title: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants
text:
Authors & Year: Bhavya Reddy, Ezgi Gursel, Katy Daniels, Anahita Khojandi, Jamie Baalis Coble, Vivek Agarwal, Ronald Boring, Vaibhav Yadav, and Mahboubeh Madadi (2024)
Venue (Journal/Conference): Nuclear Technology
DOI: 10.1080/00295450.2024.2372217
Published Online: 23 July 2024
Core Domain: Human error detection in nuclear power plant operations
Main Technical Themes: Multiclass classification, uncertainty quantification (UQ), explainable AI (XAI), Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), SHAP
Code/Data Available?: Not explicitly provided in the paper extract I reviewed
Proximity/Threat Level: Moderate to High for anyone working on trustworthy AI in safety-critical monitoring
Date Reviewed: 2026-03-13

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why this matters):

In nuclear power plants, operators must monitor many variables in short time windows and identify incidents rapidly.
This cognitive burden can itself increase the chance of human error.
If an operator incorrectly identifies an abnormal situation, the resulting mitigation action may also be wrong, which is dangerous in a safety-critical environment.

Why AI alone is not enough:

A classifier that merely predicts an error class is not sufficient in this domain.
Operators and supervisors also need to know whether the prediction is trustworthy.
In other words, the system must not only be accurate, but also transparent about its confidence.

Why Explainability is important here:

XAI is used to answer why a prediction was made.
In this paper, that means identifying which probe-location and vibration-derived features drove the model toward a given error class.
This is especially useful in operator-support settings, where a prediction should ideally be translated into actionable feedback.

Why Uncertainty Quantification is important here:

Safety-critical systems require more than point predictions.
The model should indicate when it is unsure, especially when data are limited and errors can be costly.
The paper explicitly distinguishes between aleatory uncertainty (inherent variability in data) and epistemic uncertainty (model uncertainty due to limited knowledge or limited data).

Their claim to fame / Novelty:

The paper positions itself as addressing a research gap in the joint use of XAI and UQ, specifically for human error classification in nuclear power plants.
Rather than treating explainability and uncertainty as separate post-processing ideas, the authors attempt to integrate them into one workflow.
Their emphasis is not just on explaining predictions, but also on explaining how certain the model is about those predictions.

What they actually contribute:

They compare multiple multiclass classifiers, including custom uncertainty-aware neural networks, custom XGBoost variants, ensemble combinations, and Bayesian neural networks.
They select the best-performing model not just by classification metrics, but also by UQ behavior.
They then use SHAP to analyze both:

which features drive predictions, and
which features appear linked to predictive uncertainty.


Their ultimate result:

The Bayesian neural network (BNN) was the strongest overall model.
It achieved the best balance of predictive performance and uncertainty behavior, outperforming the custom and ensemble alternatives on most metrics.
The most challenging classes were Error B and Error D, and these became the main focus of the explainability analysis.
crumbs: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#methodology-technical-details
href: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#methodology-technical-details
title: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

Problem Formulation:

Multiclass classification of operator measurement behavior into:

No error
Error A: Off-axis probe orientation
Error B: Off-position first measurement
Error C: Off-position second measurement
Error D: Swapped locations


Data Source / Testbed:

The dataset came from a physical flow loop test bed at the Department of Nuclear Engineering, University of Tennessee, Knoxville.
Surveillance data were manually collected using Fluke handheld probes.
Tri-axial acceleration data and pump speed streams were used.

Dataset Size:

Total instances: 85

45 normal
10 instances each for four error types

This is a very small dataset for a five-class classification problem.

Train/Test/Validation Split:

70% train
25% test
5% validation
In count terms:

Train: 50
Test: 24
Validation: 11


Sampling / Signal Characteristics:

Accelerometer data were collected at 25.6 kHz
60 000 samples were collected roughly every 5 minutes
Each recording covered about 2.3 seconds

Preprocessing Challenges:

The raw Fluke outputs were originally in PDF graph form
Data had to be manually extracted using Engauge Digitizer
This means the dataset is not purely sensor-native in the ML sense; it carries a manual digitization bottleneck
That introduces potential granularity loss and human preprocessing bias

Feature Construction / Signal Handling:

Frequency values were bucketed to identify informative acceleration bands
The retained bands were:

Axial: 1827 to 2327 Hz
Tangential: 41 to 541 Hz
Radial: 2249 to 2750 Hz

FFT was used to move into the frequency domain
The frequencies were then merged with amplitudes for the selected bands

Validation Strategy:

Because of the small sample size, the authors used 10-fold cross-validation
Hyperparameters were tuned using grid search constrained by the validation set

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#models-compared
href: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#models-compared
title: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants
text:
4. Models Compared
The paper compares several uncertainty-aware and ensemble-style models.

4.1 Neural Network with Custom Loss

A multilayer perceptron was trained with a custom loss:

Cross-entropy loss
plus an entropy term

The goal was to optimize not only correctness, but also confidence behavior.
A scalar lambda controlled the tradeoff between classification fit and entropy regularization.



4.2 XGBoost with Custom Loss

XGBoost was modified to include an entropy component in its objective.
This was meant to make the model uncertainty-aware while retaining the strong predictive behavior of boosted trees.



4.3 Ensemble Models
The paper constructed ensemble combinations motivated by: - XGBoost having the best traditional accuracy - Neural networks being comparatively more “certain” under the custom loss setup
The ensemble variants included combinations such as: - Traditional NN + custom XGBoost - Custom NN + XGBoost - Custom NN + custom XGBoost - Traditional XGBoost + simple neural network


4.4 Bayesian Neural Network (BNN)

The BNN is the paper’s most important model.
It uses:

Cross-entropy loss
plus KL divergence

This introduces a probabilistic treatment of weights and allows epistemic uncertainty to be modeled directly.
This is particularly suitable for:

safety-critical settings
limited data regimes
situations where calibrated confidence matters
crumbs: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#explainability-uncertainty-framework
href: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#explainability-uncertainty-framework
title: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants
text:
5. Explainability & Uncertainty Framework

Why SHAP was chosen:

The authors justify SHAP on the basis of:

cooperative game theory foundation
local accuracy
broad applicability across model families
ability to capture feature interactions

They explicitly note that gradient-based explainers would not transfer as well across all models used in the study.

How UQ was integrated:

UQ was not treated as a separate calibration add-on only.
Instead, the authors used UQ measures to understand:

prediction certainty
the relationship between accuracy and confidence
how feature contributions vary when predictions are certain vs uncertain


What this means conceptually:

The study’s main conceptual move is:

do not just explain what the model predicted
also explain how trustworthy that prediction seems to be
crumbs: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#evaluation-strategy
href: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#evaluation-strategy
title: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants
text:
6. Evaluation Strategy

6.1 Performance Metrics
The authors used metrics suitable for imbalanced multiclass classification: - Accuracy - Weighted F1 score - AUC-PR - Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC)


6.2 Uncertainty Metrics
They also used multiple UQ-oriented metrics: - Average entropy - Multiclass Brier score - Mutual information (MI) for epistemic uncertainty - Difference between the top two predicted probabilities


6.3 Why this is a good evaluation choice

This is one of the stronger parts of the paper.
They do not rely on accuracy alone.
They acknowledge that in safety-critical classification, a model that is accurate but poorly calibrated or overconfident can still be dangerous.

href: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#lambda-sensitivity
title: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants
text:
7.1 Lambda Sensitivity

For the custom-loss neural network and custom-loss XGBoost, lambda was varied between 0.1 and 0.9
As lambda increased:

entropy increased
confidence behavior changed
predictive metrics could improve or degrade depending on whether the model moved away from overconfidence or toward excessive uncertainty

Observed trend:

Higher lambda led to greater entropy, as expected
Weighted F1 gradually decreased
Brier score worsened at higher lambda values

This suggests that too much emphasis on entropy regularization can make the model overly uncertain and less effective

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#comparative-model-performance
href: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#comparative-model-performance
title: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants
text:
7.2 Comparative Model Performance

The BNN emerged as the strongest overall model.
Reported metrics for the BNN:

Accuracy: 0.95 ± 0.72
AUC-PR: 0.81 ± 0.17
Weighted F1: 0.95 ± 0.08
MCC: 0.92 ± 0.13
Brier score: 0.07 ± 0.12
MI: 1.04 ± 0.36
Average entropy: 0.07 ± 0.06

Interpretation:

The BNN had the best overall balance of:

discrimination
calibration
confidence quality
classwise balance


Interesting nuance:

Some ensemble models achieved stronger AUC-PR than the BNN
But the BNN was still preferred because its overall behavior across both predictive and uncertainty metrics was more balanced and robust

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#uncertainty-insights
href: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#uncertainty-insights
title: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants
text:
8. Uncertainty Insights

The paper provides a classwise uncertainty analysis using repeated BNN passes.


8.1 Class-Level Probability Histograms

The BNN was run 100 times per sample
The resulting probability distributions were plotted classwise



8.2 What the histograms showed

No-error class: highly concentrated near probabilities between 0.97 and 1

Very confident and stable predictions

Error A: similarly concentrated near 1

Also highly certain

Error B: much more spread out

Some predictions still peaked near 1
Others spread roughly from 0.4 to 0.88
This indicates substantial variation in certainty

Error C: mostly confident, but with some moderately uncertain points
Error D: also showed mixed certainty

Some points clustered high
Others spread between 0.40 and 0.76




8.3 Interpretation

The model handles No Error and Error A well
The main epistemic difficulty appears around Error B and Error D
This is exactly the kind of behavior that makes uncertainty-aware analysis valuable:

the model is effectively signaling where it is less trustworthy




8.4 Top-Two Probability Gap Analysis

The paper also examined the difference between the top two class probabilities
Large differences imply stronger decisiveness
Small differences imply uncertainty
Observed pattern:

No Error and Error A mostly sat in the “accurate and certain” region
Error B often showed high accuracy but lower certainty
Error D had lower decisiveness and lower accuracy more often

That distinction is important:

Error B may be recoverably ambiguous
Error D may be structurally harder for the model
crumbs: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#explainability-insights
href: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#explainability-insights
title: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants
text:
9. Explainability Insights
This is the most interesting section conceptually.

9.1 What they try to explain
The authors do not stop at “feature importance.” They specifically look at feature contributions under three scenarios: 1. Accurate and Certain 2. Accurate and Uncertain 3. Inaccurate and Certain
That is a very useful framing because it separates: - reliable decisions - cautious-but-correct decisions - confidently wrong decisions


9.2 Main classes analyzed

Error B
Error D

These were chosen because they were the most uncertainty-relevant classes.


9.3 Error B findings

For an accurate and certain Error B prediction:

surv_loc_one_tangential had a strong positive contribution
surv_loc_two_tangential contributed negatively

This aligns well with the physical definition of Error B:

the mistake is associated with the first measurement location

For accurate but uncertain Error B cases:

features such as:

surv_loc_two_tangential
surv_loc_one_radial.4
surv_loc_two_tangential.4
surv_loc_two_axial.4 appeared influential


These were moderate rather than decisive, suggesting the model sensed the correct class but without full confidence



9.4 Error D findings

For accurate and certain Error D cases:

surv_loc_one_axial contributed positively
features such as:

surv_loc_one_radial
surv_loc_one_tangential.1
surv_loc_two_tangential.4 interacted in a more balanced way


This makes intuitive sense because Error D involves swapped locations, so both measurement sites matter



9.5 High-variance SHAP features

The paper also discusses SHAP variance at a more global level
Features with high SHAP variance were interpreted as possible contributors to predictive uncertainty
The authors note that features contributing to uncertainty and inaccuracy in pointwise SHAP analysis also tended to have high variance globally



9.6 Why this is useful

This is not merely descriptive XAI
It opens the door to operator-facing decision support
A future system could potentially say things like:

“The issue likely involves probe placement at location 1”
“The model is not fully certain, so supervisor verification is advised”


That is far more useful than a raw class label alone.
crumbs: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#strengths-of-the-paper
href: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#strengths-of-the-paper
title: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants
text:
10. Strengths of the Paper

Strong safety-critical framing

The paper understands that trust, calibration, and confidence matter in nuclear settings.

Joint treatment of XAI and UQ

This is the paper’s biggest conceptual strength.
Many papers do either feature attribution or uncertainty, but not both in a unified way.

Good use of BNNs for small-data uncertainty-aware classification

The dataset is very small, so a probabilistic model class is a reasonable choice.

Thoughtful metric selection

The inclusion of MCC, AUC-PR, Brier score, entropy, MI, and top-two gap is better than a shallow accuracy-only comparison.

Operator-oriented interpretation

The authors are clearly thinking about practical deployment, not just classifier benchmarking.

Useful analysis of “accurate but uncertain” vs “inaccurate but certain”

That distinction is extremely valuable in trustworthy AI.
crumbs: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
href: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
title: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants
text:
11. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: Very small dataset

The dataset has only 85 instances total, with only 10 samples per error class.
That is extremely small for a five-class classification problem, especially one involving neural and Bayesian models.
Even with 10-fold cross-validation, instability is likely.
Some of the reported standard deviations also suggest variability.



Criticism 2: Manual digitization bottleneck

A major practical limitation is that data were manually extracted from PDF graphs using Engauge Digitizer.
That creates a preprocessing bottleneck and may introduce:

discretization error
extraction inconsistency
human preprocessing bias

This reduces confidence that the pipeline would scale cleanly to real plant settings.



Criticism 3: Explainability validation is still mostly qualitative

The SHAP analysis is interesting and plausible, but it is still largely a domain-consistency argument
The paper does not appear to use formal XAI quality metrics such as:

fidelity
stability
robustness under perturbation
explanation consistency across folds

So the explanations are persuasive, but not rigorously validated



Criticism 4: “Uncertainty-aware” does not automatically mean “well-calibrated”

The paper uses several uncertainty metrics, which is good
But there is still limited discussion of formal calibration diagnostics beyond entropy and Brier score
For a deployment paper, one might also want:

reliability diagrams
expected calibration error
risk-coverage analysis
abstention analysis




Criticism 5: Weak generalization evidence

The data come from a single experimental test bed
The paper does not establish how well the method would transfer across:

other hardware
other probe operators
other surveillance tasks
real plant conditions rather than controlled experimental conditions




Criticism 6: Limited comparator set

The comparison is useful, but still somewhat narrow
There is no comparison against stronger modern uncertainty baselines such as:

deep ensembles
Monte Carlo dropout
evidential classifiers
temperature-scaled deterministic networks
calibrated gradient boosting baselines

So while the BNN wins in this study, it is not necessarily proven superior to the broader uncertainty-aware literature



Criticism 7: Some feature names are difficult to interpret operationally

The SHAP outputs are technically informative but not yet operator-friendly
The authors acknowledge this and propose translating features into operator-understandable outputs in future work
That is a key step that is still missing for real usability
crumbs: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants

section: 12. Research Value for My Own Work
text:
12. Research Value for My Own Work

What makes this paper useful:

It is a strong example of combining predictive modeling, uncertainty analysis, and explanation in a safety-critical context
It gives a practical template for analyzing:

accurate/certain
accurate/uncertain
inaccurate/certain cases

That framing is highly reusable in other trustworthy-AI papers

What I would borrow conceptually:

Joint XAI + UQ framing
Separating classwise uncertainty behavior
Using SHAP not only to explain predictions, but also to inspect uncertainty-driving features
Highlighting “confidently wrong” predictions as a risk category

What I would improve if I built on this:

Use a larger and more realistic dataset
Add formal calibration evaluation
Add more rigorous XAI validation
Benchmark against stronger UQ baselines
Translate feature explanations into task-level, human-readable alerts

href: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#action-items-integration
title: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants
text:
13. Action Items & Integration

Cite this paper in any literature review section dealing with trustworthy AI in safety-critical systems
Use it as an example of joint XAI + UQ, rather than treating these as separate toolboxes
Reuse the paper’s framing of accurate/certain, accurate/uncertain, and inaccurate/certain predictions
Compare its BNN-based approach against stronger modern uncertainty baselines in future work
Note the limitations of very small datasets and manually digitized inputs when discussing external validity
Incorporate stronger calibration and explanation-quality metrics if extending this research direction
Consider how SHAP outputs can be transformed into operator-facing decision support rather than left as raw feature names

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#overall-takeaway
href: reviews/Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants.html#overall-takeaway
title: Uncertainty-Aware and Explainable Human Error Detection in the Operation of Nuclear Power Plants
text:
14. Overall Takeaway
This paper is not just about classifying human error in nuclear operations. Its real contribution is showing how uncertainty quantification and explainability can be combined to build a more trustworthy classifier in a safety-critical setting. The Bayesian neural network gave the strongest overall performance, and the SHAP analysis helped reveal why difficult classes like Error B and Error D remained uncertain.
The paper is strongest as a trustworthy-AI workflow paper rather than as a definitive benchmark paper. Its main weaknesses come from the tiny dataset, limited comparator set, and mainly qualitative explanation validation. Still, it is a genuinely useful contribution because it moves beyond the shallow “accurate black box” mindset and asks the far more important question: when the model makes a decision, how much should an operator trust it, and why?

objectID: reviews/UbiQTree uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/UbiQTree uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: UbiQTree: Uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why this paper exists):

SHAP is widely used to explain tree-based models, especially in healthcare and other high-stakes settings.
However, SHAP is typically treated as a point estimate, meaning it tells you what the attribution is but not how stable or trustworthy that attribution is.
This is a serious issue in practice because clinicians or decision-makers may over-trust explanations that are actually unstable across plausible model realizations.

The Motivation (Why uncertainty in XAI matters):

In high-stakes domains, it is not enough for a model to be accurate; the explanation itself must also be reliable.
A model may correctly predict a class label while the explanation behind that prediction remains unstable.
The paper argues that uncertainty in explanations must be quantified in the same way predictive uncertainty is quantified.

Their claim to fame / Novelty:

They propose UbiQTree, a framework that performs uncertainty quantification directly on SHAP values for tree ensembles.
Their key theoretical move is to decompose SHAP uncertainty into:

Aleatoric uncertainty: variability linked to irreducible noise / randomness,
Epistemic uncertainty: variability due to incomplete knowledge, limited data, or model uncertainty,
Entanglement: covariance between model-related and data-related uncertainty contributions.

They combine:

Dempster-Shafer theory for belief/plausibility-based uncertainty reasoning,
Liu’s uncertainty theory for uncertainty distributions and entropy-based reasoning,
Dirichlet process hypothesis sampling to generate plausible sub-ensemble explanations.


The paper’s main conceptual insight:

The most important features according to mean absolute SHAP are not necessarily the most stable features.
So a feature can look globally important while being epistemically fragile.

The Value Derived from Explainability (What XAI/UQ actually did here):

It moves SHAP from “importance scoring” toward reliability-aware explanation.
It allows users to inspect:

confidence intervals around SHAP,
entropy of SHAP distributions,
sign stability,
disagreement across sub-models,
whether importance and uncertainty are coupled.


Their ultimate result:

UbiQTree provides a mechanism to audit SHAP reliability rather than just SHAP magnitude.
Across several healthcare datasets, the framework shows that some top-ranked features have large epistemic uncertainty and inconsistent directional stability, meaning explanation quality cannot be inferred from feature importance alone.

objectID: reviews/UbiQTree uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles.html#methodology-technical-details
href: reviews/UbiQTree uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles.html#methodology-technical-details
title: UbiQTree: Uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

Base Modeling Setting:

The framework is developed around tree ensemble models, particularly bagging-style models such as Random Forests.
Their use case validation relies on RF classifiers trained on healthcare datasets.

Core Technical Idea: SHAP variance decomposition

The paper defines total SHAP variance as the sum of:

aleatoric component,
epistemic component,
minus an entanglement term that captures covariance between data-centric and model-centric expectations.

This is important because they argue the usual decomposition can be misleading when model and data uncertainty are not independent.

Theoretical Building Blocks:

Dempster-Shafer theory (DST):

Used to define belief and plausibility over intervals of SHAP values.
Useful for representing ambiguity and ignorance rather than only classical probability.

Uncertainty theory:

Used to define an uncertainty distribution over SHAP values and to reason about entropy and information gain.

Dirichlet process (DP) hypothesis sampling:

Used to sample plausible weighted sub-ensembles from the trained forest.
Trees are weighted using out-of-bag performance.
The concentration parameter α controls how concentrated the posterior is around stronger trees versus broader exploration of model variants.


Pipeline Summary:

Generate sub-ensembles using Dirichlet-weighted sampling.
Compute TreeSHAP for each sampled sub-ensemble.
Decompose variance into aleatoric, epistemic, and entanglement terms.
Aggregate uncertainty-aware explanation statistics:

mean SHAP,
standard deviation,
95% credible interval,
entropy,
sign stability.


Uncertainty Metrics They Emphasize:

Mean ± 2σ SHAP
95% credible intervals
Entropy of SHAP distributions
Sign stability
Conflict / ambiguity measures from evidence theory

Interpretation of their metrics:

Wide SHAP distributions imply unstable explanations.
Flat or multimodal SHAP densities imply disagreement across sub-models.
Low sign stability means the direction of feature effect is not robust.
High entropy indicates lower certainty in the explanation.
crumbs: UbiQTree: Uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles

objectID: reviews/UbiQTree uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles.html#datasets-experimental-testbed
href: reviews/UbiQTree uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles.html#datasets-experimental-testbed
title: UbiQTree: Uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles
text:
4. Datasets / Experimental Testbed
The paper validates the framework on several healthcare datasets rather than on a single benchmark. This is a strength because the method is presented as a general uncertainty-aware explanation framework rather than a dataset-specific trick.

Dataset 1: MIMIC-III

Task: Length-of-stay classification
Setting: Patients grouped into short-stay, medium-stay, and long-stay classes
Data Preparation:

Removed fields such as hadm_id, religion, marital_status, and ethnicity
Numerical features imputed with median and standardized
RF classifier with 100 estimators, class balancing, OOB scoring
70:30 train-test split with stratification

Reported predictive result: Micro-F1 of 94.70%



Dataset 2: Ovarian Cancer Risk and Progression Dataset

Task: Four-class risk classification
Class balance: Strongly imbalanced
Preprocessing / training:

Timestamp and leakage-prone progression variable removed
Median imputation, scaling, label encoding
SMOTETomek used for rebalancing
RF with 20 estimators and max depth 6

Reported predictive result: F1 score of 55.7%



Dataset 3: SEER Breast Cancer Dataset

Task: Alive vs deceased outcome classification
Scale: 4,024 instances, 16 features
Context: Longitudinal, clinically relevant survival dataset
General experimental design across datasets:

Posterior-like sub-model samples are obtained from tree ensembles
SHAP is computed repeatedly across these plausible model realizations
The resulting distributions are analyzed rather than a single SHAP vector

objectID: reviews/UbiQTree uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles.html#key-results-what-they-mean
href: reviews/UbiQTree uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles.html#key-results-what-they-mean
title: UbiQTree: Uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles
text:
5. Key Results & What They Mean

MIMIC-III findings

For short-stay, medium-stay, and long-stay predictions, the dominant features repeatedly included:

NumTransfers
NumNotes
NumCallouts

But the important point is not only that these features rank highly.
The framework shows that they also carry substantial epistemic uncertainty.
Example:

In the short-stay class, NumTransfers, NumNotes, and NumCallouts had epistemic uncertainty values of 0.133, 0.104, and 0.065 respectively.
Their sign stabilities were only 79.8%, 77.0%, and 74.5%.

So the model relies on these features, but not with fully stable reasoning.



Ovarian cancer findings

Top features varied across risk classes, but features such as:

SocioeconomicStatus
alcohol
PreviousTreatment
MenstrualHistory
symptom showed both importance and substantial variability across model subsets.

This reinforces the paper’s main message:

explanation magnitude does not imply explanation reliability.




SEER breast cancer findings

The paper examines the relationship between mean absolute SHAP and the standard deviation of SHAP values.
Their Figure 15 is especially important:

a high positive correlation means the model’s “most important” features are also the most unstable.

That is a very strong warning for real-world XAI use:

users might trust exactly the features they should scrutinize the most.

objectID: reviews/UbiQTree uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles.html#validation-strategy-predictions-explanations
href: reviews/UbiQTree uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles.html#validation-strategy-predictions-explanations
title: UbiQTree: Uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles
text:
6. Validation Strategy (Predictions & Explanations)

Predictive validation:

Standard supervised learning evaluation using held-out test sets and F1 scores.
The predictive model is not the main novelty; the explanation analysis is.

Explanation validation:

Their validation is largely internal and descriptive, not benchmarked against a formal gold standard for explanation correctness.
They evaluate explanation reliability using:

variance,
entropy,
credible intervals,
sign stability,
and visual distributional analysis.


What this means:

They do not just ask, “Which features matter?”
They ask, “How confident should we be that these features matter in the way SHAP says they do?”

Operational decision thresholds:

The paper even proposes thresholds for interpreting SHAP uncertainty in deployment settings, linking high uncertainty to expert-in-the-loop verification or retraining.

objectID: reviews/UbiQTree uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles.html#strengths
href: reviews/UbiQTree uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles.html#strengths
title: UbiQTree: Uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles
text:
7. Strengths

Strength 1: Strong problem framing

The paper identifies a real weakness in current SHAP practice: point-valued attributions are often over-interpreted.
This is especially persuasive in healthcare.

Strength 2: Moves from importance to reliability

A major conceptual strength is that it reframes XAI from “feature ranking” to “feature attribution under uncertainty.”

Strength 3: Rich uncertainty toolbox

The combination of variance decomposition, entropy, sign stability, confidence intervals, and evidence theory gives a genuinely multi-faceted view of explanation quality.

Strength 4: Practical with tree ensembles

Because it works with bagging-based tree ensembles, it stays in a setting that is still widely used in tabular healthcare ML.

Strength 5: Clear practical message

The takeaway is simple and important:

important does not mean stable.

objectID: reviews/UbiQTree uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
href: reviews/UbiQTree uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
title: UbiQTree: Uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles
text:
8. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: Heavy theory, lighter empirical proof

The paper is theoretically ambitious, but the empirical side is more illustrative than decisive.
It demonstrates that the framework produces meaningful diagnostics, but it does not fully prove that these diagnostics improve downstream human decisions or clinical outcomes.

Criticism 2: No formal external XAI ground truth

They quantify instability very carefully, but they do not establish whether a “stable” explanation is necessarily a “correct” explanation.
Stability and correctness are related, but they are not the same thing.

Criticism 3: Random Forest-centric validation

Although the motivation is stated for tree ensembles broadly, the validation is centered on RF-style bagging.
That makes sense because bagging gives natural sub-model variation, but it leaves open how well the same framework transfers to boosting methods such as XGBoost or LightGBM, where tree dependence and sequential fitting complicate the interpretation.

Criticism 4: Terminology may overstate aleatoric handling

In practice, much of what is being captured here comes from variation across trees, tree subsets, and training-induced instability.
That is very naturally epistemic/model-side.
The aleatoric interpretation is theoretically motivated, but in the experiments it may be less cleanly separated than the paper’s language suggests.

Criticism 5: Computational and conceptual overhead

Standard SHAP is attractive partly because it is already understandable to practitioners.
UbiQTree adds multiple theoretical layers:

DST,
uncertainty distributions,
Dirichlet processes,
variance decomposition,
entropy,
sign stability.

This makes it richer, but also harder to communicate and operationalize outside a research setting.

Criticism 6: Thresholds for intervention feel heuristic

Their suggested thresholds for expert review, automated decisions, and retraining are useful operationally.
But they appear more heuristic than universally validated.
In a production setting, these thresholds would need calibration for each domain and risk tolerance.

Criticism 7: More comparison to prior SHAP-UQ methods was needed

The paper discusses prior work on SHAP uncertainty, but the experimental section would have been stronger if it had directly benchmarked UbiQTree against competing SHAP-UQ methods rather than mostly demonstrating its own outputs.

title: UbiQTree: Uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles
section: 9. Research Value for My Own Work
text:
9. Research Value for My Own Work

What I can take from this paper:

It gives a very useful conceptual argument that explanation quality should itself be uncertainty-aware.
It supports the idea that feature importance rankings alone are incomplete.
It provides language and framing for discussing:

explanation robustness,
attribution stability,
uncertainty-aware interpretability.


How this could influence my literature review:

I can cite this paper as evidence that SHAP-based interpretation in critical systems should not be treated as deterministic.
It helps justify the inclusion of uncertainty-aware validation metrics for explainability methods.

How this could influence my methodology:

If I use SHAP, I should consider reporting:

confidence intervals,
attribution variance,
sign stability,
entropy or dispersion metrics, not just average SHAP scores.


Positioning insight:

This paper is not mainly about improving predictive performance.
It is about improving the trustworthiness of explanations.
That distinction is important when positioning a contribution.

title: UbiQTree: Uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles
text:
10. Action Items & Integration

Add this paper to the section of my literature review dealing with uncertainty in explanations, not just general SHAP applications.
Note explicitly that high SHAP magnitude does not imply high explanation reliability.
Consider whether my own SHAP analysis should include variance, confidence intervals, sign stability, or entropy.
Use this paper to justify a stronger critique of explanation methods that report only single attribution values.
Compare its uncertainty-aware explanation framing with other SHAP-UQ papers to identify whether UbiQTree is mainly a theoretical advance, a practical workflow, or both.
If relevant to my work, investigate whether similar decomposition can be adapted beyond bagging models to boosting-based or deep-learning explainers.

objectID: reviews/UbiQTree uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles.html#bottom-line-summary
href: reviews/UbiQTree uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles.html#bottom-line-summary
title: UbiQTree: Uncertainty quantification in XAI with tree ensembles
text:
11. Bottom-Line Summary
This paper is important because it attacks a blind spot in modern XAI practice: we often explain models as if the explanations themselves are certain. UbiQTree argues that this is unsafe, especially in healthcare, and proposes a structured framework for quantifying uncertainty in SHAP explanations. Its biggest contribution is not a new predictor, but a new way of thinking about explanation reliability. The most valuable takeaway is simple but powerful: the feature the model talks about most confidently may not be the feature it understands most reliably.

title: Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring: an operations research perspective
text:
Authors & Year: Nijat Mehdiyev, Maxim Majlatow, Peter Fettke (2025)
Venue (Journal/Conference): Annals of Operations Research (Highly reputable OR journal)
Link/DOI: 10.1007/s10479-024-05943-4
Code/Data Available?: No (Uses a proprietary real-world dataset from a German manufacturer).
Proximity/Threat Level: High / Direct Competition (Focuses on combining UQ and XAI).
Date Reviewed: 2024-05-18
crumbs: Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring: an operations research perspective

objectID: reviews/Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring: an operations research perspective
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why Probabilistic?):

In Operations Research (OR), the “predict-then-optimize” paradigm requires robust parameters. Traditional OR uses deterministic point forecasts or overly simplistic stochastic parameters. By quantifying uncertainty (predicting processing times as intervals), planners can create better worst-case/best-case production schedules and optimize resource allocation.

The Motivation (Why Explainable?):

If a system simply says “this process has high uncertainty,” the planner cannot act on it. Explaining what drives the uncertainty allows planners to intervene (e.g., if “order quantity” drives uncertainty, they can adjust batch sizes to mitigate risk).

Their claim to fame / Novelty:

Instead of just explaining the point forecast, they directly explain the prediction interval width using SHAP.
They group predictions into practical “Uncertainty Profiles” (low, medium, high) based on the relative width of the intervals to make the outputs actionable for non-technical domain experts.

The Value Derived from Explainability (What did XAI actually do?):

Identified Uncertainty Drivers: SHAP revealed that “Quantity” (number of items) actively widens the prediction interval (increases uncertainty), while the historical “Mean Processing Time” narrows the interval (increases confidence).
crumbs: Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring: an operations research perspective

objectID: reviews/Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring.html#methodology-technical-details
href: reviews/Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring.html#methodology-technical-details
title: Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring: an operations research perspective
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

Datasets / Testbed:

Real-world Manufacturing Execution System (MES) event log from a medium-sized German firm.
11,943 cases (traces), 48,577 events, 30 distinct activities.

The Model (Quantile Regression Forests):

They use QRF, a tree-based ensemble that estimates conditional quantiles rather than just a conditional mean. The prediction interval is constructed by taking the lower quantile (\(Q_{\alpha}\)) and the upper quantile (\(Q_{1-\alpha}\)).

The XAI Mechanism (Explaining the Interval Width):

To explain uncertainty, they fundamentally change the target output of the SHAP explainer. Instead of explaining the point forecast, they define the “game” to be explained as the width of the prediction interval: \(W(x) = Q_{1-\alpha}(x) - Q_{\alpha}(x)\).
By setting \(W(x)\) as the target, SHAP calculates the marginal contribution of every feature to either widening (increasing uncertainty) or narrowing (decreasing uncertainty) the interval.
crumbs: Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring: an operations research perspective

objectID: reviews/Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring.html#validation-strategy-predictions-explanations
href: reviews/Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring.html#validation-strategy-predictions-explanations
title: Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring: an operations research perspective
text:
4. Validation Strategy (Predictions & Explanations)

Validating the Predictions (Forecasting Quality):

Data Split: 10-fold overlapping sliding window cross-validation (chronological split to mimic real-world deployment).
Point Metrics: MAE, RMSE.
Uncertainty Metrics: PICP (Coverage), MPIW (Absolute Width), and MRPIW (Mean Relative Prediction Interval Width).
Statistical Rigor: Used the non-parametric Friedman-Nemenyi test to prove QRF’s superiority over BART in relative interval width.

Validating the Explanations (XAI Quality):

Approach: The validation of the explanations is purely qualitative and human-centric. There are no mathematical XAI metrics (like fidelity, robustness, or stability) used to verify that the SHAP outputs are faithful to the model.
Thoroughness of the Validation Mechanism: The extent of their XAI validation relies on two things:

A Single Expert Interview: They built a prototype dashboard and showed it to exactly one process expert from the manufacturing partner. The validation rests on this single expert stating that the outputs were “intuitively comprehensible” and “sufficiently sound and satisfactory.”
A Single Local Example: For local interpretability, the paper presents a deep dive into only one specific test instance (a “Dishing Press” activity) to show how feature values pushed the interval bounds up or down. The rest of the XAI analysis relies on aggregated global SHAP summary plots.
crumbs: Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring: an operations research perspective

objectID: reviews/Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring.html#thoughts-criticisms-author-acknowledged-limitations
href: reviews/Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring.html#thoughts-criticisms-author-acknowledged-limitations
title: Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring: an operations research perspective
text:
5. Thoughts, Criticisms & Author-Acknowledged Limitations

Criticism 1: The paper explicitly acknowledges uncertainty from both model limitations and data noise, but still leaves epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty fundamentally conflated (Most serious issue).

In Section 3.3, the authors themselves state that uncertainty arises from the model’s limitations, data noise, feature interactions, and unobserved variables. That admission is important, but it also exposes the central weakness of the paper: the framework never separates epistemic uncertainty (what the model does not know) from aleatoric uncertainty (irreducible variability in the process).
This matters because SHAP on interval width \(W(x)=Q_{1-\alpha}(x)-Q_{\alpha}(x)\) cannot tell whether a feature widens the interval because the process is genuinely noisy, because the training data are sparse in that region, or because the model is poorly specified there. As a result, the explanations are only explanations of model-estimated interval width, not clean explanations of distinct uncertainty sources.
That is a major conceptual limitation, because the paper frames the outputs as actionable uncertainty explanations for practitioners, while the method cannot distinguish whether the right response is “collect more data,” “trust the interval as inherent variability,” or “improve the model.”

Criticism 2: Explaining interval width is not the same as explaining the predictive distribution or quantile behaviour.

The paper’s key idea is to explain a derived scalar quantity, the prediction interval width, rather than the lower and upper quantiles separately. This is elegant, but it collapses a richer probabilistic object into a single number.
A feature could shift both quantiles upward with almost no change in width, or affect only the upper tail, or induce asymmetric risk, and those are meaningfully different behaviours. By focusing only on \(W(x)\), the paper explains spread, but not how features shape the location, asymmetry, or tail behaviour of the predictive distribution.
This makes the explanation layer less informative than it first appears. It is useful for saying which features widen intervals, but weaker for saying how those features alter risk structure.

Criticism 3: The explanation validation is extremely weak relative to the strength of the claims.

The paper does not evaluate explanation quality using fidelity, stability, sensitivity, perturbation, or feature-removal tests. Instead, the XAI validation is limited to a prototype dashboard discussion with a single expert and one highlighted local example.
For a paper claiming to provide actionable explanations of predictive uncertainty, this is not enough. At best, it shows that the explanations are plausible and readable; it does not show that they are reliable, faithful, or robust.
This is one of the biggest practical weaknesses in the paper, because the predictive side is evaluated carefully, while the explanation side is largely accepted on face validity.

Criticism 4: The paper’s decision-support narrative is stronger than the evidence actually provided.

The authors motivate the work through a predict-then-optimize lens and argue that uncertainty explanations can support production planning. However, they also effectively acknowledge that the work remains at the prediction stage: the forecasts may serve as inputs to later optimization models, but that integration is not actually carried out in the paper.
In other words, the study shows that one can predict intervals and visualize feature attributions, but it does not demonstrate that these explanations improve scheduling decisions, reduce cost, or change operational behaviour in a measurable way.
That makes the practitioner value proposition promising, but still only partially substantiated.

Criticism 5: The framework is heavily dependent on one proprietary dataset, which limits generalizability and reproducibility.

The authors implicitly acknowledge dataset dependence when they note that uncertainty can reveal sparse or anomalous regions of the training data. But this also means the explanations are highly tied to one event log, one firm, and one process environment.
Because the study uses a single proprietary manufacturing dataset and provides neither code nor data, it is difficult to assess whether the same method would behave similarly on other predictive process monitoring tasks, other industries, or more complex forecasting settings.
This does not invalidate the case study, but it does weaken any broad claim that the framework is generally established rather than demonstrated in one narrow context.

Criticism 6: The SHAP implementation adds approximation and scalability concerns that the paper does not fully resolve.

The authors note that exact Shapley values are computationally expensive, so they rely on KernelSHAP approximations. That is understandable, but it introduces another layer of approximation on top of an already derived target \(W(x)\).
Since the paper is working with a tree-based model, this choice also raises questions about efficiency and robustness, especially if the framework were to be scaled to larger feature spaces or real-time monitoring settings.
This is a secondary limitation compared with the conceptual issues above, but it still weakens the case for the method as a scalable operational tool.

Observation on “Uncertainty Profiles” (MRPIW):

Their use of MRPIW (Mean Relative Prediction Interval Width) to create low/medium/high profiles is still one of the most practically useful ideas in the paper. Absolute width (MPIW) naturally scales with the target size, so normalizing by the point prediction gives practitioners a more interpretable notion of whether a case is “uncertain relative to what is expected.”
So even though the uncertainty explanation story is conceptually weaker than claimed, the profiling device itself is a genuinely useful contribution for operational communication.
crumbs: Quantifying and explaining machine learning uncertainty in predictive process monitoring: an operations research perspective

title: Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers
text:
Authors & Year: Jérôme Dockès, Gaël Varoquaux, Jean-Baptiste Poline (2021)
Venue (Journal/Conference): GigaScience (Oxford University Press) (Highly reputable, peer-reviewed open-access journal).
Link/DOI: 10.1093/gigascience/giab055
Primary Topic/Concept: The mathematical breakdown of Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) under dataset shift, and why standard statistical “fixes” (like deconfounding) actually destroy predictive models.
crumbs: Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers

objectID: reviews/Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers.html#the-core-theory-what-is-the-main-concept
href: reviews/Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers.html#the-core-theory-what-is-the-main-concept
title: Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers
section: 2. The Core Theory (What is the main concept?)
text:
2. The Core Theory (What is the main concept?)

The specific theory or mechanism explained:

The paper explains how dataset shift invalidates the core assumption of Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) in machine learning: that training data \(p_{source}(X,Y)\) and deployment data \(p_{target}(X,Y)\) come from the exact same distribution.

Their main argument/conclusion:

Cross-validation on a single dataset is fundamentally insufficient to guarantee real-world generalization if the dataset was subject to selection bias. Furthermore, attempting to “fix” this shift by regressing out correlated variables (deconfounding) actively harms predictive models; instead, one must use techniques like Importance Weighting or rely on sufficiently flexible/robust models.
crumbs: Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers

objectID: reviews/Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers.html#key-arguments-evidence-the-why
href: reviews/Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers.html#key-arguments-evidence-the-why
title: Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers
text:
3. Key Arguments & Evidence (The “Why”)

Mathematical / Logical Foundation:

The ERM Failure: Machine learning models minimize empirical risk \(\hat{R}(f) = \frac{1}{n} \sum L(y_i, f(x_i))\). This is only a valid estimate of true risk if the training sample perfectly represents the target population.
Covariate vs. Prior Probability Shift: They mathematically separate Covariate Shift (where \(p(X)\) changes but \(p(Y|X)\) stays the same) from Prior Probability Shift (where \(p(Y)\) changes but \(p(X|Y)\) stays the same), noting that each requires different handling.

The “Fallacy of Deconfounding” (Crucial for Defense):

They prove (via simulated and real UKBiobank data) that tools from causal inference (like removing “confounders”) are disastrous for predictive modeling. Regressing out a shifting variable removes the predictive signal and drastically degrades accuracy.

Model Complexity Matters:

They demonstrate that highly flexible models (like Gradient Boosting or Non-linear SVMs) inherently handle covariate shifts better than over-constrained, simple linear models. In fact, applying “Importance Weighting” to a complex model can sometimes degrade performance by needlessly increasing the variance of the empirical risk.
crumbs: Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers

objectID: reviews/Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers.html#application-to-my-work-how-i-will-use-this
href: reviews/Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers.html#application-to-my-work-how-i-will-use-this
title: Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers
section: 4. Application to My Work (How I will use this)
text:
4. Application to My Work (How I will use this)

What specific decision in my paper does this justify?

1. Justifying robust evaluation: I will use this paper to argue why standard cross-validation on historical PV data is insufficient, as historical weather/generation data inherently suffers from dataset shift (e.g., changing climate, sensor degradation).
2. Defending feature selection: I will use the “fallacy of deconfounding” argument as a theoretical shield against any reviewer who suggests I should have normalized or regressed out shifting meteorological variables (like temperature or seasonality) to make the data “stationary.” This paper proves that doing so destroys predictive signal.
3. Defending model complexity: I can use their findings to justify why deploying deep/flexible neural networks (rather than simple linear baselines) is actually a safeguard against certain types of covariate shift.

Where does this belong in my paper?

Introduction (Framing dataset shift as the primary reason historical ML models fail in real-world deployment).
Background / Related Work (Defining Covariate Shift vs. Prior Probability Shift).
Methodology (Defending my feature engineering choices and my choice not to strictly deconfound the input variables).
crumbs: Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers

objectID: reviews/Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers.html#boundaries-caveats-where-does-the-theory-break
href: reviews/Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers.html#boundaries-caveats-where-does-the-theory-break
title: Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers
section: 5. Boundaries & Caveats (Where does the theory break?)
text:
5. Boundaries & Caveats (Where does the theory break?)

Assumptions made by the authors:

Importance Weighting \(\frac{p_{target}(x, y)}{p_{source}(x, y)}\) only works if there is strict distributional overlap (i.e., the support of the target distribution must be entirely included in the support of the source distribution). If a specific weather regime or failure state is completely missing from my training data, importance weighting cannot fix it.

When does this concept NOT apply?

This paper deals primarily with cross-sectional selection bias (e.g., demographic sampling in hospitals). While the math of covariate shift applies to energy, the paper does not explicitly address temporal concept drift (where the underlying physics \(p(Y|X)\) slowly changes over time, such as PV panel degradation).
crumbs: Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers

objectID: reviews/Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers.html#action-items-pre-written-assets
href: reviews/Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers.html#action-items-pre-written-assets
title: Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers
text:
6. Action Items & Pre-Written Assets
Golden Quotes: - > “If the goal of the data analysis is purely predictive, no adjustment for confounding is necessary… applying procedures meant to adjust for confounding generally degrades prediction performance without solving the dataset shift issue.” (p. 2) - > “Often, flexible models can be more robust to dataset shifts, and thus generalize better, than linear models… an over-constrained (ill-specified) model may only fit well a restricted region of the feature space.” (p. 4) - > “Dataset shift does not call for simpler models because it is not a small-sample issue. Collecting more data from the same sources will not correct systematic dataset bias.” (p. 4)
Pre-written Justification Blurb: > “In predictive forecasting, addressing dataset shift through the removal of shifting covariates—often mistakenly referred to as ‘deconfounding’—is fundamentally flawed. As demonstrated by Dockès et al. (2021), while causal inference requires adjusting for confounders, doing so in a purely predictive setting strips the model of valuable signal and degrades generalization. Therefore, rather than regressing out non-stationary meteorological features, our methodology retains these variables, relying on the inherent capacity of highly flexible, non-linear neural architectures to generalize across covariate shifts without artificial data constraints.”

text:
Authors & Year: Viktor Bengs, Eyke Hullermeier, Willem Waegeman (2022)
Venue (Journal/Conference): arXiv preprint, cs.LG
DOI / arXiv: 10.48550/arXiv.2203.06102
Primary Topic: Why direct loss-based learning of epistemic uncertainty is problematic
Contribution Type: Theoretical caution / methodological foundation for epistemic uncertainty quantification
Methods Discussed: Second-order predictors, Dirichlet distributions, evidential deep learning, posterior networks, proper scoring rules, Brier score, cross-entropy, Bayesian regularisation
Core Claim: A model cannot be reliably incentivised to report honest epistemic uncertainty merely by minimising a pointwise loss against observed labels.
Proximity / Threat Level: High relevance / supports the methodological choice to use ensemble disagreement as an epistemic uncertainty mechanism rather than relying on self-reported uncertainty from a single loss-minimising model

href: reviews/Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation.html#plain-language-explanation
title: Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation
text:
2. Plain-Language Explanation
This paper asks a deceptively simple question:

Can we train a model to output its own epistemic uncertainty just by giving it the right loss function?

The authors argue that the answer is generally no, at least for the loss functions used in several direct uncertainty-estimation methods.
The key distinction is between three levels.

Level 0: the observed label, such as class 0 or class 1.
Level 1: the true class probability, such as the probability that an input belongs to class 1.
Level 2: uncertainty about the level-1 probability itself.

Aleatoric uncertainty lives mainly at level 1. It describes randomness in the data-generating process. Even if the true class probability is known, the individual label may still be uncertain.
Epistemic uncertainty lives at level 2. It describes the learner’s lack of knowledge about the true probability or the true predictor. It should reduce when the learner receives more relevant information.
The problem is that training data usually contains level-0 observations: individual labels. It does not contain direct observations of level-1 probabilities, and it definitely does not contain direct observations of level-2 uncertainty. Therefore, if a method asks a neural network to output a distribution over class-probability distributions, there is no direct ground-truth epistemic uncertainty target for the loss to compare against.
That is the paper’s central warning:

A loss function can reward accurate predictions, but that does not mean it rewards honest epistemic uncertainty.

For my work, this is important because it supports a cautious methodological position. Epistemic uncertainty should not be treated as just another supervised target that a single model can learn because the loss says so. It needs a modelling mechanism that represents multiple plausible predictors, such as an ensemble, Bayesian posterior approximation, or another explicit model-uncertainty construction.

objectID: reviews/Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation
text:
3. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

What problem are they solving?
Many uncertainty-aware deep learning methods try to make the model predict both:

the class probabilities, and
a measure of uncertainty around those probabilities.

In classification, this is often done using a second-order distribution. Instead of predicting one probability vector, the model predicts a distribution over probability vectors. For example, a model may predict the parameters of a Dirichlet distribution. A sharp Dirichlet distribution means the model claims high certainty about the class probabilities. A broad Dirichlet distribution means the model claims more epistemic uncertainty.
This idea is attractive because it appears to let a single neural network output uncertainty directly. The authors question whether the training loss actually gives the correct incentive.


Main claim
The main claim is:

Loss minimisation over observed labels does not, by itself, give a reliable incentive to represent epistemic uncertainty faithfully.

The model may still produce uncertainty-looking numbers. But the paper shows that those numbers can be driven by the mathematical structure of the loss and regularisation, rather than by a faithful representation of the learner’s lack of knowledge.


Why this matters
This matters because epistemic uncertainty is not directly observed in the dataset. There is no ordinary label that says:

Here is the correct amount of model uncertainty for this input.

For first-order probability prediction, proper scoring rules such as log-loss or Brier score work because the expected loss is minimised by the true class probability. For second-order epistemic uncertainty, there is no equivalent ground-truth second-order target in the usual supervised data.
Therefore, methods that claim to learn epistemic uncertainty by minimising a pointwise loss need to be treated carefully.


Why this is useful for my review
This paper gives theoretical support for a methodological decision:

I should not rely only on a single model that is trained to output its own epistemic uncertainty through an auxiliary loss.
I need an uncertainty mechanism that reflects uncertainty over the predictor itself.
Deep ensembles are attractive because they express epistemic uncertainty through disagreement between multiple fitted models, rather than through a single self-reported uncertainty head.

The paper does not prove that deep ensembles are always better than MC dropout or Bayesian neural networks. Its value is more foundational: it explains why direct loss-based epistemic uncertainty is conceptually fragile.

objectID: reviews/Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation.html#methodology-technical-details
href: reviews/Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation.html#methodology-technical-details
title: Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation
text:
4. Methodology & Technical Details

The three-level uncertainty setup
The paper uses classification notation.
At level 1, the true conditional class distribution is:
[ ^*(x) = p(x) ]
A normal probabilistic classifier predicts:
[ (x) ]
and can be trained with a proper scoring rule such as cross-entropy or Brier score.
At level 2, the model predicts a distribution over possible level-1 class-probability vectors:
[ Q(x) P(P(Y)) ]
For example, in a Dirichlet-based method, (Q(x)) may be represented by Dirichlet parameters ((x)). A concentrated (Q(x)) means the model claims to know the class probabilities well. A diffuse (Q(x)) means the model claims epistemic uncertainty.


Why level-2 learning is harder than level-1 learning
For level-1 learning, the observed class labels give statistical evidence about the true class probabilities.
For level-2 learning, the learner would need evidence about distributions over probability vectors. But such evidence is not available in ordinary supervised datasets. The dataset gives labels, not repeated samples of the true probability vector.
The authors make an important point:

Learning at the epistemic level cannot be treated as ordinary frequentist learning in the same way as learning class probabilities.

This is why priors, model assumptions, hypothesis spaces, or model-sampling mechanisms matter. Epistemic uncertainty depends on the learner’s state of knowledge, not only on the data-generating distribution.


Loss form 1: Averaging first-order losses
One natural idea is to define a second-order loss by averaging a normal first-order loss over the model’s predicted second-order distribution:
[ L_2(Q, y) = _{Q}[L_1(, y)] ]
where:

(Q) is the predicted distribution over probability vectors;
() is a sampled probability vector;
(L_1) is a normal first-order loss such as cross-entropy or Brier score;
(y) is the observed label.

The problem is that if (L_1) is convex, Jensen’s inequality implies that the expected loss is at least as large as the loss at the mean prediction:
[ L_1({Q}[], y) {Q}[L_1(, y)] ]
So the loss rewards the learner for collapsing (Q) onto its mean. In other words, the model has an incentive to pretend full certainty.
This is a serious problem for epistemic uncertainty. A model with little data should often be uncertain, but the loss can still prefer a sharply peaked second-order prediction.


Loss form 2: Bayesian-style regularisation
Another idea is to add a regularisation term that penalises deviation from a prior:
[ L_2(Q, y) = {Q}[L_1(, y)] + D{KL}(Q | Q_0) ]
where:

(Q_0) is a prior distribution over probability vectors;
(D_{KL}) measures deviation from that prior;
() controls the strength of the prior/regularisation term.

If the prior is uniform, this can also be interpreted as rewarding entropy. This looks more reasonable because it prevents the model from always collapsing to a point mass.
However, the paper shows that this does not solve the problem cleanly. The amount of epistemic uncertainty now depends strongly on:

the chosen first-order loss (L_1);
the prior (Q_0);
the regularisation parameter ();
the true class probability itself.

That means the reported uncertainty can be controlled by design choices rather than by the learner’s actual state of knowledge.


What an appropriate level-2 loss should do
The authors propose two minimal requirements for a level-2 epistemic uncertainty loss.

Uncertainty should decrease as sample size increases.
With more observations, the learner should generally become less epistemically uncertain.
In the infinite-data limit, epistemic uncertainty should vanish.
If the learner receives enough relevant data, the second-order distribution should converge to a point mass at the true probability.

These requirements are deliberately modest. They do not demand a perfect uncertainty measure. They only require the uncertainty to behave in the direction epistemic uncertainty is supposed to behave.

objectID: reviews/Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation.html#main-findings
href: reviews/Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation.html#main-findings
title: Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation
text:
5. Main Findings

Finding 1: Averaging first-order losses encourages false certainty
For convex first-order losses such as Brier score and log-loss, the empirical loss minimiser becomes a Dirac distribution. In practical terms, the model reports complete certainty.
This can happen regardless of sample size.
That is exactly the opposite of what epistemic uncertainty should do. With few samples, the model should usually admit lack of knowledge. But the loss minimisation objective can still reward a collapsed distribution.


Finding 2: Regularisation can push the model toward arbitrary uncertainty
Adding a KL penalty or entropy-style regularisation prevents immediate collapse, but it introduces a different problem.
The uncertainty is now strongly controlled by the regularisation weight (). If () is too small, the model becomes too certain. If () is too large, the model can remain too uncertain even with many observations.
This means the uncertainty estimate can be tuned into existence rather than learned faithfully.


Finding 3: The problem is not only a Dirichlet problem
Although the discussion is motivated partly by Dirichlet-style second-order predictors, the formal results are broader. The issue is not just that one specific distributional family is flawed.
The deeper issue is that a pointwise loss comparing (Q(x)) with a single observed label (y) does not have enough information to judge whether (Q(x)) is an honest representation of epistemic uncertainty.


Finding 4: More data does not necessarily produce the right epistemic behaviour
In the synthetic experiments, the reported level-2 uncertainty does not reliably behave like epistemic uncertainty should.
For small regularisation values, the empirical loss minimiser collapses to a point mass. For large regularisation values, it can remain highly uncertain even at large sample sizes. The change between these behaviours can be abrupt.
This supports the theoretical result: the loss does not naturally encode the desired learning dynamic.


Finding 5: The paper questions the incentive structure, not the usefulness of uncertainty
The authors are not arguing that epistemic uncertainty is unimportant. They argue the opposite: epistemic uncertainty is important, but difficult.
Their concern is that some methods produce uncertainty values without a trustworthy reason to believe those values are faithful.

href: reviews/Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation.html#why-this-paper-supports-an-ensemble-based-methodology
title: Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation
section: 6. Why This Paper Supports an Ensemble-Based Methodology
text:
6. Why This Paper Supports an Ensemble-Based Methodology
This paper is useful for justifying ensembles because it clarifies what epistemic uncertainty is uncertainty about.
Epistemic uncertainty is not just another output variable. It is uncertainty about the predictor, the hypothesis, or the class-probability function that should be used. Therefore, a method for epistemic uncertainty should represent multiple plausible predictors or model states.
Deep ensembles do this in a direct and practical way:

train multiple models independently;
let each model represent a plausible fitted function;
use disagreement between models as evidence of model uncertainty;
treat agreement as evidence that the prediction is more stable under the modelling procedure.

This is methodologically different from asking one model to produce a second-order uncertainty value through a pointwise loss. The ensemble does not need a direct epistemic uncertainty label. Its uncertainty signal comes from variation across fitted predictors.

The argument this paper gives me
The paper supports the following chain of reasoning:

Epistemic uncertainty has no direct supervised ground truth.
A loss against observed labels can reward predictive accuracy without rewarding honest epistemic uncertainty.
Direct second-order uncertainty heads can therefore be overconfident, underconfident, or strongly controlled by regularisation.
A more defensible epistemic uncertainty mechanism should represent alternative plausible predictors.
Deep ensembles are a practical way to approximate this by using independently trained models and measuring their disagreement.



How this helps position ensembles against MC dropout
This paper is not mainly an MC dropout paper, so I should not cite it as direct empirical evidence that ensembles outperform MC dropout.
Instead, I should use it for the deeper methodological point:

Epistemic uncertainty should come from uncertainty over predictors, not merely from a single model being trained to output an uncertainty score.

That point pairs naturally with the deep-ensemble literature. Compared with MC dropout, which samples stochastic subnetworks around one trained model and depends on dropout design choices, deep ensembles make the model-plurality mechanism more explicit. Each independently trained model can occupy a different fitted solution, and disagreement between those fitted solutions is easier to interpret as epistemic uncertainty.
So this paper is best used together with:

Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles
Deep Ensembles: A Loss Landscape Perspective
Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift

The combined argument is:

Bengs et al. explain why direct loss-based epistemic uncertainty is conceptually fragile.
Lakshminarayanan et al. show that deep ensembles work well empirically for predictive uncertainty.
Fort et al. explain why independently trained ensembles generate useful function-space diversity.
Ovadia et al. show why epistemic uncertainty matters under dataset shift.
