title: Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation
section: 7. Scope Notes Rather Than Heavy Criticism
text:
7. Scope Notes Rather Than Heavy Criticism
I am using this paper as methodological support, so the important caveats are scope notes rather than reasons to dismiss it.

Scope note 1: The formal results target specific loss families
The authors are careful to say that their formal results apply to the proposed loss functions they analyse. They do not prove that no possible level-2 loss could ever work.
For my review, the fair claim is:

Existing direct loss-minimisation approaches to second-order epistemic uncertainty can fail to provide faithful epistemic incentives.

not:

All possible direct uncertainty losses are impossible.



Scope note 2: The paper focuses on classification
The technical setup is classification, with probability vectors and Dirichlet-style second-order distributions.
My work may involve regression, prediction intervals, or forecasting. The exact theorems do not transfer automatically. However, the conceptual warning does transfer well:

If the training target does not contain epistemic uncertainty labels, the loss may not be able to validate epistemic uncertainty directly.



Scope note 3: The paper is not a direct ensemble benchmark
The paper does not compare deep ensembles, MC dropout, and Bayesian neural networks in an empirical benchmark.
It supports ensembles indirectly by clarifying why epistemic uncertainty should be tied to uncertainty over predictors. For direct ensemble evidence, I should cite the ensemble papers alongside this one.


Scope note 4: It does not remove the need to validate ensemble uncertainty
Using ensembles avoids the specific pitfall of a single model self-reporting epistemic uncertainty through a level-2 loss, but it does not automatically guarantee perfect uncertainty quality.
An ensemble still needs:

calibration checks;
interval coverage checks;
uncertainty-error relationship tests;
dataset-shift or sparse-regime evaluation;
evidence that ensemble members are meaningfully diverse.

section: 8. Relevance to My Research / How I Will Use It
text:
8. Relevance to My Research / How I Will Use It

Why I would cite this paper
I would cite this paper when motivating why epistemic uncertainty should not be treated as an ordinary supervised prediction target.
The most useful citation claim is:

Bengs, Hullermeier, and Waegeman show that loss functions proposed for direct second-order epistemic uncertainty prediction can fail to incentivise faithful epistemic uncertainty, because observed labels do not provide direct feedback about the learner’s uncertainty over the true probability distribution.



How it supports my methodology
This paper supports a methodology where epistemic uncertainty is estimated from a mechanism that represents multiple plausible predictors.
For my work, that points toward:

deep ensembles;
ensemble disagreement;
function-space diversity;
uncertainty validation under shift;
caution toward uncertainty values produced only by an auxiliary loss head.



How it connects to explainability
The paper is not an XAI paper in the feature-attribution sense. Its relevance to explainability is methodological.
If I want to explain uncertainty, I first need the uncertainty estimate itself to be meaningful. This paper warns that an uncertainty output can look interpretable while being produced by a loss incentive that does not actually reward honest epistemic uncertainty.
That supports the idea that explainable uncertainty should start with a defensible uncertainty-generation mechanism.


Best use in my literature review
This paper should sit in the methodological-foundation part of the review, close to:

deep ensembles as a practical epistemic uncertainty mechanism;
loss landscape explanations for ensemble diversity;
uncertainty under dataset shift;
papers that distinguish aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty.

It is not mainly a paper about energy forecasting or SHAP. It is a theoretical support paper for why the epistemic uncertainty mechanism matters.

title: Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation
text:
9. Pre-Written Assets

Literature review paragraph
Bengs, Hullermeier, and Waegeman provide an important methodological caution for epistemic uncertainty quantification. They argue that, unlike first-order probability estimation, second-order epistemic uncertainty cannot be learned faithfully by simply minimising a pointwise loss against observed labels. Their analysis shows that losses used for direct second-order uncertainty prediction can incentivise a model to become artificially overconfident, remain arbitrarily uncertain under regularisation, or report uncertainty that depends more on loss design choices than on the learner’s actual state of knowledge. This motivates the use of epistemic uncertainty mechanisms that represent uncertainty over predictors themselves, such as deep ensembles, rather than relying only on a single model’s self-reported uncertainty head.


Methodology justification sentence
Because epistemic uncertainty has no direct supervised target, I use ensemble disagreement as a practical model-uncertainty mechanism rather than relying solely on a single model trained to output epistemic uncertainty through loss minimisation.


Ensemble justification sentence
Deep ensembles are methodologically attractive for epistemic uncertainty because they represent multiple plausible fitted functions, so disagreement between ensemble members provides a more direct signal of model uncertainty than a loss-trained self-reported confidence score.


MC dropout comparison sentence
This paper does not directly benchmark MC dropout, but it supports the broader concern that epistemic uncertainty should be represented through uncertainty over predictors; this favours ensemble-based disagreement when a transparent and defensible epistemic mechanism is needed.


Caution sentence
The paper should not be used to claim that all non-ensemble uncertainty methods are invalid; its strongest use is to show that direct loss-based second-order uncertainty estimates need careful justification and validation.


One-line review
This paper explains why epistemic uncertainty cannot simply be learned as another loss-minimising output: without direct uncertainty labels, the loss can reward confidence behaviour that is mathematically convenient but epistemically unfaithful.

title: Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation
text:
10. Bottom-Line Takeaway
The core value of this paper is that it strengthens the methodological case for being careful about where epistemic uncertainty comes from.
It tells me not to treat an uncertainty number as trustworthy merely because a neural network was trained to output it. For epistemic uncertainty, the model must somehow represent uncertainty over possible predictors. Deep ensembles provide a practical way to do that through disagreement between independently fitted models.
For my review, this paper supports the theoretical justification for using ensembles as an epistemic uncertainty mechanism, especially when paired with papers that show ensembles are empirically strong and functionally diverse.

Study Type: Journal article
Code/Data Available?: No public code repository reported in the paper. The meteorological dataset is not publicly available and must be requested from the Turkish State Meteorological Service (MGM) through official channels.
Primary Domain: Short-term wind speed forecasting
Core Methods: Adaptive VMD, dual-stream CNN–BiLSTM, quantile regression, SHAP

Proximity/Threat Level: Medium to High / Relevant methodological neighbor

href: reviews/Multiscale Wind Forecasting Using Explainable-Adaptive Hybrid Deep Learning.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: Multiscale Wind Forecasting Using Explainable-Adaptive Hybrid Deep Learning
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why wind forecasting matters):

Wind speed forecasting is central to reliable renewable generation scheduling, reserve planning, grid stability, and short-term operational decision-making.
Wind is highly stochastic, nonlinear, irregular, and multiscale, so classical forecasting methods often struggle to capture its behavior.

The Motivation (Why probabilistic forecasting?):

The paper explicitly argues that point forecasts alone are operationally insufficient.
Grid operators need not just a single estimate, but a sense of forecast uncertainty, especially under unstable wind conditions.
The model therefore outputs adaptive quantile bands rather than fixed uncertainty intervals.

The Motivation (Why explainability?):

The authors argue that many deep learning models in wind forecasting remain black boxes.
Existing XAI work in this area tends to focus only on meteorological feature importance and does not really explain decomposition components, multiscale signal behavior, or dual-stream model internals.
Their SHAP analysis is meant to show that the model learns physically meaningful drivers rather than merely fitting patterns blindly.

Their claim to fame / Novelty:

They combine four things in one framework:

Adaptive VMD to determine the number of decomposition modes in a data-driven way,
Dual-stream CNN–BiLSTM to separately process decomposed wind dynamics and meteorological/temporal drivers,
Quantile regression for uncertainty-aware forecasting,
Mode-aware SHAP analysis for interpretability across both exogenous variables and decomposed modes.

Their main novelty is not raw RMSE minimization, but the integration of multiscale decomposition + probabilistic learning + explainability.

The Value Derived from Explainability (What did XAI actually do?):

It showed that seasonal periodicity and solar-related variables strongly influence predictions.
It demonstrated that lower-frequency VMD modes dominate the model’s decision process, while higher-frequency modes mainly help with sudden local variations.
It supported the authors’ claim that the internal behavior of the model aligns with physical wind-generation mechanisms.

Their ultimate result:

The final proposed hybrid quantile model achieved:

RMSE = 0.700 m/s
MAE = 0.545 m/s
Pinball Loss = 0.1367
PICP = 0.8846
PINAW = 0.3445
Approx. CRPS = 0.136

The model’s main contribution is therefore calibrated uncertainty and interpretability, rather than best-in-class point error.

href: reviews/Multiscale Wind Forecasting Using Explainable-Adaptive Hybrid Deep Learning.html#methodology-technical-details
title: Multiscale Wind Forecasting Using Explainable-Adaptive Hybrid Deep Learning
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

3.1 Dataset / Study Area

The study uses four years of hourly meteorological data (2021–2025) from the Afyonkarahisar Meteorology Directorate in Türkiye.
Target and inputs include:

Wind speed (WS)
Global horizontal irradiance (GHI)
Direct normal irradiance (DNI)
Diffuse irradiance (DIF)
Air temperature (T)
Time variables:

hour
day of year (DOY)
hour_sin, hour_cos
doy_sin, doy_cos





3.2 Data Characteristics

The wind regime is mostly low-speed, with the highest frequencies concentrated in the 0–2 m/s range.
Higher wind speeds above 4 m/s are rare.
This means the dataset is right-skewed, noisy, and hard to forecast, especially for sudden peaks.
The series also exhibits:

daily periodicity,
seasonal structure,
long-term trend, which motivates multiscale decomposition.




3.3 Data Cleaning & Preprocessing

Around 1.1% missing values were present, mainly from intermittent solar-radiation sensor outages.
Missing values were handled using time-based linear interpolation.
Invalid values were corrected using physically motivated rules:

wind speed < 0 m/s set to 0,
temperatures outside −40°C to 60°C removed before interpolation,
negative radiation values set to 0.

Wind speed was normalized with Min–Max scaling before VMD.
Separate MinMaxScalers were used for:

VMD mode inputs,
meteorological/temporal inputs,
target wind speed.




3.4 Forecasting Setup

Data split:

70% training
15% validation
15% test

Forecast horizon:

1 hour ahead

Input window:

Primary setup uses 24 hours historical data to predict the next hour.

A later performance-comparison table mentions a common comparison setup using:

input window = 12
forecast horizon = 1
same 70/15/15 split




3.5 Adaptive VMD

The paper uses Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD) rather than fixed decomposition methods like EMD/CEEMDAN.
Key idea:

Decompose the wind-speed signal into band-limited modes with different center frequencies.

The important hyperparameter is the number of modes K.
Instead of setting this manually, the authors test:

K ∈ {3, 4, 5, 6, 7}

For each K:

the signal is decomposed,
a lightweight feed-forward neural proxy model is trained,
validation RMSE is checked,
the best K is selected.

Final choice:

K = 4

Interpretation of the four modes:

IMF1: noise-like, high-frequency surges
IMF2: medium-frequency short-term behavior
IMF3: more regular daily-cycle variation
IMF4: low-frequency long-term trend

They also discuss spectral flatness as a guiding criterion to avoid over-decomposition.



3.6 Model Architecture
The model is a dual-stream CNN–BiLSTM:

Wind-Stream

Input: VMD modes
Purpose: learn multiscale wind dynamics
Components:

1D Conv layer
BiLSTM layers
Dense projection




Met-Stream

Input: meteorological and temporal variables
Purpose: learn external environmental and seasonal drivers
Components:

1D Conv layer
BiLSTM layers
Dense projection




Fusion & Output

The latent representations from both streams are concatenated.
Then passed through:

Dense(64, ReLU)
Dense(32, ReLU)

Final output layer predicts three quantiles:

Q0.05
Q0.50
Q0.95





3.7 Detailed Architecture Notes

CNN:

1 × Conv1D
32 filters
kernel size = 3
same padding
ReLU activation

BiLSTM:

2 stacked layers
units = 64 → 32
first layer returns sequences
second returns final representation

Training details:

Adam optimizer
learning rate = 1e-4
clipnorm = 1.0
EarlyStopping with patience = 5

Additional regularization:

dropout = 0.2
recurrent dropout = 0.2

The discussion section notes the architecture has roughly 3.1 million trainable parameters.



3.8 Quantile Regression

Instead of only minimizing MSE, the model is trained to estimate quantiles.
The 0.05–0.95 interval corresponds to a 90% prediction interval.
The authors justify this choice as a good trade-off between:

uncertainty coverage,
sharpness,
operational usefulness for reserve allocation and scheduling.




3.9 Evaluation Metrics
The study evaluates both deterministic and probabilistic performance.

Deterministic metrics:

RMSE
MAE

Probabilistic metrics:

Pinball Loss
PICP
PINAW
Approximate CRPS




3.10 Explainability Strategy

SHAP is applied to the median output (Q0.5).
SHAP values are computed for:

meteorological and temporal features,
VMD modes

Their goal is not only ranking variables, but explaining the contribution of decomposed multiscale components.

4. Validation Strategy (Predictions & Explanations)

4.1 Validating the Predictions

Standard train/validation/test split with sliding windows.
Deterministic accuracy is derived from the median forecast.
Probabilistic quality is evaluated through interval coverage and width.



4.2 Validating the Uncertainty

The 0.05–0.95 quantile band is inspected visually and numerically.
The authors emphasize that the band:

widens during unstable periods,
narrows during quiet periods,
adapts over time rather than staying fixed.

This is their evidence that the model captures time-varying volatility.



4.3 Validating the Explanations

The paper mostly relies on qualitative physical consistency checks.
It argues that explanation outputs align with known atmospheric and seasonal behavior.
There is no formal quantitative XAI validation such as:

fidelity,
stability,
robustness,
sensitivity tests,
perturbation-based explanation evaluation.

5. Results

5.1 Deterministic Performance

Final model:

MAE = 0.545 m/s

The median forecast tracks:

general trend,
diurnal periodicity,
seasonal variation, but smooths sharp peaks.

The model produces non-symmetric, dynamically changing quantile bands.
Reported interpretation:

observations fall within the band a large portion of the time,
intervals widen under unstable wind conditions,
intervals narrow during calm periods.




5.3 Coverage

The paper reports:

PICP = 87.4% for the 90% interval in one section.

In the comparison table, the final hybrid model is reported as:

PICP = 0.8846

So the calibration is close to but slightly below ideal 90% coverage.



5.4 SHAP Findings for Meteorological / Temporal Inputs

The paper first states:

GHI is the most dominant meteorological variable,
Temperature is also influential,
DNI and DIF matter less but still contribute,
hour_sin and hour_cos show the model learns daily periodicity.

Later, a more detailed SHAP interpretation states:

doy_sin is actually the most important overall feature,
followed by GHI,
then hourly harmonics.


This suggests that the dominant explanatory story is: 1. Seasonality 2. Solar forcing 3. Diurnal periodicity 4. Secondary atmospheric features


5.5 SHAP Findings for VMD Modes

Importance ranking:

IMF4 highest
IMF3 second
IMF1 / IMF2 lower

Interpretation:

low-frequency trend and smooth persistent modes are the main forecasting signal,

title: Multiscale Wind Forecasting Using Explainable-Adaptive Hybrid Deep Learning
text:
6. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: The strongest baseline actually appears to beat the proposed model

The most obvious issue in the results table is that the TCN-Quantile baseline appears substantially better than the proposed method on nearly every reported metric:

much lower RMSE,
much lower MAE,
lower pinball loss,
better coverage,
narrower intervals,
lower CRPS.

That creates a major tension in the paper’s narrative.
The authors try to reposition the contribution around uncertainty-awareness and interpretability rather than best raw error, but the TCN baseline is also probabilistic.
So unless there is some hidden mismatch in experimental protocol or implementation complexity, this table weakens the claim that the proposed framework is a stronger forecasting model.



Criticism 2: Internal inconsistency in the architecture description

There is a noticeable inconsistency between sections.
In one place, the authors say pooling is intentionally omitted to avoid losing peak information.
In later architecture subsections, both wind-stream and met-stream include MaxPooling1D.
That is a methodological inconsistency that should not appear in a polished paper.
It makes the exact implemented architecture slightly ambiguous.



Criticism 3: Input window inconsistency

The main methodology says the model predicts the next hour from 24 hours of historical data.
The performance comparison table states that all models were evaluated under a common setup with input window = 12.
That is another reproducibility issue.
A reader cannot be completely certain whether the final reported numbers come from the 24-step design, the 12-step benchmark protocol, or mixed settings.



Criticism 4: “Adaptive” VMD is only partially adaptive

The paper markets the decomposition stage as adaptive, which is fair to a degree.
But the adaptivity is limited to searching over a small discrete set:

K ∈ {3,4,5,6,7}

That is more like a validation-based hyperparameter sweep than fully adaptive mode discovery.
It is better than manually fixing K once, but it is still a fairly narrow search strategy.



Criticism 5: SHAP validation is still mostly qualitative

The explainability section is interesting and useful, but it is not rigorously validated.
The authors mainly argue that the SHAP outputs “make physical sense.”
That is helpful, but it does not tell us:

whether explanations are stable across seeds,
whether they are robust to small perturbations,
whether the model is explanation-faithful,
whether similar samples get similar explanations.




Criticism 6: Point-forecasting weakness is partially excused rather than solved

The authors openly acknowledge that decomposition and quantile learning smooth the signal and reduce pointwise responsiveness to peaks.
That honesty is good.
But it also means the proposed architecture is not especially strong at one of the most standard forecasting tasks: exact next-step point accuracy.
The paper reframes this as a design choice, which is partly fair, but it remains a practical limitation.



Criticism 7: Single-site, low-wind regional scope limits generalization

The entire model is validated on one regional dataset from Afyonkarahisar.
The authors themselves acknowledge that offshore and high-wind environments have very different turbulence characteristics and spectral properties.
So the model’s broader generalizability is not demonstrated.



Criticism 8: The non-public dataset limits reproducibility

Since the dataset is not publicly released, independent replication is difficult.
That weakens the experimental transparency of the work.



Criticism 9: No stronger ablation on the value of each ingredient

The paper does compare several variants, which is good.
But it still does not fully isolate:

adaptive vs fixed VMD,
SHAP’s practical value beyond explanation,
meteorology stream vs time stream vs decomposition stream,
hybrid loss vs pure quantile loss in a deeper ablation sense.

A more systematic ablation would have made the contribution clearer.



Criticism 10: The paper slightly overstates its interpretability advantage

It is fair to say this study gives more interpretability than a plain CNN–LSTM.
But SHAP on the median output is still a partial explanation of a fairly complex hybrid architecture.
It does not completely “open the black box.”
It gives useful attribution insights, especially feature- and mode-level importance, but not full mechanistic transparency.

text:
9. Relevance to My Work / Integration Notes

Why it matters to my literature review:

This paper is useful as an example of a study that treats uncertainty quantification and explainability as first-class objectives rather than just add-ons.
It is particularly relevant if I want to position my own work against:

deterministic-only deep forecasting papers,
fixed decomposition pipelines,
shallow XAI analyses that only rank raw features.


What I can adopt:

The framing that point accuracy alone is not enough for operational forecasting.
The use of quantile outputs instead of only point estimates.
The idea of explaining not only exogenous variables, but also decomposed latent signal components.
The insight that lower-frequency modes often dominate predictive utility.

What I should improve beyond this paper:

Use public or reproducible datasets where possible.
Add formal XAI evaluation:

stability,
robustness,
fidelity,
perturbation sensitivity.

Make the experimental setup fully consistent and reproducible.
Benchmark against stronger modern baselines and make sure the proposed method actually wins, or clearly explain why it is still valuable if it does not.
Perform better ablations to isolate the value of each design choice.

text:
Authors & Year: Xiaodong Shen, Huixin Liu, Gao Qiu, Youbo Liu, Junyong Liu, and Shixiong Fan (2024)
Venue (Journal/Conference): IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics

DOI: 10.1109/TII.2024.3355105
Primary Topic/Concept: Interpretable outlier-adaptive day-ahead electricity price forecasting using cross-market features and interval prediction
Study Region / Testbed: Danish day-ahead electricity market, specifically DK1 and DK2
Core Methods: GMM, LightGBM, LSTNet, KDE, SHAP
Code/Data Available?: The paper cites public data sources for market variables, but it does not present a dedicated public code repository in the paper itself
Proximity/Threat Level: High / Directly relevant if your work concerns probabilistic or interpretable forecasting under extreme events
Date Reviewed: 2026-03-13

objectID: reviews/Interpretable Interval Prediction-Based Outlier-Adaptive Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/Interpretable Interval Prediction-Based Outlier-Adaptive Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: Interpretable Interval Prediction-Based Outlier-Adaptive Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting Involving Cross-Market Features
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why this problem matters)

Electricity prices in European markets have become far more erratic due to geopolitical shocks, fuel price volatility, renewable penetration, and tighter cross-market coupling.
Traditional price forecasting models often focus only on the internal electricity market and ignore cross-market spillovers from gas, coal, and neighboring electricity markets.
Extreme prices, including sharp spikes and negative prices, are no longer rare edge cases. They are increasingly central to the forecasting problem.
Standard point forecasting is not enough because it does not quantify uncertainty, and it tends to break down exactly where market participants care most: during extreme or abnormal events.



The Motivation (Why interval prediction?)

The authors argue that outlier prices are fundamentally harder to predict with a single point model because outliers are sparse and induce large generalization errors.
Their solution is not to replace point forecasting entirely, but to combine:

point prediction for regular price regimes, and

interval prediction for abnormal or outlier regimes.

This “divide-and-rule” logic is a key conceptual contribution of the paper.



The Motivation (Why explainability?)

They explicitly position interpretability as a trust and validation mechanism for electricity market forecasting.
In their framing, market participants need to know why the model is relying on certain features, especially when economic and geopolitical events dominate the market.
SHAP is not used only as a descriptive dashboard. It is used as a cross-validation mechanism to check whether the LSTNet learned sensible market structure or whether it overfit to outlier-driven noise.



Their claim to fame / Novelty
The paper’s novelty rests on the combination of four ideas: 1. Cross-market feature fusion across electricity, gas, and coal markets, including mixed temporal granularities. 2. A GMM-LightGBM outlier detector, where GMM identifies historical outliers and LightGBM forecasts future outlier timestamps. 3. An LSTNet-KDE hybrid predictor, where one LSTNet forecasts the main price trend and another estimates outlier prediction errors, which KDE then converts into intervals. 4. SHAP-based interpretability as a model reliability check, not just a posthoc illustration.


Their ultimate result

The framework shows that:

LightGBM is the best outlier forecaster among the tested classifiers.
LSTNet is the strongest point predictor among the tested baselines.
Interval prediction for isolated outliers yields empirically valid and stable coverage.
SHAP identifies natural gas as the dominant cross-market driver of electricity price trends in the Danish case study.

objectID: reviews/Interpretable Interval Prediction-Based Outlier-Adaptive Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting.html#methodology-technical-details
href: reviews/Interpretable Interval Prediction-Based Outlier-Adaptive Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting.html#methodology-technical-details
title: Interpretable Interval Prediction-Based Outlier-Adaptive Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting Involving Cross-Market Features
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

Overall Pipeline
The framework has five modules:

Data preparation / multitemporal syncretism

Builds a unified database across electricity and primary energy markets.
Electricity inputs use hourly sequences.
Gas and coal inputs use daily sequences, aligned into 24-step windows.

Outlier detection and forecasting

Historical outliers are detected using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM).
A scaled outlier score is computed, and timestamps with scaled score ≥ 9 are labeled as outliers.
These historical labels are then appended to the feature set.
LightGBM is trained to predict outlier timestamps for the next 24-hour forecasting horizon.

Principal trend capture / point forecasting

A base LSTNet is trained on the outlier-fused input set.
It captures short-term local dependencies via convolution, long-term structure via recurrent and skip-recurrent components, and local sharp behavior via an autoregressive layer.

Error estimation and interval prediction

A second, error-oriented LSTNet predicts forecasting errors for future outliers.
KDE is then used on recent outlier errors plus the predicted error to construct a predictive interval for outlier timestamps.

Interpretability-based cross-validation

SHAP is applied to the base LSTNet.
If the learned feature dependence looks unreasonable, the authors propose retraining with:

outlier smoothing, and
cost-sensitive weighting.





Inputs Used
The paper defines three main input subsets:

RIS (Raw Input Subset):

previous 24 hours of electricity-related curves
previous 24 days of gas and coal prices

OFIS (Outlier-Fused Input Subset):

RIS plus historical outlier identification labels

FEPS (Forecasting Error Prediction Subset):

OFIS
the 24-hour point forecast
predictive errors for the most recent outliers




Key Features
The paper uses a broad set of variables, including: - historical electricity prices - electricity production / consumption-type market features - neighboring or interconnected market electricity features - energy exchange features - gas prices - coal prices
This is important: the study is not just “price forecasting with lagged prices.” It is explicitly a cross-market, multitemporal forecasting problem.


Dataset / Case Study

Market: Danish day-ahead market, DK1 and DK2
Period: May 1, 2021 to August 31, 2022
Split:

Training: May 1, 2021 to May 31, 2022
Validation: June 1, 2022 to July 31, 2022
Testing: August 1, 2022 to August 31, 2022




Why isolate outliers?
One of the paper’s strongest ideas is that outliers are not treated as random contamination. The authors explicitly argue that outlier prices still have temporal patterning, and therefore deserve their own specialized treatment rather than being discarded or flattened.

text:
4. Validation Strategy (Predictions & Explanations)

Validating the Outlier Detector
For outlier timestamp prediction, they use: - Accuracy - Recall
They compare: - SVM - XGBoost - LightGBM
Takeaway: LightGBM is selected as the best detector, especially due to stronger Recall.


Validating the Point Predictor
For point forecasting, they use: - MAE - sMAPE - RRMSE
They compare the proposed LSTNet setup against: - CNN-LSTM - Informer - LightGBM
Takeaway: LSTNet performs best overall for both DK1 and DK2.


Validating the Interval Predictor
For interval forecasting, they use: - PICP (Prediction Interval Coverage Percentage) - PINAW (Prediction Interval Normalized Average Width)
They evaluate prediction intervals built: - on all samples - on outlier samples only
They also run a sensitivity experiment on outlier sample size.
Takeaway: The interval method achieves empirical coverage close to the nominal level and remains relatively stable.


Validating the Explanations
The paper validates SHAP mainly through: - feature ranking consistency, - economic plausibility, - cross-checking with known market structure.
This is not a formal XAI benchmark. It is a domain-knowledge plausibility validation approach.

title: Interpretable Interval Prediction-Based Outlier-Adaptive Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting Involving Cross-Market Features
section: 5. Main Results & What They Actually Mean
text:
5. Main Results & What They Actually Mean

5.1 Outlier Detection Results

LightGBM outperforms SVM and is competitive or better than XGBoost on Accuracy.
More importantly, LightGBM substantially improves Recall, which matters because missing rare but important price outliers is especially costly.
This supports the use of a two-stage detector:

unsupervised GMM for labeling historical anomalies,
supervised LightGBM for forecasting future abnormal timestamps.




5.2 Point Forecasting Results

LSTNet beats CNN-LSTM, Informer, and LightGBM on the reported point metrics.
The authors highlight that the AR component helps LSTNet stay closer to local outlier behavior than the other models.
However, the paper also shows something more interesting:

when the models are tested on regular points only, LSTNet still performs best,
but its performance changes more noticeably when outliers are present.

That means the model is strong, but also meaningfully stressed by outlier structure.



5.3 Interval Forecasting Results

The interval module reaches empirical coverage close to the target confidence levels.
When trained only on outlier samples, prediction intervals become wider, which the authors interpret as appropriate because outlier generalization error is larger.
Their claim is subtle:

wider intervals are not necessarily a weakness here,
because the point of the interval is to absorb the uncertainty caused by rare, poorly learned, extreme prices.




5.4 Interpretable Findings (SHAP)
This is one of the most valuable parts of the paper.

Global ranking

Gas is the most important feature overall.
DK1 and DK2 are also highly important.
Interconnected market features such as DE and SE4 rank among the top features.
Coal ranks much lower, which the authors attribute to its relatively low variation during the test period.



Why this matters
This is a strong result because it tells you the model is not only using local electricity history. It is relying strongly on: - domestic price dynamics, - cross-border electricity market interactions, - and especially gas market conditions.


Gas ablation logic
The authors compare forecasting performance with and without the gas feature, and show a clear degradation when gas is removed. That is an important validation step because it links: - SHAP explanation, - feature ranking, - and actual forecast performance.


Temporal SHAP insight for gas
They go further and analyze the 24 gas trading days used as inputs: - the SHAP values are consistently positive, - the first to fourth trading days matter most, - the first trading day has the strongest impact, - days 5–11 have almost no effect, - days 12–24 have small but fluctuating influence.
This is one of the most interesting interpretability findings in the paper because it suggests the model is not just saying “gas matters,” but that recent gas market information matters disproportionately more.

objectID: reviews/Interpretable Interval Prediction-Based Outlier-Adaptive Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting.html#strengths-of-the-paper
href: reviews/Interpretable Interval Prediction-Based Outlier-Adaptive Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting.html#strengths-of-the-paper
title: Interpretable Interval Prediction-Based Outlier-Adaptive Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting Involving Cross-Market Features
text:
6. Strengths of the Paper

Strength 1: It tackles the real problem, not the clean one
A lot of electricity forecasting papers still operate in relatively stable market settings or frame extremes as nuisances. This paper directly targets volatile, deregulated, shock-prone markets.


Strength 2: Good problem decomposition
The split into: - outlier detection, - point forecasting, - outlier interval prediction, - interpretability-based cross-validation
is conceptually neat and practically defensible.


Strength 3: Cross-market thinking is a genuine contribution
The inclusion of gas, coal, and neighboring electricity markets is not cosmetic. It is central to the study’s argument and is supported by the SHAP analysis.


Strength 4: The explainability is actually tied to model governance
The paper does more than produce SHAP beeswarm plots. It frames interpretability as a tool for: - checking whether the predictor learned sensible structure, - spotting overfitting, - and deciding whether retraining is necessary.


Strength 5: Sensible argument for hybrid point + interval forecasting
Their “do not use a single unified prediction mode for everything” argument is persuasive: - point forecasts are more intuitive and efficient in regular periods, - interval forecasts are more robust in outlier periods.

objectID: reviews/Interpretable Interval Prediction-Based Outlier-Adaptive Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
href: reviews/Interpretable Interval Prediction-Based Outlier-Adaptive Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
title: Interpretable Interval Prediction-Based Outlier-Adaptive Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting Involving Cross-Market Features
text:
7. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: SHAP is used as a trust mechanism, but not formally validated
The paper uses SHAP for cross-validation and decision support, but the validation remains mostly qualitative and economically intuitive. - There is no formal stability analysis of explanations. - There is no faithfulness or robustness testing. - There is no comparison against alternative explanation methods.
So while the interpretability story is compelling, it is not rigorously benchmarked.


Criticism 2: The “cross-validation” role of SHAP is still somewhat heuristic
The paper says that if SHAP reveals an unreasonable dependence structure, retraining is triggered with outlier smoothing and cost-sensitive learning. That is an interesting idea, but the paper does not fully operationalize it: - What exact threshold defines “untrustworthy”? - How often is retraining triggered? - How sensitive is the procedure to subjective expert judgment?
This means the interpretability-to-correction loop is more of a promising framework than a fully reproducible protocol.


Criticism 3: The outlier definition is still threshold-based after transformation
Although GMM is used, the final outlier labeling still depends on a scaled score threshold. That makes the “outlier” concept partly model-driven and partly arbitrary. A different threshold might materially alter: - class balance, - LightGBM training, - interval width behavior, - and the apparent success of the outlier-specialized branch.


Criticism 4: Baseline set is good, but not exhaustive
The paper compares against: - SVM / XGBoost for outlier detection - CNN-LSTM / Informer / LightGBM for point prediction
This is respectable, but for a paper centered on interval prediction and uncertainty, stronger interval/probabilistic baselines could have made the evidence more decisive, for example: - quantile regression networks, - conformal interval methods, - mixture density approaches, - direct probabilistic transformers.


Criticism 5: Interval prediction is targeted, not fully distributional
Their framework is best understood as outlier-adaptive interval forecasting, not a full probabilistic density forecasting system across all timestamps. That is fine, but it limits the generality of the uncertainty modeling story.


Criticism 6: One month of testing is not very long for a volatile market claim
The full data period is decent, but the actual test window is still relatively short. For highly unstable markets, longer rolling-origin testing across multiple stress regimes would have strengthened the conclusions.


Criticism 7: Potential complexity cost
The framework is powerful, but it is also layered: - GMM - LightGBM - base LSTNet - error LSTNet - KDE - SHAP - possible retraining loop
That may be acceptable in research, but deployment complexity is much higher than with a single unified forecaster.

8. What This Paper Means for My Own Research

If I am working on probabilistic forecasting
This paper is useful because it shows a strong alternative to “predict a full distribution everywhere.”
Instead, I can: - use point forecasting in regular regimes, - reserve special uncertainty machinery for abnormal regimes, - and thereby reduce unnecessary stochastic modeling overhead.


If I am working on XAI for forecasting
This paper is especially relevant because it treats SHAP as more than an explanation layer. It uses SHAP to: - rank cross-market drivers, - verify economic plausibility, - and supervise model reliability.
That is a strong framing move for a literature review.


If I am working on energy market coupling
The paper supports the argument that electricity price forecasting in modern European markets cannot be treated as a closed single-market time-series problem. Gas and cross-border electricity features matter materially.

text:
9. Best Summary in Plain English
This paper proposes a forecasting system for volatile electricity markets that first asks:

Will tomorrow contain abnormal price points?

What is the normal price trend?

How uncertain should I be specifically at those abnormal points?

Did the model learn sensible market logic, or did it overfit?

To answer those questions, it combines: - GMM + LightGBM to identify and forecast outliers, - LSTNet to forecast the main trend, - another LSTNet + KDE to build intervals for future outliers, - and SHAP to explain and verify what the model learned.
Its most important empirical finding is that natural gas is the dominant cross-market feature shaping Danish electricity price forecasts during the studied period, and that explicitly separating outlier handling from normal forecasting improves robustness.

href: reviews/Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why hybrid modeling?):

The paper starts from a very practical tension in building energy forecasting:

Pure physical simulation is interpretable and grounded in real building physics, but it often fails to match actual operational behavior accurately.
Pure data-driven models can fit measured demand more accurately, but they behave like black boxes and ignore explicit physical structure.

Their central argument is that building electricity demand is fundamentally governed by physical mechanisms, but actual usage also contains hidden operational patterns that only data-driven learning can uncover.

The Motivation (Why this matters specifically for buildings?):

Building electricity forecasting supports optimal control, energy management, and cost reduction.
Even small forecasting improvements can translate into meaningful operational and economic benefits.
In commercial buildings, actual demand is shaped not only by climate and HVAC physics, but also by occupancy behavior and irregular working patterns, which are difficult to represent in a purely simulation-based framework.

Their claim to fame / Novelty:

They propose a hybrid forecasting framework that explicitly combines:

Physical software simulation for heating and cooling loads,
EMD for decomposing complex demand signals,
K-means clustering for inferring work-state intensity,
Deep learning via LSTM or TCN-GRU,
SHAP + Pearson correlation for interpretability,
Monte Carlo weather-error propagation for prediction intervals,
Transfer learning for floors with limited historical data.

The novelty is not any single component alone, but the system-level integration of physical priors, data decomposition, learned representations, interpretability, uncertainty quantification, and data-efficiency strategies into one building forecasting pipeline.

The Value Derived from Explainability and Hybridization:

Physical relevance: The model does not rely purely on opaque learned correlations; it explicitly incorporates simulated heating and cooling loads.
Operational relevance: It discovers a more realistic “work” feature from the electricity data itself, rather than relying only on fixed calendar schedules.
Interpretability: SHAP and correlation analysis show which features matter most, especially work-state, lag terms, and cooling load.
Practical deployment value: The framework is extended beyond point forecasting to include uncertainty intervals and transfer learning for incomplete-data settings.

Their ultimate result:

The hybrid models achieve R² above 0.85, reaching up to about 0.9, while pure physical simulation alone only reaches about 0.3.
MAE, MSE, and RMSE remain below 0.07, and SMAPE stays around 0.2 in the main hybrid setup.
In transfer learning settings, R² remains above 0.8, with somewhat higher errors but still workable performance.

objectID: reviews/Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods.html#methodology-technical-details
href: reviews/Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods.html#methodology-technical-details
title: Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

Dataset / Testbed:

The study uses hourly electricity demand data from the air-conditioning terminals on each floor of the Glodon Xi’an Digital Architecture R&D Building.
The building is a large office building with 12 floors above ground and 3 below, with substantial HVAC infrastructure and a central ecological atrium.
The example time span shown in the paper covers data from April 17, 2023 to November 27, 2023.

Physical Model Component:

A BIM model is constructed in Autodesk Revit and imported into the Hongye Building Performance Analysis Platform, which uses EnergyPlus, OpenFOAM, and Radiance as core engines.
The software computes annual dynamic heating and cooling loads based on building envelope, weather, HVAC design, and occupancy-related conditions.
From this simulation, the paper extracts:

Cooling load: (L_c)
Heating load: (L_h)


Deep Learning Component:

Two learning backbones are tested:

LSTM
TCN-GRU

Both models include dropout and dense layers, and use Adam optimization with MSE as validation loss.
The paper positions:

LSTM as stronger for long-range temporal dependencies and expressive sequence learning,
TCN-GRU as combining local temporal extraction through dilated convolutions with sequential memory through GRU units.


Input Features:

The hybrid model uses six main external features:

Temperature
Humidity
Holiday
Work-state
Cooling load (L_c)
Heating load (L_h)

Lagged demand features are also used in the interpretability analysis, particularly lag-1 and lag-2.

EMD Pre-processing:

They use Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) to break complex electricity demand data into simpler Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs).
The motivation is that raw electricity demand contains overlapping oscillatory structures that are difficult for deep learning models to learn directly.
The IMFs are ranked by energy, and the higher-energy modes are selected to reduce computational cost while preserving most of the informative structure.
Prediction is done IMF-by-IMF, and the final forecast is reconstructed by summing the predicted IMFs.

K-means Work-State Extraction:

A major contribution is the introduction of a learned “work” feature.
Instead of assuming that working hours are fixed by calendar, they cluster electricity demand behavior using K-means.
The electricity demand is first split into clusters, then mapped into three work-intensity classes: 0, 1, and 2.
This lets the model infer actual operational intensity from load patterns rather than imposing a rigid schedule.

Prediction Interval Method:

Instead of using residual-based prediction intervals, they use weather forecast error intervals and a Monte Carlo process.
The idea is to perturb the weather inputs, generate many temperature scenarios, run them through the model, and then derive the forecast interval from the resulting predictive distribution.
This is conceptually different from the more standard residual-distribution approach.

Transfer Learning Setup:

Transfer learning is tested between floors.
The paper uses decomposed IMFs from one floor as the source task and fine-tunes models for another floor with limited data.
Initial layers are frozen, source weights are transferred, and remaining layers are fine-tuned.
They specifically compare training with 5 IMFs versus 8 IMFs.

href: reviews/Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods.html#validation-strategy-predictions-interpretability-uncertainty
title: Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods
text:
4. Validation Strategy (Predictions, Interpretability & Uncertainty)

Validating the Predictions (Forecasting Quality):

The paper evaluates performance using:

MAE
MSE
RMSE
SMAPE
R²

These are used both to assess the effect of pre-processing and the final hybrid forecasting models.

Validating EMD Pre-processing:

They test model performance with and without EMD.
For LSTM, adding EMD reduces errors and increases R² from 0.056 to 0.2938.
For TCN-GRU, EMD also improves performance, increasing R² from 0.2964 to 0.3588.
Their interpretation is that EMD makes hidden structure easier for the models to learn.

Validating the Work-State Feature:

Two approaches are compared:

A manually fixed work-hour schedule,
A K-means-derived work-state.

The fixed schedule gives R² = 0.3040.
The K-means-derived feature improves performance dramatically to R² = 0.8417.
Residual plots, Q-Q plots, and residual density plots all favor the K-means approach, suggesting that it captures real operational regimes more faithfully.

Validating the Final Hybrid Model:

On the 8th-floor dataset, both hybrid models achieve roughly R² ≈ 0.85.
Errors are low, with RMSE and MAE below 0.07, and SMAPE below 0.25.
The paper says TCN-GRU appears slightly better overall in the main hybrid forecasting experiment, especially from residual distribution behavior.

Validating the Explanations (XAI Quality):

They use SHAP values and Pearson correlation heatmaps.
This is not a formal XAI benchmarking framework; it is mainly a feature-importance and domain-consistency analysis.
For the third floor, the top features are:

work
(L_c)
lag-1
lag-2

For the eighth floor, the top features are:

work
lag-1
lag-2
(L_c)

The ranking shift is interpreted as a time-scale effect: lag terms dominate at shorter scales, while physically simulated cooling load becomes more influential at larger scales.

Validating Prediction Intervals:

They generate intervals using Monte Carlo propagation of weather uncertainty.
The reported PINAW is 0.7513 for the shown LSTM interval example.
The paper argues that this is more practically aligned with real forecasting conditions than intervals based only on residual assumptions.

Validating Transfer Learning:

With transfer learning, R² remains above 0.8.
Increasing IMF count from 5 to 8 improves R², for example from 0.83 to 0.88 in the LSTM setup.
Errors remain below 0.2, while SMAPE stays around 0.4.
The paper concludes that LSTM performs slightly better than TCN-GRU in the transfer learning setting, especially in residual normality and generalization.

title: Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods
text:
5. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: The “hybrid” idea is strong, but causality is still limited.

The paper is better than a purely black-box demand model because it injects physically simulated cooling and heating loads.
However, the final predictive mechanism is still primarily correlational rather than causal.
The physical model provides useful priors, but the deep model does not explicitly enforce thermodynamic consistency or energy-balance constraints during learning.

Criticism 2: The XAI is useful, but still shallow.

SHAP and Pearson correlation are helpful for identifying influential features, but this is still a relatively lightweight form of interpretability.
The paper does not evaluate:

explanation stability,
sensitivity to perturbations,
faithfulness/fidelity,
robustness across retraining runs.

So the interpretability story is persuasive, but not especially rigorous.

Criticism 3: Their strongest gain may come from feature engineering, not necessarily architecture.

A big jump in performance comes from the K-means-derived work-state feature.
That suggests the paper’s real contribution may be less about LSTM vs TCN-GRU and more about constructing better operational features.
In that sense, the “hybrid” framework is partly a feature-engineering framework disguised as a forecasting architecture.

Criticism 4: The comparison against pure physical simulation is somewhat easy to win.

The paper emphasizes that pure physical simulation only reaches R² ≈ 0.3.
That result is believable, but it is also not surprising.
Whole-building or floor-level electricity demand includes many operational irregularities, occupancy deviations, and control behaviors that calibrated simulation alone often misses.
So the comparison is valid, but not especially demanding as a benchmark.

Criticism 5: The uncertainty modeling is interesting, but incomplete.

Their Monte Carlo interval method based on weather forecast error is novel in context and practically meaningful.
But it only propagates uncertainty from weather forecasts, mainly temperature and humidity.
It does not fully capture:

model uncertainty,
occupancy uncertainty,
control-system uncertainty,
sensor noise,
structural misspecification.

So the interval is not a full predictive uncertainty distribution, but rather a partial uncertainty analysis.

Criticism 6: The transfer learning claim is promising, but narrow.

Transfer learning is only demonstrated across floors within the same building.
This is useful, but still a relatively favorable transfer setting because the floors share infrastructure, climate, schedule patterns, and building envelope assumptions.
True generalization to different buildings, HVAC systems, climates, or usage types is not shown.

Criticism 7: The weather feature set is thin.

The authors themselves acknowledge that only temperature and humidity are used from weather data.
For building electricity demand, especially cooling-dominated operation, omitted variables such as:

solar radiation,
wind speed,
cloud cover,
occupancy proxies,
internal equipment gains, could materially affect performance and feature interpretation.


Criticism 8: Residual normality is slightly overused as a quality signal.

The paper repeatedly treats approximately normal residuals as evidence of good generalization and model validity.
That is not completely wrong, but it is a weak standard on its own.
A model can still have operationally important biases, heteroscedasticity, or poor tail behavior even if residual plots look roughly normal.

text:
6. Why This Paper Matters for My Research

What is genuinely useful here:

It offers a strong example of how to combine:

physical priors,
decomposed time-series structure,
learned operational states,
explainability,
interval forecasting,
and data-efficiency techniques.

This is especially valuable if I want to argue that interpretable forecasting should not be framed as purely “post-hoc XAI on black-box models,” but can also come from hybridization with domain structure.

What I would borrow:

The idea of using derived operational-state features instead of relying only on calendar variables.
The use of simulation outputs as explanatory auxiliary features rather than as standalone forecasts.
The framing that interpretability can also be about verifying whether physically meaningful variables rise in importance.

What I would improve:

Add stronger baselines.
Add formal explanation-quality tests.
Compare residual-based vs weather-error-based intervals more directly.
Use richer exogenous features.
Test transfer learning across more diverse domains, not just neighboring floors.

This paper is a strong example of a practically motivated hybrid forecasting framework: it shows that physically simulated HVAC loads, data-driven decomposition, learned work-state features, and post-hoc interpretability can be combined to produce accurate and operationally meaningful building electricity forecasts, but its claims about interpretability, uncertainty, and transferability remain more promising than fully proven.

title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
Authors & Year: Chenbei Lu, Jinhao Liang, Wenqian Jiang, Jiaye Teng, Chenye Wu (2023)
Venue (Journal/Conference): Journal of the Franklin Institute
DOI: 10.1016/j.jfranklin.2023.02.010
Primary Topic: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting using a nonlinear ensemble learner
Core Technical Theme: Replacing conventional linear ensemble rules with a learned nonlinear combiner, then using Shapley values to quantify how much each base model contributes
Date Reviewed: 2026-03-13
Proximity / Threat Level: Moderate to high, especially if my work involves probabilistic forecasting, ensemble design, or SHAP/Shapley-based interpretation of model contributions
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why probabilistic load forecasting?)
The paper starts from the standard but important argument that deterministic forecasts are not enough for power-system operations. Operators need uncertainty-aware forecasts to support dispatch, planning, and investment, especially under increasing renewable penetration. The authors argue that high-resolution probabilistic forecasting is especially useful because it captures both short-term dynamics and uncertainty structure more comprehensively than coarser or point-only approaches.


The Motivation (Why ensemble learning?)
Their central motivation is that no single forecasting model performs best on every dataset, so model combination is attractive for improving robustness and generalization. However, they argue that most existing ensemble methods in load forecasting are still essentially linear combinations of base-model outputs, such as: - mean value ensemble, - median value ensemble, - weighted average ensemble, and - quantile regression combination.
Their key complaint is that these linear rules are too restrictive and cannot fully exploit complementary strengths across heterogeneous base learners.


Their main novelty / claim to fame
The paper makes three main claims: 1. A learning ensemble framework for probabilistic load forecasting, where a machine learning model learns the nonlinear mapping from the predictions of several base models to the final probabilistic forecast. 2. A theoretical argument that nonlinear learning-based ensemble methods can overcome a fundamental limitation of linear ensembles. 3. A Shapley value-based contribution analysis to quantify the value of each base forecaster inside the ensemble.


What is actually novel here?
The most important novelty is not simply “using an ensemble,” since ensembles are already common. The real novelty is the argument that: - prior probabilistic load-forecast ensembles are mostly linear, - nonlinear ensemble learning can do better, - and this is supported by both theoretical results and empirical experiments.
This theoretical layer is important because many papers propose hybrid or stacked models purely as an engineering heuristic. Here, the authors try to give the nonlinear ensemble idea a formal foundation.


Their ultimate result
The learning ensemble, especially the DNN-based and LSTM-based versions, outperformed conventional ensemble methods across multiple forecasting horizons. Compared with the average single model, improvements approached 50% in some settings, and even compared with the best single model, the learning ensemble still achieved around 10% to 20% improvement. The paper also found that FCDNN and LSTM models contributed the most to the ensemble according to Shapley-value analysis.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#problem-formulation-methodology
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#problem-formulation-methodology
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text: 3. Problem Formulation & Methodology
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#forecasting-formulation
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#forecasting-formulation
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
3.1 Forecasting formulation
The paper frames the task as quantile-based probabilistic forecasting rather than directly predicting full parametric distributions. This is sensible because: - quantile forecasting is flexible, - it avoids assuming a specific output distribution family, - and it can be evaluated using pinball loss.
The forecasting model receives: - historical load, - day-type information, - weather and temperature-related variables,
and predicts future load quantiles over multiple time horizons.

Loss function
The paper uses the pinball loss as the core optimization and evaluation objective for probabilistic forecasts. This is a standard and defensible choice for quantile prediction.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#data-splitting-strategy
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#data-splitting-strategy
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
3.2 Data splitting strategy
A slightly unusual but important part of the methodology is the dataset partitioning: - one half is used to train/validate the base models, - the other half is split into: - an ensemble training set (S), and - a final evaluation set (E).
So the workflow is:

Train multiple base forecasting models,
collect their predictions on the ensemble-training subset,
train the ensemble combiner on those predictions,
evaluate the final ensemble on a held-out test subset.

This is conceptually clean because it avoids training the meta-learner on the same data used to fit the base models.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#base-forecasting-models
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#base-forecasting-models
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
3.3 Base forecasting models
The ensemble is built from four model families:

1. FCDNN
A fully connected deep neural network trained with pinball loss plus regularization.


2. LSTM
A recurrent neural model intended to capture temporal dependencies in load time series.


3. RFQR
Random Forest Quantile Regression, which derives predictive quantiles from the distribution of tree outputs.


4. LightGBM
A gradient-boosted tree model adapted for the forecasting task.


Why this model set matters
This is a reasonably diverse base-model library: - neural networks for flexible nonlinear function approximation, - LSTM for temporal dependence, - tree ensembles for structured nonlinearities and robustness.
That diversity is exactly what makes ensemble learning potentially useful.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#conventional-ensembles-they-compare-against
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#conventional-ensembles-they-compare-against
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
3.4 Conventional ensembles they compare against
They benchmark the learning ensemble against four conventional combination rules:

MVE: Mean Value Ensemble
MdVE: Median Value Ensemble
WAE: Weighted Average Ensemble
QR: Quantile Regression ensemble

This comparison is important because the paper is not asking whether ensembles help at all. It is asking whether learned nonlinear combination helps more than standard linear aggregation.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#their-proposed-learning-ensemble
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#their-proposed-learning-ensemble
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
3.5 Their proposed learning ensemble
The proposed learning ensemble takes the outputs of all trained base models as inputs and learns a nonlinear mapping:

base predictions go in,
final probabilistic forecast comes out,
training is performed by minimizing pinball loss on the ensemble-training set.

They test three neural meta-learners for this role: - DNN - LSTM - CNN
So the paper is really about stacked nonlinear probabilistic forecasting, with a neural combiner on top of heterogeneous base predictors.

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#theoretical-contribution
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#theoretical-contribution
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
4. Theoretical Contribution
This is the most distinctive part of the paper.

4.1 Critique of linear ensembles
The authors derive expressions for the mean and variance of the error of a linear ensemble. They then show that the expected pinball loss of a linear ensemble remains strictly larger than zero, which they interpret as evidence of a systematic approximation gap between a linear ensemble and the true forecasting function.


4.2 Approximation argument for nonlinear ensemble
They then argue that a neural network can approximate the ideal nonlinear mapping from base predictions to the true target arbitrarily well under certain assumptions, including: - the existence of an injective Lipschitz-continuous mapping from base predictions to the true output, - and enough model capacity.
They first show this for a simple two-layer network, then extend it to a deeper multi-model setting.


Why this matters
Whether or not one accepts every assumption literally, the theoretical message is clear:

linear combination is fundamentally restrictive, while nonlinear learned combination is expressive enough to approximate a much richer class of mappings.

That is the real conceptual backbone of the paper.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#shapley-value-component
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#shapley-value-component
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
5. Shapley Value Component
A second important contribution is the Shapley value-based evaluation of base-model contributions.

What they do
For each subset of candidate forecasting models, they: 1. train the corresponding ensemble, 2. evaluate its pinball loss, 3. compute marginal contributions across coalitions, 4. aggregate those marginal contributions into Shapley values.


Why this is useful
This is not feature attribution in the usual SHAP sense. Instead, it is model-level contribution attribution: - Which base forecasters are most useful to the ensemble? - Which ones actually reduce loss meaningfully? - Which ones are mostly redundant?
This is a useful perspective because it helps interpret the ensemble architecture itself, not only the forecasted outputs.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#experimental-setup
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#experimental-setup
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text: 6. Experimental Setup

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#dataset-testbed
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#dataset-testbed
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
6.1 Dataset / testbed
The study uses aggregated load data from a coastal industrial city in Guangdong, China, with 5-minute resolution data from January 2019 to June 2022.

Inputs
The input features include: - previous two days of 5-minute load history, - day type, - date information, - future temperature, - future apparent temperature.


Outputs
The model predicts probabilistic forecasts at quantiles: - 20% - 50% - 80%
for horizons: - 1 hour - 3 hours - 6 hours - 12 hours - 24 hours
This is a genuinely high-resolution setting, and the multi-horizon design makes the evaluation more convincing.

href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#training-details
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
6.2 Training details
For the meta-learners, the paper uses: - random search for hyperparameters, - Adam optimizer, - early stopping, - ReLU as the general activation function.
This is standard and reasonable, although not especially exhaustive.

href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#key-results

text: 7. Key Results

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#single-model-performance
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#single-model-performance
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
7.1 Single-model performance
Among the 40 single models tested, FCDNN and LSTM perform significantly better than LightGBM and RFQR overall. Performance worsens as the forecast horizon increases, which is exactly what one would expect.
An interesting observation is that the deep learning models are more sensitive to hyperparameter choices than the more conventional tree-based models.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#ensemble-performance
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#ensemble-performance
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
7.2 Ensemble performance
This is where the paper’s main claim is supported.

Compared with the average single model
Even simple mean ensembling improves over the average single model by more than 20%.


Compared with conventional ensemble methods
The learning ensemble methods outperform all four conventional linear ensemble approaches across all forecast windows.


Best-performing meta-ensembles
The strongest performance comes from: - LE (DNN) - LE (LSTM)
The DNN-based learning ensemble can achieve improvements approaching 50% relative to the average single model.


Compared with the best single model
This is the more meaningful comparison. Conventional ensemble methods sometimes fail to improve over the best single model. In contrast, the learning ensemble still shows 10%–20% gains.
This is probably the most practically relevant empirical result in the paper.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#robustness-checks
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#robustness-checks
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
7.3 Robustness checks
The authors shuffle the dataset five times to produce different training/validation/ensemble/evaluation splits. The learning ensemble maintains similar performance across these shuffled datasets.
This is not a very deep robustness test, but it does at least suggest that the gains are not due to one lucky split.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#temporal-behavior
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#temporal-behavior
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
7.4 Temporal behavior
In their week-long visualization, the probabilistic forecasts track the real load closely. The paper notes that: - 1-hour forecasts have small average loss but larger fluctuation, - and larger forecast errors tend to occur from 13:00 to 20:00.
This kind of time-localized error analysis is useful because it hints at structural difficulty in certain daily operating periods.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#shapley-results
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#shapley-results
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
7.5 Shapley results
The Shapley-value analysis shows: - FCDNN and LSTM contribute much more than LightGBM and RFQR, - their contributions increase with forecasting difficulty, - and together they account for more than 70% of the total contribution share.
This aligns with the single-model results and adds internal consistency to the study.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#strengths-of-the-paper
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#strengths-of-the-paper
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
8. Strengths of the Paper

Strength 1: Clear problem framing
The paper is very clear about the gap it wants to fill: existing probabilistic ensembles are mostly linear, and that may be too restrictive.


Strength 2: Theoretical + empirical integration
Many forecasting papers are either theoretical or empirical. This one tries to do both: - formalize why linear ensembles are limited, - then validate the nonlinear alternative experimentally.


Strength 3: Strong experimental comparisons within the chosen framing
The comparisons against MVE, MdVE, WAE, and QR are fair and directly tied to the paper’s stated research question.


Strength 4: Model-level interpretability
The Shapley-value analysis is a nice addition because it helps explain why the ensemble works, not only whether it works.


Strength 5: Multi-horizon, high-resolution setting
Testing at 1h, 3h, 6h, 12h, and 24h horizons with 5-minute load data gives the study practical depth.
