objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#criticism-1-the-theory-depends-on-strong-assumptions
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#criticism-1-the-theory-depends-on-strong-assumptions
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
section: Criticism 1: The theory depends on strong assumptions
text:
Criticism 1: The theory depends on strong assumptions
The theoretical superiority of the nonlinear ensemble depends on assumptions like the existence of an injective Lipschitz mapping from base-model predictions to the true target. That is mathematically useful, but in practice it is a strong assumption.
This means the theory is best interpreted as an expressivity argument, not a guarantee that the proposed approach will always achieve near-zero pinball loss in real data.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#criticism-2-can-approach-zero-is-not-the-same-as-will-train-well
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#criticism-2-can-approach-zero-is-not-the-same-as-will-train-well
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
section: Criticism 2: “Can approach zero” is not the same as “will train well”
text:
Criticism 2: “Can approach zero” is not the same as “will train well”
The paper is careful in places, but the overall tone could make readers overestimate the practical implications of the approximation theorems. Real neural training is: - non-convex, - data-limited, - sensitive to hyperparameters, - and prone to optimization failure.
So the theory supports the possibility of superior nonlinear combination, not necessarily its routine attainment.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#criticism-3-the-evaluation-is-narrow-in-terms-of-uncertainty-quality
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#criticism-3-the-evaluation-is-narrow-in-terms-of-uncertainty-quality
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
section: Criticism 3: The evaluation is narrow in terms of uncertainty quality
text:
Criticism 3: The evaluation is narrow in terms of uncertainty quality
The paper focuses almost entirely on pinball loss. That is appropriate for quantile forecasting, but still somewhat narrow.
It does not deeply assess: - calibration quality across many quantile levels, - sharpness-vs-calibration tradeoff beyond pinball loss, - interval coverage diagnostics, - or full distributional consistency.
Because they only forecast the 20%, 50%, and 80% quantiles, the uncertainty representation is also fairly sparse.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#criticism-4-limited-comparison-to-more-modern-probabilistic-deep-baselines
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#criticism-4-limited-comparison-to-more-modern-probabilistic-deep-baselines
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
section: Criticism 4: Limited comparison to more modern probabilistic deep baselines
text:
Criticism 4: Limited comparison to more modern probabilistic deep baselines
The base model set is useful, but the benchmark space is still limited. The paper does not compare against stronger end-to-end probabilistic deep learning baselines such as: - modern quantile sequence models, - conformal methods, - mixture density models, - deep state-space approaches, - or transformer-style probabilistic forecasters.
So the claim is strongest within the ensemble-combination setting they define, not necessarily against the current full frontier of probabilistic forecasting.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#criticism-5-interpretation-is-at-the-model-level-not-the-feature-level
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#criticism-5-interpretation-is-at-the-model-level-not-the-feature-level
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
section: Criticism 5: Interpretation is at the model level, not the feature level
text:
Criticism 5: Interpretation is at the model level, not the feature level
The Shapley analysis explains which base models matter most, but not: - which input variables drive uncertainty, - which temporal patterns are most influential, - or how external weather variables affect different horizons.
So this is useful interpretability, but it is not the same as the richer feature-level XAI used in SHAP-style forecasting papers.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#criticism-6-computational-scalability-of-shapley-analysis-may-become-painful
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#criticism-6-computational-scalability-of-shapley-analysis-may-become-painful
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
section: Criticism 6: Computational scalability of Shapley analysis may become painful
text:
Criticism 6: Computational scalability of Shapley analysis may become painful
For only four selected model types, enumerating all subsets is manageable. But exact Shapley computation scales poorly as the number of candidate models grows.
So the method is elegant for a small library of base models, but may become cumbersome for larger ensemble pools unless approximation methods are used.

href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#criticism-7-generalization-evidence-is-still-geographically-narrow
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
section: Criticism 7: Generalization evidence is still geographically narrow
text:
Criticism 7: Generalization evidence is still geographically narrow
The study uses one city-level dataset from Guangdong. It is a meaningful real-world dataset, but still only one operating environment.
So the paper demonstrates that the method works well here, but not yet that it transfers robustly across: - different climates, - residential vs industrial systems, - national-scale demand, - markets with stronger weather volatility, - or different calendar/load behaviors.

href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#what-i-would-take-forward-from-this-paper
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
section: 10. What I Would Take Forward From This Paper
text:
10. What I Would Take Forward From This Paper

Research takeaway 1
A nonlinear meta-learner on top of diverse probabilistic forecasters is a serious benchmark and should not be ignored.


Research takeaway 2
If I am comparing forecasting pipelines, I should distinguish clearly between: - single-model improvement, and - combination-rule improvement.
This paper is primarily about the second.


Research takeaway 3
Model-level Shapley analysis is a useful way to justify which base learners are worth keeping in an ensemble.


Research takeaway 4
There is room to extend this framework by adding stronger uncertainty diagnostics and richer probabilistic baselines.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#action-items-integration
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#action-items-integration
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
11. Action Items & Integration

Consider using a nonlinear stacking ensemble as a benchmark in my own probabilistic forecasting work, especially when I already have heterogeneous base learners.
When reviewing this paper in a literature review, position it as a nonlinear probabilistic ensemble paper rather than a general “XAI forecasting” paper.
Note that its interpretability contribution is model-contribution attribution, not feature-level explanation.
If I build on this idea, add stronger uncertainty-quality diagnostics such as coverage, calibration curves, interval scores, CRPS, or conformal validity checks.
Treat the theoretical claims as capacity and approximation arguments, not as practical guarantees.
Use this paper to justify that linear ensemble rules may be too restrictive for probabilistic forecasting, especially in high-resolution settings.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

objectID: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#bottom-line-summary
href: reviews/High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting.html#bottom-line-summary
title: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach
text:
12. Bottom-Line Summary
This is a strong and well-structured paper whose main message is simple but important:

In probabilistic load forecasting, it is not enough to have many good base models.
The rule used to combine them matters, and a learned nonlinear ensemble can outperform standard linear combination methods.

Its best contribution is the combination of: - a clear ensemble-learning argument, - a formal theoretical justification, - and a Shapley-based analysis of model contribution.
Its main weaknesses are: - strong theoretical assumptions, - limited uncertainty evaluation breadth, - and a benchmark space that does not fully cover newer probabilistic deep learning alternatives.
Overall, this is a worthwhile paper and a solid citation if I need support for: - nonlinear ensemble learning, - probabilistic load forecasting, - or Shapley-based attribution of base-model contributions in ensemble systems.
crumbs: High-resolution probabilistic load forecasting: A learning ensemble approach

title: Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression
text:
Authors & Year: Ilias Chronopoulos, Aristeidis Raftapostolos, and George Kapetanios (2024 journal version; advance access 2023)
Venue (Journal/Conference): Journal of Financial Econometrics
DOI: 10.1093/jjfinec/nbad014
Primary Topic: Deep neural network quantile regression for non-linear VaR forecasting
Secondary Topics: Mixed-frequency modeling, MIDAS, Monte Carlo validation, interpretability of quantile neural networks, SHAP, partial derivatives
Code/Data Available?: Not emphasized in the core paper text I reviewed
Proximity/Threat Level: Medium to High, especially if my work involves deep quantile forecasting, explainability, or benchmarking non-linear quantile models
Date Reviewed: 2026-03-13
crumbs: Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression

objectID: reviews/Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why Quantiles / Why VaR?)

The paper starts from the classical argument that mean regression is often inadequate when the real interest is in the conditional tails of a distribution.
In finance, this matters because risk management is fundamentally about downside extremes rather than average behavior.
Value-at-Risk (VaR) is directly linked to conditional quantiles of returns, so a quantile regression framework is a natural modeling choice.
The authors argue that standard linear quantile regression may be too restrictive for financial markets, where relationships between returns and predictors are often non-linear, asymmetric, and unstable over time.



The Motivation (Why Deep Learning?)

The central justification is that feed-forward neural networks have strong universal approximation properties, so they can approximate highly non-linear conditional quantile functions much more flexibly than linear or low-order sieve approaches.
They position neural networks not just as generic predictors, but as a way to estimate a conditional quantile function directly through the quantile loss.



The Motivation (Why Explainability?)

The authors explicitly acknowledge the “black-box” criticism of neural networks.
Their response is not merely to forecast better, but also to make the neural quantile model more interpretable through:

SHAP values, and
partial derivatives of the fitted network output with respect to inputs.

This is important because in risk forecasting, users want to know not only what the VaR forecast is, but also why it changed.



Their claim to fame / Novelty

They propose a deep quantile estimator that directly models non-linear conditional quantiles via feed-forward neural networks.
They extend the setup to allow mixed-frequency inputs through a MIDAS-style architecture.
They also contribute to explainable ML in finance by comparing SHAP with partial-derivative-based interpretation.
The paper frames itself as, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, the first finance application using a neural network quantile estimator specifically for VaR forecasting.



Their ultimate result

The deep quantile estimator outperforms linear quantile, MIDAS, and other non-parametric quantile competitors in their VaR forecasting exercise.
They report predictive gains of up to 98% relative to the linear quantile benchmark, and up to 84% for the non-linear MIDAS model, depending on the setup.
Their interpretability comparison also concludes that partial derivatives are more stable and much cheaper computationally than SHAP, while still being informative.
crumbs: Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression

objectID: reviews/Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression.html#methodology-technical-details
href: reviews/Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression.html#methodology-technical-details
title: Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

Core modeling idea

Standard quantile regression estimates the conditional quantile by minimizing the pinball / check loss.
The authors replace the linear predictor (x_t^()) with a neural network (G_(x_t; w)), yielding a non-linear quantile regression estimator: [ Q_y(x_t) = G_(x_t; w) ]
The model is trained by minimizing the quantile loss over the neural network parameters.



Network structure

They focus on feed-forward neural networks.
Hidden layers use ReLU activations.
The output layer is linear.
They frame the model as ranging from relatively parametric to more non-parametric depending on network width/depth.



Regularization
To control overfitting, they consider: - No regularization - Deep LASSO - Deep Ridge - Deep Elastic Net
This is a strong part of the paper because they do not present “deep learning” as a single monolithic model; they explicitly examine how different penalties affect finite-sample behavior and forecast quality.


Hyperparameter tuning
They use a time-series cross-validation framework rather than random CV, which is the correct choice for dependent data.
Tuned components include: - number of hidden layers - number of neurons - learning rate - batch size - dropout - regularization strength - Elastic Net mixing parameter - MIDAS polynomial parameters for mixed-frequency models


Optimization

They use ADAM
Maximum epochs: 5000
Early stopping is used to reduce overfitting

objectID: reviews/Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression.html#monte-carlo-design-what-it-actually-shows
href: reviews/Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression.html#monte-carlo-design-what-it-actually-shows
title: Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression
section: 4. Monte Carlo Design & What It Actually Shows
text:
4. Monte Carlo Design & What It Actually Shows

Why the Monte Carlo section matters
This is one of the more valuable parts of the paper.
The authors do not jump straight to empirical finance results. They first ask whether the proposed deep quantile estimator behaves sensibly in controlled settings.


Monte Carlo setup
They study finite-sample performance over: - quantiles ( {1%, 2.5%, 5%, 10%, 20%} ) - sample sizes ( T {100, 300, 500, 1000} ) - 1000 replications
They compare: - deep quantile - deep LASSO - deep Ridge - deep Elastic Net - shallow counterparts - linear quantile regression - polynomial quantile regression - spline-based quantile regression


Simulation cases
They test five settings: 1. Simple non-linear sinusoidal function with i.i.d. Gaussian regressor 2. AR(1) regressor 3. GARCH-type regressor 4. A function generated from a neural-network-like composition 5. Serially correlated errors


What they find

Both shallow and deep neural quantile estimators generally show good finite-sample performance
Shallow networks often outperform deeper ones in the simulation study
Linear quantile regression fails badly when the true quantile function is non-linear
Polynomial and spline alternatives also generally underperform in these non-linear settings
Penalization is often helpful, especially in more difficult settings and extreme quantiles



My interpretation of this section
This Monte Carlo exercise gives the paper real methodological credibility.
It is not merely “deep learning won on one dataset.” The authors show that the model class itself is able to recover non-linear quantile functions under several stylized but meaningful data-generating processes.
That said, the simulations are still relatively low-dimensional and controlled. They do not stress-test the method under severe regime change, covariate shift, heavy tails beyond Gaussian innovations, or highly multivariate predictor spaces of the kind now common in financial ML.
crumbs: Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression

objectID: reviews/Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression.html#empirical-application-var-forecasting-setup
href: reviews/Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression.html#empirical-application-var-forecasting-setup
title: Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression
text:
5. Empirical Application: VaR Forecasting Setup

Target problem

Forecast 10-day-ahead VaR using daily data
U.S. stock return losses over a long historical sample
Sample period discussed in the paper: September 1985 to August 2020



Out-of-sample design

Last 2000 observations reserved for out-of-sample evaluation
Remaining 7053 observations used for tuning and estimation
This split is chosen partly to make the conditional quantile forecast encompassing results comparable with earlier literature



Quantiles forecasted

( = 1%, 5%, 10% )



VaR model classes used as inputs / structures
They examine four VaR specifications: 1. GARCH(1,1)-style VaR 2. RiskMetrics 3. CAViaR symmetric absolute value (SV) 4. CAViaR asymmetric slope (ASV)
Then they build: - linear quantile versions - MIDAS versions - non-linear deep quantile versions - non-linear deep MIDAS versions


What is important here
This is not a totally unconstrained “throw raw data into a neural net” paper.
The authors still organize the forecasting problem around well-known VaR structures from the econometrics literature. In that sense, the paper is trying to bridge: - classical risk econometrics, and - modern non-linear function approximation.
That makes it much stronger than a purely black-box finance paper.
crumbs: Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression

objectID: reviews/Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression.html#validation-strategy-predictions-explanations
href: reviews/Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression.html#validation-strategy-predictions-explanations
title: Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression
text:
6. Validation Strategy (Predictions & Explanations)

Validating the predictions
They use several forecast-comparison tools: - Diebold–Mariano (DM) test - Giacomini–White (GW) test - quantile score test - conditional quantile forecast encompassing test (Giacomini and Komunjer framework)


What they conclude from these tests

The deep quantile estimator generally has higher forecasting accuracy
It often encompasses competing forecasts more often than the reverse
In some cases, the encompassing tests are inconclusive, suggesting that forecast combinations may outperform any single model



Validating the explanations
This is much less rigorous.
They compare: - SHAP values - partial derivatives
And judge them on: - interpretability - stability over time - computational cost - ability to reflect known stress periods like the 2008 financial crisis and COVID-19
This is useful, but it is still mostly qualitative validation rather than a formal XAI evaluation framework.
crumbs: Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression

objectID: reviews/Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression.html#explainability-contribution-what-did-xai-actually-do
href: reviews/Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression.html#explainability-contribution-what-did-xai-actually-do
title: Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression
section: 7. Explainability Contribution: What Did XAI Actually Do?
text:
7. Explainability Contribution: What Did XAI Actually Do?

Their two interpretation tools

SHAP values

Used as a standard post-hoc feature attribution framework

Partial derivatives

Used to examine marginal sensitivity of the predicted quantile to each input




Their main interpretability findings

Partial derivatives are more stable over time
Partial derivatives are far cheaper computationally than SHAP
The derivative-based interpretation fluctuates around the linear quantile estimate and can capture time variation linked to major market stress events



Why this matters
This is an interesting contribution because most finance explainability papers default to SHAP and stop there.
These authors ask whether a simpler structural sensitivity measure may actually be more practical.


My interpretation
The paper’s most interesting XAI insight is not that SHAP works, but that SHAP may not be the most useful interpretability tool in this setting.
For continuously differentiable models, partial derivatives can provide: - a faster, - more stable, - more directly sensitivity-based view of model behavior.
That is a very useful takeaway for any forecasting paper where interpretability has to be repeated over many rolling windows or over long historical horizons.
crumbs: Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression

objectID: reviews/Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression.html#main-strengths-of-the-paper
href: reviews/Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression.html#main-strengths-of-the-paper
title: Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression
text:
8. Main Strengths of the Paper

Strength 1: It is methodologically balanced
The paper combines: - theory motivation, - simulation evidence, - empirical forecasting, - and interpretability.
That gives it a more complete arc than many ML-for-finance papers.


Strength 2: It respects time-series structure
Their use of: - time-series cross-validation, - proper out-of-sample design, - formal forecast comparison tests, makes the work much stronger than papers that only report in-sample fit or random train/test splits.


Strength 3: It benchmarks against econometric baselines
The authors do not compare only against strawman mean models.
They include: - linear quantile models, - MIDAS variants, - CAViaR-type structures, - and non-parametric alternatives.


Strength 4: It gives an actual interpretability discussion
Even if not fully rigorous, the paper takes the interpretability problem seriously and tests two different tools rather than treating explainability as an afterthought.


Strength 5: It explicitly studies regularization
The paper acknowledges that neural quantile estimators can overfit, and it studies how penalties change performance. That is a mature methodological move.

title: Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression
text:
9. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: The paper still uses a fairly narrow input structure
Although the authors motivate high-dimensional flexibility, the actual VaR specifications remain relatively low-dimensional and structurally tied to traditional VaR equations.
This is not necessarily bad, but it means the paper does not fully demonstrate how the method behaves in genuinely high-dimensional financial forecasting environments with many covariates, macro variables, realized measures, order-book features, or alternative data.


Criticism 2: The interpretability evaluation is still mostly qualitative
The comparison between SHAP and partial derivatives is interesting, but it is not validated with: - faithfulness metrics, - stability metrics, - perturbation tests, - agreement under resampling, - or formal sensitivity benchmarks.
So while the conclusion that partial derivatives are “better” is plausible and practically useful, it is not fully established in a rigorous XAI-evaluation sense.


Criticism 3: The forecasting victory may partly reflect flexible function approximation rather than a uniquely finance-specific insight
The deep quantile model wins because it can represent non-linear conditional quantiles better than linear models.
That is a valid result, but it is also somewhat unsurprising.
The paper is stronger as a demonstration of the value of non-linear quantile function estimation than as a finance-theory breakthrough.


Criticism 4: The deep-vs-shallow message is awkward
In Monte Carlo, shallow models often look better than deeper ones, yet the paper is framed around “deep” quantile regression. That does not invalidate the work, but it does weaken any simplistic narrative that more depth is inherently better.


Criticism 5: No broader uncertainty discussion beyond quantiles
This paper is about quantile forecasting, not full probabilistic density estimation.
That is fine, but it means it does not engage with: - calibration of full predictive distributions, - tail dependence structures, - extreme value theory integration, - or whether the estimated quantiles remain coherent across levels.


Criticism 6: Potential monotonicity / quantile crossing issues are not the main focus
Whenever multiple quantiles are estimated, one wants to know whether the resulting quantile curves are coherent and non-crossing.
This paper does not foreground that issue as a central methodological challenge.


Criticism 7: The benchmark set is respectable, but not modern by 2026 standards
For historical context the benchmark suite is reasonable.
But by current standards, one would also want comparisons against: - quantile gradient boosting, - quantile random forests, - distributional boosting, - modern sequence models, - conformalized quantile methods, - and perhaps heavy-tail parametric or semi-parametric baselines.

The most useful takeaway may actually be the partial-derivative vs SHAP comparison.
That gives me a strong precedent for arguing that: - SHAP is not the only route to explainability, - and in some forecasting settings, derivative-based explanations may be more stable and computationally realistic.


If my work is on energy forecasting rather than finance
Even though the domain is financial VaR, the methodological structure is transferable: - tail-focused forecasting, - quantile loss, - neural non-linearity, - time-series CV, - benchmarking against linear and structured baselines, - and interpretability of conditional quantile dynamics.
This is especially relevant if I want to forecast: - reserve requirements, - net-load risk, - renewable underproduction risk, - demand peaks, - or other lower/upper tail events.

As a bridge paper
It is best positioned as a bridge between: - classical econometric quantile/VaR methods, and - modern ML non-linear function approximation.

text:
14. Bottom-Line Review
This is a strong and thoughtful paper that does more than just apply a neural network to a finance problem.
Its main contribution is to show that direct neural quantile estimation can materially improve VaR forecasting when the conditional quantile function is non-linear, and that this can be studied in a reasonably disciplined way through simulation, out-of-sample testing, and interpretability analysis.
Its most interesting conceptual contribution is not merely “deep learning beats linear models,” but rather: 1. conditional quantiles are often non-linear,
2. neural networks provide a practical estimator for them, and
3. partial-derivative-based explanations may be a more stable alternative to SHAP in this context.
The paper’s main weaknesses are that the interpretability validation remains mostly qualitative, the input space is not especially high-dimensional in practice, and the benchmark set, while solid, is no longer exhaustive by modern standards.
Still, as a literature-review source, it is highly useful and deserves to be treated as an important reference for any research sitting at the intersection of: - quantile forecasting, - tail-risk prediction, - neural non-linear regression, - and explainable probabilistic modeling.

Venue (Journal/Conference): Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (PMLR 266), Conformal and Probabilistic Prediction with Applications
Primary Topic: Interpreting conformal classification outputs using SHAP
Core Methods: Class-conditional conformal prediction, Random Forest, Tree SHAP
Application Domain: Benchmark classification datasets (Iris, Wisconsin Breast Cancer, Pima Diabetes)
Code/Data Available?: Not emphasized as a core contribution in the paper

objectID: reviews/Explaining Set-Valued Predictions.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/Explaining Set-Valued Predictions.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: Explaining Set-Valued Predictions: SHAP Analysis for Conformal Classification
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why Conformal Prediction?):

Standard classifiers usually return a single label, and probabilistic models return normalized probabilities, but neither necessarily communicates uncertainty in a cautious, decision-support-oriented way.
Conformal classification instead outputs a prediction set with formal error control, allowing the model to say that multiple labels are plausible, or in rare cases that no label is plausible enough.

The Motivation (Why Explainability?):

Even though conformal predictors provide stronger uncertainty quantification than ordinary classifiers, their outputs can still be hard for users to interpret, especially when the prediction set is non-trivial, such as:

multiple labels included,
a surprising label excluded,
or an empty prediction set.

The authors argue that practical usefulness depends not only on calibrated uncertainty, but also on understanding why labels were included or rejected.

Their claim to fame / Novelty:

The paper argues that previous work mostly used conformal methods to quantify uncertainty in explanations, not to explain conformal predictions themselves.
Their key novelty is to apply SHAP directly to class-wise conformal p-values, treating each p-value as an explainable output.
This creates class-specific, asymmetric explanations, which is a major departure from ordinary probabilistic classifiers where class probabilities are coupled by the sum-to-one constraint.

The central conceptual contribution:

SHAP is not limited to explaining raw model scores.
By defining different target functions, the same SHAP framework can explain:

class-wise p-values,
class inclusion or exclusion,
the full prediction set,
confidence,
credibility.


The value derived from explainability (What did XAI actually do?):

It reveals why specific labels are included or excluded from the conformal set.
It allows the analyst to identify ambiguity, atypicality, and possible out-of-distribution-like behavior.
It provides both local explanations for individual uncertain predictions and global explanations of how features influence class-wise conformal behavior across the dataset.
It gives a more faithful picture of uncertainty reasoning than standard softmax explanations, because each class p-value is explained independently.

Their ultimate result:

The paper is a proof-of-concept, not a benchmarking paper focused on predictive superiority.
Its main result is conceptual and interpretive: SHAP-enhanced conformal classification can make set-valued predictions much more transparent and decision-useful.
crumbs: Explaining Set-Valued Predictions: SHAP Analysis for Conformal Classification

objectID: reviews/Explaining Set-Valued Predictions.html#methodology-technical-details
href: reviews/Explaining Set-Valued Predictions.html#methodology-technical-details
title: Explaining Set-Valued Predictions: SHAP Analysis for Conformal Classification
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

3.1 Overall framework
The paper combines: 1. an underlying classifier, 2. class-conditional conformal calibration, 3. SHAP explanations applied to conformal outputs.
The base learner is a Random Forest classifier with 300 trees, and explanations are computed using Tree SHAP.


3.2 Conformal classification setup

The study uses inductive conformal prediction (ICP).
A trained classifier first produces class probabilities.
These probabilities are transformed into nonconformity scores using a hinge-loss-style definition: [ = 1 - _h( x_i) ]
For each candidate label, a conformal p-value is computed by comparing the test nonconformity score against calibration nonconformity scores.
Labels with ( p_y(x) < ) are rejected, and the remaining labels form the prediction set.



3.3 Class-conditional calibration

The conformal predictors are calibrated in a class-conditional manner.
That matters because it provides more label-aware validity and makes the p-values especially suitable for class-wise interpretation.



3.4 Confidence and credibility
The study also emphasizes two derived conformal quantities:

Credibility:

the largest p-value across all labels,
interpreted as how well the instance conforms to the most plausible class.

Confidence:

one minus the second-largest p-value,
interpreted as how decisively the most plausible class stands apart from the runner-up.


This distinction is important: - a prediction can be confident but not credible, meaning the model is decisive, but the instance is still atypical; - or credible but not confident, meaning multiple classes look plausible.


3.5 What exactly is explained with SHAP?
The strongest methodological point in the paper is that the object being explained is determined by the prediction function passed into SHAP.
Their main choice is: - for each class ( y ), define ( f_y(x) = p_y(x) )
This lets SHAP explain how each feature pushes a class’s conformal p-value up or down.
They then outline four additional explainable targets:

Class inclusion
[ f_y(x) = [p_y(x) > ] ] Explains why a class crossed the inclusion threshold.
Full prediction set as structured output
Encodes the entire set of included labels and explains why that set was returned.
Confidence
Explains why the model is decisive or indecisive.
Credibility
Explains why an instance is typical or atypical relative to calibration data.



3.6 Datasets / Testbed
The experiments use three standard benchmark datasets:

Iris
Wisconsin Breast Cancer
Pima Indian Diabetes

These were likely chosen because: - the features are understandable, - the problems are familiar, - and local explanations are easy to narrate.


3.7 Train / calibration / test split
The paper uses a simple stratified hold-out split: - 60% training - 30% calibration - 10% testing
This is important because the work is positioned as a demonstration study, not a large-scale statistical evaluation.

objectID: reviews/Explaining Set-Valued Predictions.html#validation-strategy-predictions-explanations
href: reviews/Explaining Set-Valued Predictions.html#validation-strategy-predictions-explanations
title: Explaining Set-Valued Predictions: SHAP Analysis for Conformal Classification
text:
4. Validation Strategy (Predictions & Explanations)

4.1 Validating the predictions
The paper does not primarily validate predictive performance against a strong set of SOTA baselines. Instead, the focus is on: - constructing conformal predictors correctly, - showing realistic conformal outputs, - and demonstrating how SHAP can interpret them.
So this is more of an interpretability-method paper than a predictive benchmarking paper.


4.2 Validating the explanations
The explanations are validated mainly through: - qualitative consistency checks, - dataset semantics, - and human interpretability.
Examples include: - In Iris, petal width and petal length behave in ways consistent with known class geometry. - In Breast Cancer, high-risk cellular features support malignancy while also revealing more nuanced effects on credibility. - In Diabetes, the explanations reveal that a case can still be uncertain even when confidence might initially look moderately high.


4.3 Local and global explanation modes
The study uses: - waterfall plots for local explanations, - beeswarm plots for global explanations.
This is a good design choice because the method aims to explain both: - why a particular instance produced a certain set-valued prediction, - and how features generally influence conformal p-values across the population.
crumbs: Explaining Set-Valued Predictions: SHAP Analysis for Conformal Classification

objectID: reviews/Explaining Set-Valued Predictions.html#main-findings-interpretive-insights
href: reviews/Explaining Set-Valued Predictions.html#main-findings-interpretive-insights
title: Explaining Set-Valued Predictions: SHAP Analysis for Conformal Classification
text:
5. Main Findings & Interpretive Insights

5.1 Explaining p-values is richer than explaining probabilities
A central insight is that explaining class-wise conformal p-values gives more flexibility than explaining ordinary class probabilities.
Why? - Probabilities must sum to one. - P-values for different classes are not locked into that zero-sum structure.
That means: - the same feature can lower both classes’ plausibility, - or support one class without acting as a simple mirror image for another.
This is one of the strongest conceptual contributions in the paper.


5.2 It supports asymmetric, class-specific reasoning
In binary and multiclass settings, SHAP on p-values allows: - a separate rationale for why class A was included, - and a different rationale for why class B was excluded.
That is especially valuable in high-stakes settings like diagnosis or triage, where the reason a dangerous class was rejected may matter just as much as the reason another class was selected.


5.3 It helps interpret ambiguous predictions
The framework is particularly useful when: - multiple labels remain in the prediction set, - credibility is low, - or the instance looks atypical.
The method helps make uncertainty diagnostic, not just descriptive.


5.4 It may help flag out-of-distribution-like cases
The authors explicitly note that empty prediction sets or very low credibility can indicate: - out-of-distribution behavior, - extreme uncertainty, - or corrupted/unusual inputs.
Their SHAP framework then offers a way to inspect which features caused that breakdown in conformity.


5.5 Threshold-aware explanations are different from p-value explanations
One subtle and useful insight appears in the explanation of set inclusion: - a feature that lowers a p-value can still have a positive contribution to inclusion if the class remains above the threshold.
This is an important distinction. It means the semantics of the explanation change depending on the target: - explaining the p-value, - versus explaining threshold crossing.
That is a sophisticated point, and one of the paper’s most practically useful methodological clarifications.
crumbs: Explaining Set-Valued Predictions: SHAP Analysis for Conformal Classification

objectID: reviews/Explaining Set-Valued Predictions.html#dataset-specific-results
href: reviews/Explaining Set-Valued Predictions.html#dataset-specific-results
title: Explaining Set-Valued Predictions: SHAP Analysis for Conformal Classification
text:
6. Dataset-Specific Results

6.1 Iris

The method shows that SHAP explanations align well with known Iris class structure.
In one case, Virginica receives a high conformal p-value and strong confidence/credibility, with petal width, petal length, and sepal length supporting the result.
In another case, the conformal predictor shifts the prediction from Versicolor to Virginica, and SHAP explains why the p-values justify that change.
The global beeswarm plot shows class-specific patterns that match known geometry of the dataset.

Why this matters:
It demonstrates that the method is not merely mathematically possible, but also semantically sensible.


6.2 Wisconsin Breast Cancer

A malignant case receives high confidence but lower credibility.
SHAP shows that some features strongly support exclusion of the benign class.
At the same time, for the malignant class, some features raise the p-value while others lower it.
The credibility explanation highlights that some features make the case somewhat atypical relative to calibration data.
The set inclusion explanation shows how threshold-based explanations differ from raw p-value explanations.

Why this matters:
This is probably the cleanest demonstration that the framework can separate: - plausibility of a class, - atypicality of the instance, - and threshold-based inclusion logic.


6.3 Pima Diabetes

The base classifier leans toward Non-Diabetic, but conformal calibration shifts the output toward Diabetic, which is correct.
However, neither class can be strongly rejected at modest significance thresholds, so the case is genuinely uncertain.
SHAP reveals which features reduce or increase the p-values for each class.
The confidence explanation shows that even a confidence value that looks decent in isolation can still represent substantial uncertainty relative to the rest of the dataset.
The full set explanation shows why the returned prediction set contains both labels.

Why this matters:
This is a strong example of conformal prediction correcting or reframing a conventional classifier output, while SHAP explains the resulting uncertainty structure.
crumbs: Explaining Set-Valued Predictions: SHAP Analysis for Conformal Classification

objectID: reviews/Explaining Set-Valued Predictions.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
href: reviews/Explaining Set-Valued Predictions.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
title: Explaining Set-Valued Predictions: SHAP Analysis for Conformal Classification
text:
7. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: This is a proof-of-concept, not a rigorous empirical benchmark
The paper is explicitly a proof-of-concept. That is fair, but it means the empirical claims should be interpreted cautiously. The method is shown to be plausible and interesting, not comprehensively validated.


Criticism 2: There is no formal evaluation of explanation quality
The paper does not use rigorous XAI evaluation criteria such as: - faithfulness, - stability, - robustness, - consistency under perturbation, - or human-centered utility studies.
That is a major gap, especially because the paper’s core contribution is interpretability.


Criticism 3: Small benchmark datasets make the examples readable but limit external validity
Iris, WBC, and Pima are pedagogically useful, but they are relatively small and familiar. This makes the examples easy to understand, but it also means the study does not yet prove that the method scales well to: - high-dimensional tabular data, - sparse features, - image or text domains, - or modern deep classifiers.


Criticism 4: Random Forest + Tree SHAP is a comfortable setting
The underlying model is a Random Forest, and the explanation engine is Tree SHAP, which is one of the most mature and convenient SHAP settings. That makes sense for a first study, but it leaves open the harder question: - how well does this framework behave with deep models, approximate explainers, or more unstable p-value structures?


Criticism 5: The method explains outputs derived from calibration, not just the base model
This is conceptually powerful, but it also complicates interpretation. SHAP is not explaining the base classifier directly; it is explaining a downstream conformal quantity. That means the explanation now blends: - model behavior, - calibration effects, - dataset structure, - and thresholding logic.
This is not a flaw, but it means practitioners may overinterpret the explanations as “why the model predicted class Y,” when the true target is subtler: “why the conformal system assigned this p-value / inclusion status / confidence / credibility.”


Criticism 6: OOD detection is suggested more than proven
The authors mention that empty sets or low credibility may support detection of out-of-distribution or anomalous cases. That is a compelling idea, but the paper does not perform a dedicated OOD experiment. So at this stage, OOD usefulness remains more of a conceptual promise than an empirically established result.


Criticism 7: The paper does not compare against other explanation strategies for conformal outputs
The paper presents SHAP as the explanation mechanism, but does not compare it against: - LIME, - Integrated Gradients, - counterfactual explanations, - prototype-based methods, - or dedicated conformal explanation techniques.
So we do not yet know whether SHAP is best, merely that it works and is flexible.
crumbs: Explaining Set-Valued Predictions: SHAP Analysis for Conformal Classification

text:
8. Research Value for My Own Work

Why this paper matters conceptually:

It strengthens the idea that uncertainty-aware model outputs themselves can be the target of explanation, not only raw model predictions.
That is highly relevant if I want to explain:

uncertainty scores,
quantile behavior,
interval inclusion,
or calibration-derived outputs in my own forecasting work.


Direct methodological takeaway:

SHAP can explain any deterministic function of the model, not just the original prediction.
That opens a major design space for explaining:

interval width,
conformal coverage decisions,
anomaly scores,
forecast sharpness,
quantile crossing corrections,
or custom uncertainty metrics.


Important conceptual insight for probabilistic forecasting:

The paper shows the value of explaining outputs that are not forced into normalized competition.
This is highly relevant if I am thinking about explaining multiple uncertainty quantities independently rather than relying only on probability-simplex outputs.

Potential relevance to my literature review:

This paper is useful for a section on:

explainability of uncertainty-aware prediction systems,
explanation of set-valued or structured outputs,
and post-hoc interpretation of conformal prediction.

title: Explaining Set-Valued Predictions: SHAP Analysis for Conformal Classification
text:
10. Final Verdict
This is a clever, original, and conceptually important paper, even though it is still an early-stage demonstration rather than a full empirical validation study.
Its biggest strength is not predictive novelty, but interpretive reframing: it shows that conformal prediction outputs, especially class-wise p-values, can be treated as first-class explainable objects.
That move is important.
Instead of merely saying: - “here is the predicted set,”
the method can now say: - “here is why this label was almost included,” - “here is why that one was excluded,” - “here is why the instance is atypical,” - and “here is why the model is uncertain.”
For anyone working on explainable uncertainty quantification, this paper is highly relevant. Its limitations are mostly about evaluation depth, scale, and empirical breadth, not about the originality of the idea itself.

title: Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model: Factoring climate predictors for accuracy and deeper insights with probabilistic confidence interval and point-based forecasts
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why this study matters)
The paper starts from a very practical power-systems problem: electricity demand is nonlinear, climate-sensitive, and inherently uncertain. Pure point forecasting is not enough for operational decision-making, because operators, aggregators, and traders also need a sense of forecast uncertainty. The authors therefore position their work around two needs: 1. Higher predictive accuracy for daily electricity demand. 2. Better uncertainty quantification and interpretability for real-world energy decision-making.
The paper explicitly argues that demand models should not only predict future load accurately, but should also quantify uncertainty and explain which factors drive those forecasts. This is framed as important for electricity market planning, grid operation, demand response, and trading.


Their claim to fame / novelty
The main novelty is the adaptation of Deeply Fused Nets (FNET), originally used in image/text domains, to a time-series electricity demand forecasting setting. The authors argue that this is the first use of this specific deep fusion idea for electricity demand forecasting, and they extend it with: - CNN + BILSTM deep fusion - Residual bootstrapping for 95% prediction intervals - SHAP analysis for explainability
So the novelty is not just “another hybrid CNN-LSTM,” but specifically a deep fusion architecture where intermediate representations from multiple branches are fused repeatedly, instead of only at the final stage. The study also adds a probabilistic layer via bootstrap intervals and an interpretability layer via SHAP.


Why the explainability part is important here
The explainability contribution is not treated as decorative. The authors use SHAP to make the model more transparent and to identify the role of lagged demand and climate predictors in the final forecast. Their results suggest that historical demand and evapotranspiration are among the most influential predictors, with SHAP also revealing interaction effects, especially between lagged demand and evapotranspiration.


Why the uncertainty part is important here
Instead of assuming a fixed parametric output distribution, the study uses bootstrap residual resampling to generate 95% prediction intervals. This is important because electricity demand is chaotic and nonstationary, and the authors explicitly argue that making strong distributional assumptions may distort risk estimates.
crumbs: Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model: Factoring climate predictors for accuracy and deeper insights with probabilistic confidence interval and point-based forecasts

text:
3.1 Dataset / testbed
The study uses electricity demand data from four substations in Southeast Queensland, Australia: - Annerley - Heathwood - Laidley - Zillmere
The raw dataset spans 01/07/2011 to 30/06/2021, with 280,560 measurements sampled at 30-minute intervals, later downsampled to daily resolution. This results in a 10-year daily forecasting problem.

objectID: reviews/Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model.html#input-variables
href: reviews/Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model.html#input-variables
title: Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model: Factoring climate predictors for accuracy and deeper insights with probabilistic confidence interval and point-based forecasts
text:
3.2 Input variables
The model does not rely on lagged demand alone. It combines historical electricity demand with 10 climate variables from the SILO database. These include: - Maximum temperature - Minimum temperature - Vapour pressure - Vapour pressure deficit - Synthetic evaporation - Solar radiation - Relative humidity at maximum temperature - Relative humidity at minimum temperature - Evapotranspiration - Mean sea level pressure
The lag structure is chosen using PACF and Mutual Information Function (MIF) analysis. The chosen lag depths differ by substation: - Annerley: 4 lag days - Heathwood: 6 lag days - Laidley: 5 lag days - Zillmere: 6 lag days
This is one of the better methodological choices in the paper, because the lag structure is not arbitrarily imposed.
crumbs: Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model: Factoring climate predictors for accuracy and deeper insights with probabilistic confidence interval and point-based forecasts

text:
3.3 Preprocessing and data split
The authors use min-max normalization and split the data into: - 90% training/validation: 01/07/2011 to 30/06/2020 - 10% testing: 01/07/2020 to 30/06/2021
Within the training portion, 20% is used as a validation set for hyperparameter tuning.

title: Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model: Factoring climate predictors for accuracy and deeper insights with probabilistic confidence interval and point-based forecasts
text:
3.4 The proposed model
The proposed model is a Deeply Fused Network (FNET) built from: - 1D CNN - BILSTM - repeated deep fusion of intermediate representations
Key architectural details include: - CNN filters ranging from 32 to 128 - a 4-layer BILSTM branch - a final single BILSTM regression layer - SeLU activation in the CNN branch - ReLU activation in the dense layer - Adam optimizer
The authors argue that deep fusion offers several benefits over shallow fusion: - better information flow, - learning at intermediate representation levels, - more representative feature embeddings, - extraction of multi-scale features.

title: Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model: Factoring climate predictors for accuracy and deeper insights with probabilistic confidence interval and point-based forecasts
text:
4. Validation Strategy

4.1 Point forecast validation
The deterministic evaluation includes multiple metrics, including: - Correlation coefficient (r) - RMSE - MAE - additional efficiency and bias-related metrics later in the paper, such as Willmott’s Index, Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency, Legates–McCabe index, KGE, GPI, and CPI.
This is a strength of the study: it does not rely on a single accuracy measure.


4.2 Probabilistic validation
The prediction intervals are evaluated with several uncertainty metrics, including: - PICP - MPIW - PINAW - ARIL - Winkler Score - CRPS - F-value
This is a strong point. The paper treats uncertainty quality as multi-dimensional rather than reducing it to just one interval metric.


4.3 Explainability validation
The XAI validation is primarily qualitative and domain-informed. The authors use SHAP plots to interpret: - the dominance of lagged load, - the importance of evapotranspiration, - interaction effects between lagged demand and climate drivers.
This gives meaningful interpretive insight, but it is not a formal XAI evaluation in the robustness/fidelity sense.

title: Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model: Factoring climate predictors for accuracy and deeper insights with probabilistic confidence interval and point-based forecasts
text:
5.1 Deterministic forecasting performance
The paper reports that FNET consistently performs best or among the best across the four substations and across multiple deterministic metrics.
A few concrete examples: - Annerley: FNET achieved r = 0.974, RMSE = 15.136 MW, MAE = 11.641 MW - On the same substation, the nearest deep baselines were slightly worse: - LSTMCNN: r = 0.967, RMSE = 16.233 MW, MAE = 12.482 MW - BILSTM: r = 0.965, RMSE = 16.481 MW, MAE = 12.484 MW - Weakest Annerley performers included: - KRR: r = 0.926, RMSE = 23.480 MW, MAE = 17.593 MW - MARS: r = 0.936, RMSE = 21.984 MW, MAE = 17.219 MW - MLP: r = 0.950, RMSE = 19.579 MW, MAE = 14.889 MW
For Laidley, FNET again performs strongly: - FNET: r = 0.963, RMSE = 13.038 MW, MAE = 10.266 MW - This is better than: - BILSTM: r = 0.957, RMSE = 14.449 MW, MAE = 11.488 MW - LSTMCNN: r = 0.961, RMSE = 14.370 MW, MAE = 11.425 MW
Across the paper’s wider set of metrics, the proposed FNET is repeatedly ranked first or near first, while shallow baselines such as MLP, KRR, and MARS tend to perform worst.

text:
5.2 Additional performance metrics
The paper also shows strong FNET results on: - Willmott’s Index - Nash–Sutcliffe coefficient - Legates & McCabe index - APB - KGE - GPI - CPI
For example, at Laidley, FNET achieves: - EWI ≈ 0.891 - ENS ≈ 0.859 - ELM ≈ 0.603
The authors use these broader metrics to argue that FNET is not just slightly better in one narrow sense, but more robust overall.

title: Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model: Factoring climate predictors for accuracy and deeper insights with probabilistic confidence interval and point-based forecasts
text:
5.3 Probabilistic forecasting performance
The probabilistic evaluation also favours FNET. The paper states that the model’s prediction intervals perform well across multiple uncertainty metrics and that the empirical error distribution and ECDF analyses show clearer separation in favour of FNET. The FNET intervals appear to maintain stronger performance when judged jointly by coverage and width, rather than only one of these.
The broader takeaway is that the proposed architecture is not only a better point forecaster, but also a more useful uncertainty-aware forecaster.

href: reviews/Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model.html#explainability-findings
title: Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model: Factoring climate predictors for accuracy and deeper insights with probabilistic confidence interval and point-based forecasts
text:
5.4 Explainability findings
The SHAP analysis identifies lagged electricity demand and evapotranspiration as especially influential variables. A major interpretive insight is that evapotranspiration generally contributes positively, but its contribution becomes stronger when lagged demand is high. In other words, the model is not simply learning isolated one-feature effects; SHAP suggests interaction structure between demand history and climate variables.
This is useful because it shows the model is not behaving as a totally opaque black box. The paper’s interpretation implies the network is capturing a meaningful coupling between thermal/climatic conditions and consumption patterns.

5.5 Computational cost
One downside is computational efficiency. The paper explicitly states that FNET is less computationally efficient than the benchmark models. However, it also argues that once trained, the model can remain in service for an extended period and that testing time is under one minute, which makes deployment still practical for real applications.

href: reviews/Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model.html#what-the-paper-does-well
title: Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model: Factoring climate predictors for accuracy and deeper insights with probabilistic confidence interval and point-based forecasts
text:
6. What the Paper Does Well

6.1 Strong methodological breadth
This is one of the stronger papers in the space because it combines: - advanced hybrid deep learning, - probabilistic uncertainty estimation, - multiple deterministic and probabilistic evaluation metrics, - and explainability.
A lot of studies do only one or two of these.


6.2 Good feature engineering logic
The use of PACF and MIF to select lag structure is a sound step and gives the model design more credibility than arbitrary lag selection.


6.3 Sensible uncertainty method
Bootstrap residual intervals are a good fit for this application because they avoid strong parametric output assumptions. That is a sensible design choice for a volatile real-world demand signal.


6.4 Explainability is tied to domain meaning
The SHAP analysis is not merely decorative. It identifies influential climate variables and interaction effects that can plausibly matter in real electricity demand dynamics.


6.5 Broad evaluation
The paper evaluates performance from many angles, which makes its conclusion more convincing than papers that rely only on RMSE or only on one interval metric.

objectID: reviews/Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
href: reviews/Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
title: Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model: Factoring climate predictors for accuracy and deeper insights with probabilistic confidence interval and point-based forecasts
text:
7. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: “Explainable” does not mean rigorously validated explainability
The paper uses SHAP well for qualitative interpretation, but it does not formally evaluate explanation quality using metrics such as: - explanation stability, - robustness, - fidelity, - sensitivity to perturbations, - or agreement across runs/background choices.
So although the SHAP figures are insightful, the study does not prove that the explanations themselves are stable or trustworthy in a stricter XAI sense.


Criticism 2: Residual bootstrap intervals are practical, but still limited
Bootstrap intervals are attractive because they are distribution-light, but they are still built on residual behaviour learned from past model errors. That means they may underperform under structural change, abrupt demand regime shifts, or unseen climate-demand patterns. The paper does not deeply interrogate whether residual bootstrap remains well calibrated under distribution shift.


Criticism 3: The benchmark set is broad, but not cutting-edge
The comparison is fair across several classical and hybrid baselines, but from a current forecasting perspective, the paper still omits stronger modern sequence models and probabilistic methods, for example: - quantile neural networks, - transformer-based forecasters, - mixture density approaches, - conformal prediction baselines, - distributional deep learning alternatives.
So while FNET beats the included baselines, the broader state-of-the-art comparison remains incomplete.


Criticism 4: Limited external generalization
All experiments are conducted on four substations in one regional context in Queensland. That is useful, but it does leave open the question of whether the same gains hold across: - different countries, - different climates, - larger transmission-level systems, - more abrupt socio-economic demand patterns, - or higher renewable penetration settings.


Criticism 5: Interpretability is still mostly feature attribution, not mechanistic understanding
The SHAP analysis tells us which features matter and how they trend, but it still does not fully reveal the internal mechanics of the deep fused representation. So the model becomes more interpretable, but not truly transparent in a structural sense.


Criticism 6: Computational cost matters more than the paper admits
The authors acknowledge that FNET is slower than alternatives. That is important. In operational environments where models must be retrained frequently, or where many substations/regions must be modeled simultaneously, this cost can become a real deployment bottleneck.
crumbs: Explainable deeply-fused nets electricity demand prediction model: Factoring climate predictors for accuracy and deeper insights with probabilistic confidence interval and point-based forecasts

section: 8. Positioning This Paper in the Literature
text:
8. Positioning This Paper in the Literature
This paper is best positioned as a high-quality hybrid deep learning paper that sits at the intersection of: - load forecasting, - uncertainty quantification, - and post-hoc interpretability.
Its biggest contribution is not that it invents uncertainty quantification or SHAP for forecasting, but that it integrates: 1. a deep fusion architecture, 2. bootstrap-based interval prediction, 3. and SHAP-based interpretation into one forecasting workflow.
Relative to weaker forecasting papers, it is stronger because it goes beyond point accuracy. Relative to cutting-edge probabilistic forecasting research, it is still somewhat transitional, because its uncertainty layer is bootstrap-based rather than intrinsically distributional or conformal.

9. Relevance to My Own Research / Why This Paper Matters
This paper is highly relevant if my research is about: - interpretable probabilistic demand forecasting, - climate-aware load prediction, - comparing point vs interval forecasting performance, - integrating SHAP into forecasting pipelines, - or arguing for more transparent forecasting tools in energy systems.
It is especially useful as a citation for the claim that accurate load prediction alone is insufficient and that uncertainty and interpretability must also be incorporated.

text:
11. Bottom-Line Takeaway
This is a strong and relevant paper. Its main achievement is showing that a deeply fused CNN-BILSTM model, augmented with bootstrap prediction intervals and SHAP explanations, can outperform a wide set of classical and neural baselines for daily electricity demand forecasting. The paper is methodologically richer than many load forecasting studies because it treats forecasting as a three-part problem: accuracy, uncertainty, and interpretability.
Its main weaknesses are that the explainability is validated only qualitatively, the probabilistic method is still residual-bootstrap rather than a more modern intrinsically probabilistic framework, and the benchmark set does not fully represent the strongest current state of the art. Even so, it is a very useful paper and a strong reference point for any work on explainable probabilistic energy forecasting.

title: Enhancing energy prediction in variable refrigerant flow cooling systems: A hybrid grey-box model integrating thermodynamic knowledge, experimental data and machine learning
text:
Authors & Year: Muhammad Reshaeel, Mohamed I. Hassan Ali (2026)
Venue (Journal/Conference): Energy

DOI: 10.1016/j.energy.2025.139895
Primary Domain: HVAC / VRF system energy prediction
Core Modelling Family: XGBoost
Model Types Compared: Pure black-box ML vs hybrid grey-box ML
Interpretability Tool: SHAP, including SHAP interaction values
Uncertainty Treatment: Aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty quantification
Dataset Type: Limited experimental data from a VRF laboratory test bench
Proximity/Threat Level: High for any research involving interpretable, physics-informed HVAC or energy prediction under small-data conditions
Why this paper matters: It is one of the clearest demonstrations that embedding thermodynamic structure into a machine learning model can materially improve not only predictive accuracy, but also uncertainty behaviour and interpretability.
crumbs: Enhancing energy prediction in variable refrigerant flow cooling systems: A hybrid grey-box model integrating thermodynamic knowledge, experimental data and machine learning

objectID: reviews/Enhancing energy prediction in variable refrigerant flow cooling systems.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/Enhancing energy prediction in variable refrigerant flow cooling systems.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: Enhancing energy prediction in variable refrigerant flow cooling systems: A hybrid grey-box model integrating thermodynamic knowledge, experimental data and machine learning
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation
The paper starts from a very practical energy systems problem: HVAC systems account for a major fraction of building energy use, and VRF systems are increasingly attractive because of their energy efficiency and part-load performance. However, to operate, optimize, diagnose, or control VRF systems well, one needs accurate energy prediction models. The authors argue that existing modelling approaches each have serious weaknesses: - White-box models are physically grounded and generalizable, but they require detailed system knowledge and are computationally intensive. - Black-box ML models can be accurate, but they depend heavily on rich, representative data and are often hard to interpret. - Existing grey-box models help bridge the gap, but the literature still lacks a model that is simultaneously accurate, robust, uncertainty-aware, and interpretable when trained on limited experimental data.


Their Main Research Gap
The paper identifies three specific gaps: 1. Small-data robustness in VRF prediction is still weak. 2. Comprehensive uncertainty quantification is rare in VRF energy prediction. 3. SHAP-based interpretability had not yet been explored in this VRF prediction context.


Their Claim to Fame / Novelty
The novelty is not just “use XGBoost for VRF prediction.” The real novelty is the comparison framework: - build a pure black-box XGBoost model using only operational variables, - build a hybrid grey-box XGBoost model using operational variables plus thermodynamic state variables and engineered thermodynamic features, - compare both on: - predictive accuracy, - residual behaviour, - robustness under distribution shift, - aleatoric uncertainty, - epistemic uncertainty, - interpretability via SHAP.


Why the Grey-Box Framing Matters
The hybrid model embeds VRF cycle domain knowledge into the learning pipeline. This is not done by replacing ML with physics, but by augmenting the feature space with physically meaningful quantities such as: - suction and discharge temperatures, - pressure ratio, - part-load ratio, - degrees of subcooling and superheating, - refrigerant mass flow rates.
This is the key philosophical contribution of the paper:
the model remains data-driven, but the representation is physically informed.

text:
3.1 Experimental Testbed
The study uses a laboratory VRF test bench developed with LAB-TECH International. It includes: - two indoor units, - one outdoor unit, - an inverter-driven variable-speed compressor, - temperature, pressure, and refrigerant flow sensors, - a thermodynamic cycle simulation interface, - cooling-mode operation only.
The system uses R410A refrigerant and has a rated cooling capacity of 11.2 kW.

Data Collection Context

Location: Khalifa University, Abu Dhabi
Duration: two days
Time window: 8:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.
Resolution: minute-wise measurements
Raw data points: 1320
Stable data points retained after cleaning: 1080

The paper explicitly removes stabilization-period data, following HVAC testing recommendations.

objectID: reviews/Enhancing energy prediction in variable refrigerant flow cooling systems.html#feature-design
href: reviews/Enhancing energy prediction in variable refrigerant flow cooling systems.html#feature-design
title: Enhancing energy prediction in variable refrigerant flow cooling systems: A hybrid grey-box model integrating thermodynamic knowledge, experimental data and machine learning
text:
3.2 Feature Design

Black-box Model Inputs
The pure black-box model uses only four operational features: - room temperature (Troom) - mean set-point temperature (Tmean) - ambient temperature (Tamb) - relative humidity (RH)
These are essentially external/operational proxies for system behaviour.


Hybrid Grey-box Model Inputs
The hybrid model uses the above operational variables plus thermodynamic state and engineered features.

Thermodynamic State Features

suction temperature (Tsuc)
discharge temperature (Tdis)



Engineered Thermodynamic Features

pressure ratio (PR)
part-load ratio (PLR)
condenser subcooling (DSC-cond)
liquid-line subcooling 1 and 2 (DSC-L1, DSC-L2)
superheating in evaporator 1 and 2 (DSH-E1, DSH-E2)
suction-line superheating (DSH-suc)
refrigerant mass flow rates (RF1, RF2)

These engineered variables are derived from measured pressures, temperatures, and refrigerant flow quantities through thermodynamic relations and energy balances.



Why This Matters
This is where the paper becomes much more than a standard ML application. The authors are effectively arguing that: - operational variables tell you what conditions the system sees, - thermodynamic variables tell you how the cycle is actually responding.
That distinction becomes very important later in the accuracy, uncertainty, and SHAP results.

text:
3.3 Correlation Analysis
The authors use Spearman correlation before model development.

Black-box Correlation Findings
For the black-box dataset: - Troom is the strongest positive correlate with compressor input power, - Tamb is also positively related, - Tmean and RH are negatively related.
The black-box model therefore relies heavily on indirect empirical trends.


Hybrid Correlation Findings
For the hybrid dataset, the dominant variables shift away from raw operating conditions toward: - PLR - PR - Tdis - RF1 - RF2 - DSC-cond
This is a major conceptual result. Once thermodynamic variables are introduced, the model no longer needs to rely mainly on environmental proxies. Instead, it can learn from variables that are much closer to the underlying physics of compressor workload.


Important Observation
The paper notes some collinearity, especially: - DSC-L1 vs DSC-L2 - RF1 vs RF2
But the authors keep them because they encode distinct thermodynamic interactions.

text:
3.4 Learning Algorithm & Training
Both models use XGBoost with the same overall pipeline. The main difference is only the feature set.

Hyperparameter Tuning
They tune hyperparameters using GridSearchCV.
Best values included: - learning rate = 0.1 for both - max_depth = 3 for black-box, 6 for hybrid - n_estimators = 75 for both - stronger regularization for the hybrid model (reg_alpha = 0.5, reg_lambda = 2)
That stronger regularization in the hybrid model is interesting: even though the hybrid model has many more features, it still ends up performing substantially better, suggesting that the added variables are not just noise but genuinely informative structure.

text:
4. Validation Strategy

Performance Metrics
The paper evaluates models using: - R² - RMSE - CV-RMSE


Validation Procedure
Because the dataset is small, the authors use k-fold cross-validation instead of a single fixed split, varying k from 2 to 10.


Additional Robustness Test
They also perform an out-of-distribution evaluation using a 4-hour operational dataset with significant distributional shift, quantified using Population Stability Index (PSI).
This is a strong aspect of the paper. Many small-data ML studies stop at cross-validation, but here the authors go a step further and explicitly test how the models behave under shifted conditions.

text:
5.1 Main Predictive Performance
Across cross-validation folds, the hybrid grey-box model outperforms the black-box model consistently.

Average Gains of the Hybrid Model

R² improvement: 7.26%
RMSE reduction: 71.86%
CV-RMSE reduction: 71.87%



Typical Metric Values
Black-box model: - R² ≈ 0.924–0.930 - RMSE ≈ 0.082–0.086 kW - CV-RMSE ≈ 6.74–7.02%
Hybrid grey-box model: - R² ≈ 0.993–0.995 - RMSE ≈ 0.022–0.025 kW - CV-RMSE ≈ 1.82–2.05%


Interpretation
This is a large gain, not a marginal one. The hybrid model is not just “a little better”; it is in a materially different regime of accuracy.
The paper also explains why the percentage gain in R² looks modest relative to the dramatic drop in RMSE: - R² is bounded and variance-based, - RMSE and CV-RMSE reflect absolute and relative error magnitude.
That explanation is sensible and technically correct.

The hybrid model has: - 98.33% of predictions within the ±10% error bounds.
The black-box model has: - 87.22% within the ±10% error bounds.
This is a visually intuitive way of showing that the grey-box model is much more tightly aligned with true compressor input power.

5.3 Residual Behaviour
This is one of the strongest sections of the paper.

Black-box Residuals

residuals spread roughly from -0.80 to 0.30 kW
heteroscedastic pattern
larger errors at higher predicted power



Hybrid Residuals

residuals roughly confined to -0.30 to 0.10 kW
much tighter spread
more homoscedastic pattern



Why this matters
This indicates the hybrid model is not just more accurate on average, but also more stable across the operating range. That is especially important for control-oriented energy models.

text:
5.4 Robustness Under Distribution Shift
This section significantly strengthens the paper.
The authors freeze hyperparameters and evaluate both models on a new dataset with significant shift in many variables. PSI values indicate strong shift in features such as: - Tdis - PR - PLR - DSC-cond - RF1 - RF2 - Troom - Tmean - Tamb - RH

Shifted-Data Performance
Black-box: - RMSE = 0.1753 kW - CV-RMSE = 17.13% - R² = 0.8017 - 48.75% within ±10% error
Hybrid grey-box: - RMSE = 0.1130 kW - CV-RMSE = 11.04% - R² = 0.9176 - 63.75% within ±10% error


Interpretation
Both models degrade under shift, which is expected. But the hybrid model degrades more gracefully. This is a strong result because it supports the core grey-box argument: physically informed representations generalize better when the operating distribution changes.

title: Enhancing energy prediction in variable refrigerant flow cooling systems: A hybrid grey-box model integrating thermodynamic knowledge, experimental data and machine learning
text:
6.1 Aleatoric Uncertainty
The authors estimate aleatoric uncertainty in two stages: 1. train a model to estimate the median compressor power, 2. model the absolute residuals as a proxy for irreducible noise.

Results
Black-box average aleatoric uncertainty: - 0.0315 kW
Hybrid grey-box average aleatoric uncertainty: - 0.0038 kW


Reduction

87.94% lower aleatoric uncertainty



Interpretation
This is a striking result. Strictly speaking, aleatoric uncertainty is supposed to reflect irreducible noise, but in practice its estimated value depends on how well the model isolates signal from noise. The hybrid model’s lower estimated aleatoric uncertainty suggests that the thermodynamic features help explain variance that would otherwise be dumped into the residual/noise term.
That is one of the central messages of the paper: better physics-aware features reduce what looks like “noise.”
