href: reviews/Enhancing energy prediction in variable refrigerant flow cooling systems.html#epistemic-uncertainty
title: Enhancing energy prediction in variable refrigerant flow cooling systems: A hybrid grey-box model integrating thermodynamic knowledge, experimental data and machine learning
text:
6.2 Epistemic Uncertainty
Because XGBoost does not provide epistemic uncertainty directly, the authors use an ensemble-based perturbation approach: - inject Gaussian noise into input features, - retrain multiple perturbed models, - compute variance in predictions.

Results
Black-box average epistemic uncertainty: - 0.0140 kW
Hybrid grey-box average epistemic uncertainty: - 0.0080 kW


Reduction

42.86% lower epistemic uncertainty



Noise Sensitivity Test
The hybrid model remains less sensitive to input perturbation across all tested noise levels. The authors report that the average percentage change in epistemic uncertainty across noise levels is 20.45% lower for the hybrid model.


Interpretation
This is a very nice result because the hybrid model actually has more input features, so one might initially expect more perturbation sensitivity. Instead, the opposite happens. The paper’s explanation is that the thermodynamic variables act as structural constraints that stabilize the learned function.
That is a convincing interpretation.

7.1 What SHAP Shows at a High Level
The hybrid model’s SHAP results are more physically meaningful than those of the pure black-box model. In the hybrid model: - operational features become secondary, - thermodynamic variables dominate, - feature effects align much more clearly with VRF thermodynamics.
This is exactly what you would hope to see in a genuinely useful grey-box model.

text:
7.2 Key Physically Meaningful Findings
The SHAP dependency analysis shows: - higher PLR strongly increases predicted compressor power, - higher Tdis is associated with greater compressor workload, - higher PR is positively related to compressor power, - higher DSC-cond also shows a meaningful positive role under load.
These are not arbitrary ML patterns. They line up with expected compressor-cycle behaviour: - more load leads to higher refrigerant throughput, - higher pressure ratio means harder compression, - higher discharge temperature accompanies harder compressor operation.

PR × PLR

positive interaction in the mid-range,

text:
Criticism 1: The dataset is still very small
The study uses only 1080 stable data points collected over two days from a single laboratory test bench. That is not trivial data, but it is still a very constrained setting. The results are promising, but one should be careful about calling the approach “state-of-the-art” in a broad field sense without wider external validation.

Criticism 2: Cooling-only operation limits generality
The test bench operates in cooling mode only. VRF systems in practice often operate across cooling, heating, transition, and defrost conditions. So the learned relationships may not transfer cleanly across all practical modes.

Criticism 4: Uncertainty quantification is useful, but not fully Bayesian
Their aleatoric and epistemic pipelines are thoughtful and practical, but they are still approximation schemes, not principled probabilistic posterior inference. That is not a flaw per se, but it is important to keep in mind. The paper should be read as providing operational uncertainty indicators, not exact uncertainty decomposition in a formal Bayesian sense.

Criticism 5: No comparison against stronger temporal models in equivalent conditions
The authors cite LSTM literature, but they do not benchmark directly against a strong temporal deep learning model on the same dataset. Their justification is understandable because the dataset is short, but it still leaves open the question: - how much of the gain comes from physics-informed features, - and how much could also be captured by a carefully regularized temporal model if longer histories were available?

Criticism 6: SHAP is used persuasively, but not validated formally
The SHAP results are highly interpretable and physically sensible. But the validation remains qualitative: - “does this look thermodynamically reasonable?”
That is a good start, but there is no explicit testing of: - explanation stability, - faithfulness, - robustness under perturbations, - agreement with independent physical sensitivity analysis.

section: Criticism 7: The black-box baseline is intentionally weak in representation
text:
Criticism 7: The black-box baseline is intentionally weak in representation
This is perhaps the biggest scientific caveat. The black-box model uses only four operational variables. That creates a very stark contrast with the hybrid model, which has sixteen features including cycle-informed quantities. So the study convincingly proves: adding thermodynamic structure helps.
But it does not fully prove: grey-box learning is superior to all strong black-box alternatives,
because the “black-box” here is also deprived of potentially richer measured inputs.

section: 9. What This Paper Really Tells Us
text:
9. What This Paper Really Tells Us
The paper’s deepest contribution is not just a performance table. It shows that in small-data engineering settings: - feature design matters more than blindly increasing model complexity, - physics-informed variables can reduce both prediction error and estimated uncertainty, - interpretability improves when the feature space reflects the actual system physics, - robustness under shift improves when the model is grounded in physical state representation rather than only operational proxies.
In other words:

The paper argues, quite convincingly, that the real strength of hybrid grey-box modelling is not merely “better accuracy,” but a better representation of causally meaningful system behaviour.

That is why the approach works.

Cite this paper in any literature review section discussing physics-informed or grey-box energy prediction for HVAC/VRF systems.
Use it as a key reference when arguing that embedding thermodynamic state variables into ML models improves robustness and interpretability under limited data.
Reuse its structure of comparing:

residual behaviour,

aleatoric uncertainty,
epistemic uncertainty,

In my own work, consider whether engineered physics features are reducing what is currently being interpreted as “noise.”
If I build a comparable model, include stronger external validation than this paper:

multiple seasons,

Consider adding formal interpretability checks beyond visual SHAP plausibility.

title: Enhancing energy prediction in variable refrigerant flow cooling systems: A hybrid grey-box model integrating thermodynamic knowledge, experimental data and machine learning
text:
11. One-Paragraph Literature Review Summary
Reshaeel and Hassan Ali (2026) present a strong case for hybrid grey-box machine learning in VRF compressor power prediction by comparing a pure black-box XGBoost model trained on operational variables with a grey-box XGBoost model augmented by thermodynamic state and engineered cycle features. Using limited experimental data from a laboratory VRF test bench, the hybrid model substantially outperformed the black-box model, achieving a 7.26% improvement in R² and roughly 72% reductions in RMSE and CV-RMSE, while also exhibiting more stable residuals and stronger robustness under distribution shift. A major contribution of the study is its explicit uncertainty analysis, where the grey-box model reduced estimated aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty by 87.94% and 42.86%, respectively. SHAP analysis further showed that the hybrid model learned physically meaningful relationships centered on part-load ratio, pressure ratio, discharge temperature, and condenser subcooling, providing interpretable insight into VRF control behaviour. Although the study is limited by small-scale, cooling-only, single-system data, it offers compelling evidence that thermodynamic feature engineering can improve accuracy, reliability, and interpretability in small-data HVAC modelling.

Main Topic: Probabilistic day-ahead electricity price forecasting

Dataset / Market: Danish electricity market, forecasting the DK1 day-ahead tariff

objectID: reviews/Day-Ahead Electricity Price Probabilistic Forecasting Based on SHAP Feature Selection and LSTNet Quantile Regression.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/Day-Ahead Electricity Price Probabilistic Forecasting Based on SHAP Feature Selection and LSTNet Quantile Regression.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: Day-Ahead Electricity Price Probabilistic Forecasting Based on SHAP Feature Selection and LSTNet Quantile Regression
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why electricity price forecasting matters):

Electricity prices are central to electricity-market decision making and directly influence resource allocation, bidding, and operational planning.
Rising renewable penetration has increased volatility and uncertainty, making price behavior harder to model accurately.
The authors argue that deterministic forecasting alone is insufficient because it produces only a single point estimate and does not quantify uncertainty.

The Motivation (Why probabilistic forecasting):

Electricity prices in modern power systems are noisy, volatile, and influenced by many interacting drivers.
Probabilistic forecasting provides richer information than point forecasts by estimating quantiles, intervals, and density functions.
This is especially useful for market participants making risk-sensitive decisions under uncertainty.

The Motivation (Why SHAP / interpretability):

The input feature space in integrated electricity markets can become large and redundant.
The authors use SHAP not only as an interpretation tool, but also as a feature selection mechanism.
Their framing is that SHAP helps reveal both which variables matter most and how they influence the final forecast, including directionality.

Their claim to novelty:

They propose a new probabilistic electricity price forecasting framework that combines:

SHAP-based feature selection,
LSTNet quantile regression,
KDE-based recovery of probability density functions and prediction intervals.

Their novelty is less about inventing a brand-new model family and more about integrating interpretable feature selection with nonparametric probabilistic forecasting in a structured pipeline.

What the paper is really contributing:

A feature-selection stage using SHAP values to reduce redundancy and overfitting.
A probabilistic forecasting stage where LSTNet predicts multiple quantiles.
A nonparametric density reconstruction step using Gaussian kernel density estimation.
Qualitative market interpretation through SHAP feature-importance and dependence analysis.

title: Day-Ahead Electricity Price Probabilistic Forecasting Based on SHAP Feature Selection and LSTNet Quantile Regression
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

3.1 Forecasting Philosophy

The paper positions itself explicitly in the nonparametric probabilistic forecasting camp.
The authors criticize parametric probabilistic methods because real power-system outputs can be highly stochastic, fat-tailed, and polymorphic, making rigid parametric assumptions unreliable.
Their workaround is:

estimate quantiles directly via quantile regression,
then reconstruct the implied probability density using KDE.




3.2 SHAP for Feature Selection and Analysis

SHAP is used in two distinct ways:

Feature selection: rank variables by average absolute SHAP value,
Feature analysis: inspect whether features increase or decrease price and how this depends on feature magnitude.

The feature importance score is computed as the average absolute SHAP contribution for a feature across samples.
Unlike plain correlation-based ranking, SHAP preserves both:

magnitude of influence, and
direction of influence.




3.3 LSTNet Architecture

The forecasting backbone is LSTNet, chosen because electricity prices exhibit:

short-term local dependencies,
long-term cyclical dependencies,
nonlinear behavior.

LSTNet contains:

a CNN module for short-term local feature extraction,
a recurrent / recurrent-skip module for long-term temporal dependence,
an autoregressive linear module to restore sensitivity to scale changes.

This last point is important: the authors explicitly note that the nonlinear components can become insensitive to input scale, so the AR branch is added to correct that weakness.



3.4 Quantile Regression Layer

The paper explains quantile regression from the ground up:

standard linear quantile regression,
neural-network quantile regression,
then LSTNet quantile regression.

In practice, the model predicts a set of electricity-price quantiles rather than a single expected value.
The paper states that the inter-quantile interval is 0.1, so they appear to forecast quantiles on a coarse grid such as 0.1, 0.2, …, 0.9.



3.5 Density Reconstruction with KDE

After obtaining predicted quantiles, the authors use Gaussian kernel density estimation to reconstruct a continuous predictive distribution.
Bandwidth is chosen via the Rule-of-Thumb formula.
This step lets them move from a discrete set of predicted quantiles to:

a probability density function,
and prediction intervals at different confidence levels.




3.6 Evaluation Metrics

Point forecasting metrics: RMSE and MAPE
Interval / probabilistic metrics:

PICP: Prediction Interval Coverage Probability
PINAW: Prediction Interval Average Width
AL: Average pinball loss

The paper emphasizes the trade-off between:

coverage / reliability and
sharpness / narrow intervals

They use average pinball loss as the tie-breaker when PICP and PINAW point in opposite directions.

text:
4. Dataset / Testbed

Market: Danish electricity market
Target: DK1 day-ahead tariff
Data source: www.energidataservice.dk
Time span: 1 May 2019 to 31 August 2019
Training period: 1 May 2019 to 31 July 2019
Testing period: 1 August 2019 to 31 August 2019


Input Features
The paper includes lagged regional electricity prices and market/renewable/exchange variables such as: - DK1, DK2 lagged prices, - neighboring market prices: DE, NO2, SE3, SE4, SYS, - DK1 production and consumption, - wind, solar, and hydropower, - exchange variables between DK1 and neighboring regions/countries.


Important practical note

This is a very short study period for electricity price forecasting: only about four months in total, with roughly three months used for training.
That makes the paper more of a method demonstration than a strong stress-test across seasons, years, structural breaks, and market regime shifts.

href: reviews/Day-Ahead Electricity Price Probabilistic Forecasting Based on SHAP Feature Selection and LSTNet Quantile Regression.html#feature-selection-findings-interpretability-results
title: Day-Ahead Electricity Price Probabilistic Forecasting Based on SHAP Feature Selection and LSTNet Quantile Regression
text:
5. Feature Selection Findings & Interpretability Results

5.1 Top-ranked Features
The top SHAP-ranked inputs are: 1. DK2_7 2. DK1_7 3. DK1_1 4. DE_1 5. DK2_1 6. ExGE_1 7. HydroPower_1
The authors then keep the top seven features as the final input set.


5.2 Market Interpretation from SHAP

DK2_7 was the most influential feature overall.
Among neighboring-country variables, Germany (DE_1) had the strongest influence on Danish prices.
Among renewables, hydropower ranked above wind and solar.
Among exchange variables, ExGE_1 (exchange between DK1 and Germany) was most important.



5.3 Directional effects found by SHAP

For DK2_7:

lower historical DK2 prices tended to push predictions down,
higher historical DK2 prices tended to push predictions up.

For SE4_1:

lower values tended to increase predicted DK1 prices,
higher values tended to reduce them.

For Wind_1:

the paper identifies a threshold around 1000,
below this value, wind tended to reduce price,
above it, wind tended to increase price.

For ExGE_1:

below roughly 800, exchange with Germany increased price,
above roughly 1000, it decreased price.




5.4 What is useful here

This is one of the stronger parts of the paper.
The authors do not just rank features; they try to interpret market mechanisms.
Even if the interpretations are simplified, the workflow is useful:

global ranking,
local directional analysis,
threshold-style dependence plots.

href: reviews/Day-Ahead Electricity Price Probabilistic Forecasting Based on SHAP Feature Selection and LSTNet Quantile Regression.html#forecasting-results
title: Day-Ahead Electricity Price Probabilistic Forecasting Based on SHAP Feature Selection and LSTNet Quantile Regression
text:
6. Forecasting Results

6.1 Point Forecasting Results
The paper compares BPNN, LSTM, LSTNet, and their SHAP-selected variants.

Table: Point forecasting metrics

BPNN: RMSE = 8.35, MAPE = 13.02
LSTM: RMSE = 7.80, MAPE = 14.62
LSTNet: RMSE = 4.96, MAPE = 8.39
SHAP–BPNN: RMSE = 4.27, MAPE = 10.34
SHAP–LSTM: RMSE = 3.62, MAPE = 9.28
SHAP–LSTNet: RMSE = 2.35, MAPE = 5.39




Key takeaway

LSTNet was the best base model.
SHAP-based feature selection improved all three model families.
The best overall point forecasting model was SHAP–LSTNet.



6.2 Probabilistic Forecasting Results
The benchmark probabilistic models are SHAP–BPNN, SHAP–LSTM, and SHAP–LSTNet.

At confidence level 0.9:

SHAP–BPNN: PINAW = 22.22, PICP = 10.87, AL = 2.61
SHAP–LSTM: PINAW = 72.22, PICP = 32.74, AL = 0.88
SHAP–LSTNet: PINAW = 97.22, PICP = 35.79, AL = 0.41



At confidence level 0.8:

SHAP–BPNN: PINAW = 15.28, PICP = 7.42, AL = 2.25
SHAP–LSTM: PINAW = 44.44, PICP = 25.72, AL = 1.58
SHAP–LSTNet: PINAW = 80.56, PICP = 27.13, AL = 0.80



At confidence level 0.7:

SHAP–BPNN: PINAW = 9.72, PICP = 5.77, AL = 4.88
SHAP–LSTM: PINAW = 34.72, PICP = 17.42, AL = 1.85
SHAP–LSTNet: PINAW = 77.78, PICP = 24.13, AL = 1.14




Their conclusion from probabilistic results

The authors conclude that SHAP–LSTNet at 0.9 confidence is the best probabilistic model, mainly because it achieves the smallest average pinball loss.
They argue that narrow intervals alone are not desirable if they fail to cover the actual observations.

Forecasting validation: straightforward hold-out split

train on May–July 2019,
test on August 2019.

Point forecasting validation: RMSE and MAPE
Probabilistic validation: PICP, PINAW, AL
Interpretability validation: qualitative SHAP plots and market-based reasoning

No rolling-origin evaluation
No walk-forward backtesting across multiple months or seasons
No repeated experiments across years
No robustness analysis under price spikes, regime shifts, or extreme events

title: Day-Ahead Electricity Price Probabilistic Forecasting Based on SHAP Feature Selection and LSTNet Quantile Regression
text:
8. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: The dataset is too short for strong claims

The training window is only three months and the test window is only one month.
Electricity price forecasting is highly regime-sensitive.
A model that works over one August test month may not generalize across winter, fuel shocks, transmission events, or unusual renewable conditions.
This is a serious limitation if the paper is read as evidence of broad practical superiority.



Criticism 2: SHAP is used on top of a small-sample setup

SHAP rankings can be useful, but with limited data, feature-importance estimates can become unstable.
The paper does not test whether the selected top-seven feature set is stable across:

different train/test splits,
different random seeds,
or different model initializations.

So the feature-selection conclusions may be more fragile than the paper suggests.



Criticism 3: The probabilistic evaluation looks odd

The reported PICP values are surprisingly low relative to the stated confidence levels.
For example, at a 0.9 confidence level, a PICP of 35.79 is far below what one would expect if the intervals were calibrated in the usual sense.
That raises at least one of three possibilities:

unusual scaling/definition,
reporting inconsistency,
poor calibration despite low pinball loss.

The paper does not fully unpack this tension.



Criticism 4: KDE after quantile prediction is a practical workaround, not a fully coherent probabilistic model

The framework first predicts quantiles and then reconstructs a density with KDE.
This can be useful, but it is a somewhat stitched-together pipeline.
It does not guarantee the same degree of internal probabilistic coherence as methods that directly learn a full conditional distribution.



Criticism 5: Baselines are weak and narrow

The comparison set is mainly BPNN, LSTM, and LSTNet variants.
That is not enough to establish state-of-the-art superiority in electricity price forecasting.
Stronger baselines could have included:

quantile gradient boosting,
quantile random forests,
LightGBM/XGBoost quantile models,
conformalized interval methods,
transformer-based time-series models,
modern probabilistic deep learning baselines.




Criticism 6: Interpretability is descriptive, not rigorously validated

The SHAP analysis is interesting and readable.
But the paper treats plausible feature plots as sufficient evidence of interpretability quality.
It does not test:

explanation stability,
explanation fidelity,
sensitivity to background distribution choice,
or whether the explanations remain consistent across retraining runs.




Criticism 7: No explicit treatment of quantile crossing

Since the method predicts multiple quantiles, quantile crossing is a natural concern.
The paper does not clearly discuss whether the predicted quantiles were constrained or post-processed to remain monotonic.
That matters if the quantiles are later fed into KDE.



Criticism 8: Market interpretation may be overly literal

The paper interprets SHAP dependence plots as if they reveal stable market thresholds, such as wind = 1000 or exchange = 800.
These thresholds may just reflect local patterns in this dataset rather than deep structural market truths.
The paper could have been more careful in separating:

data-specific empirical patterns,
from broadly generalizable market mechanisms.

It gives a clean and understandable pipeline from feature selection to probabilistic output.
It uses SHAP in a more meaningful way than many papers that only include one generic feature-importance plot.
It combines prediction and interpretation in a way that is easy to explain to readers.
It shows clearly that feature selection can materially improve forecasting accuracy.
It is a useful reference paper if your own work involves:

SHAP-based screening,
quantile forecasting,
probabilistic time-series modeling,
or energy-market XAI.

This paper sits at the intersection of three threads:

Electricity price forecasting

moving from classical statistical models toward deep learning.

11. Relevance to My Own Research / How I Could Use It

Useful as a citation for:

SHAP-based feature selection in energy forecasting,
probabilistic forecasting using quantile regression,
combining interpretability with deep temporal models,
nonparametric density reconstruction after quantile estimation.

Useful as a methodological stepping stone:

It provides a precedent for using SHAP before a deep forecasting model.
It supports the idea that reducing redundant inputs can improve both accuracy and interpretability.

text:
13. Final Verdict
This is a useful and well-structured applied paper rather than a definitive state-of-the-art benchmark. Its main strength is not that it proves the best possible probabilistic electricity price forecaster, but that it presents a clear and intuitive SHAP + LSTNet + quantile/KDE pipeline that is easy to understand, easy to cite, and reasonably convincing as a proof of concept.
Its key message is: > SHAP-guided dimensionality reduction can improve deep probabilistic electricity price forecasting, while also making the model more interpretable.
Its main weakness is: > the experimental setup is too limited to fully justify strong general claims about robustness, calibration, and state-of-the-art performance.

title: Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift
text:
Authors & Year: Yaniv Ovadia, Emily Fertig, Jie Ren, et al. (2019)
Venue (Journal/Conference): NeurIPS 2019 (Highly authoritative; foundational paper from Google Research/DeepMind on dataset shift).
Link/DOI: arXiv:1906.02530
Primary Topic/Concept: The failure of post-hoc calibration under dataset shift, the danger of models being “confidently wrong,” and the necessity of capturing epistemic uncertainty.
crumbs: Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift

objectID: reviews/Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift.html#the-core-theory-what-is-the-main-concept
href: reviews/Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift.html#the-core-theory-what-is-the-main-concept
title: Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift
section: 2. The Core Theory (What is the main concept?)
text:
2. The Core Theory (What is the main concept?)

The specific theory or mechanism explained:

Standard machine learning models (and those calibrated via post-hoc methods like Temperature Scaling) only effectively capture aleatoric uncertainty (data noise). When exposed to out-of-distribution (OOD) data or dataset shift, these models do not naturally increase their uncertainty; instead, they become “confidently wrong.”

Their main argument/conclusion:

Achieving perfect calibration on an i.i.d. (independent and identically distributed) validation set does not guarantee calibration under real-world distribution shifts. Only methods that explicitly capture epistemic uncertainty (like Deep Ensembles) are robust enough to “know what they don’t know” as data shifts.
crumbs: Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift

objectID: reviews/Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift.html#key-arguments-evidence-the-why
href: reviews/Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift.html#key-arguments-evidence-the-why
title: Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift
text:
3. Key Arguments & Evidence (The “Why”)

Mathematical / Logical Foundation:

They decouple accuracy from prediction reliability using Proper Scoring Rules (Brier Score, Negative Log-Likelihood) and Expected Calibration Error (ECE). This allows them to mathematically prove that as shift increases, a model’s calibration degrades faster than its accuracy.

Key Evidence & Testing Mechanics:

Progressive Shift: They didn’t just test “in vs. out”. They applied synthetic corruptions (e.g., blur, rotation) at progressive levels of intensity to image (MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet), text, and tabular datasets.
Completely OOD Data: They tested models on entirely different datasets (e.g., training on MNIST, testing on NotMNIST) to see if predictive entropy spiked. It often didn’t.
The Deep Ensemble Finding: Across almost all tests, Deep Ensembles (using as few as 5 models) consistently provided the most reliable uncertainty estimates under shift.

Terminology / Definitions:

Aleatoric Uncertainty: Inherent noise or randomness in the data (what standard single models capture).
Epistemic Uncertainty: Uncertainty due to a lack of knowledge or lack of data (what ensembles or Bayesian methods capture).
Dataset Shift / Covariate Shift: When the test input distribution diverges from the training distribution.
crumbs: Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift

section: 4. Application to My Work (How I will use this)
text:
4. Application to My Work (How I will use this)

What specific decision in my paper does this justify?

I will use this paper to mathematically and empirically justify why my methodology cannot rely on standard single-model outputs or simple post-hoc calibration. Because PV forecasting operates in environments prone to severe covariate shift (changing weather, sensor drift), models that only output aleatoric uncertainty are dangerous. I need a framework (like ensembles or direct interval optimization) that inherently accounts for epistemic uncertainty to prevent “confidently wrong” predictions.

Where does this belong in my paper?

Introduction (Setting up the problem: standard ML uncertainty is dangerous in real-world grids due to the “confidently wrong” phenomenon).
Background / Related Work (Defining Epistemic vs. Aleatoric uncertainty and highlighting the limits of post-hoc calibration).
Methodology (Defending the choice of robust, uncertainty-aware loss functions or ensemble architectures).
crumbs: Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift

objectID: reviews/Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift.html#boundaries-caveats-where-does-the-theory-break
href: reviews/Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift.html#boundaries-caveats-where-does-the-theory-break
title: Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift
section: 5. Boundaries & Caveats (Where does the theory break?)
text:
5. Boundaries & Caveats (Where does the theory break?)

The “Relativity Problem” of Entropy (Crucial Insight):

The authors prove that models fail by comparing entropy/confidence on an in-distribution set versus a known shifted set. However, in the real world, uncertainty metrics like entropy are purely relative. If you don’t have a known OOD dataset to benchmark against, how do you set the threshold for “too much entropy”? The paper highlights the failure under shift, but it does not solve the operational problem of defining absolute OOD thresholds in production without reference data.

Assumptions made by the authors:

The study evaluates classification tasks (discrete distribution over \(k\) classes). Metrics like discrete ECE or softmax entropy do not perfectly translate to continuous regression intervals without adaptation (e.g., adapting to PICP/PINAW or CWC).
crumbs: Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift

title: Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift
text:
6. Action Items & Pre-Written Assets
Golden Quotes: - > “Better calibration and accuracy on the i.i.d. test dataset does not usually translate to better calibration under dataset shift (shifted versions as well as completely different OOD data).” (p. 9) - > “Post-hoc calibration (on i.i.d validation) with temperature scaling leads to well-calibrated uncertainty on the i.i.d. test set and small values of shift, but is significantly outperformed by methods that take epistemic uncertainty into account as the shift increases.” (p. 9)
Pre-written Justification Blurb: > “Standard machine learning models typically capture only aleatoric uncertainty, leading to highly overconfident predictions when exposed to out-of-distribution inputs. As demonstrated by Ovadia et al. (2019), methods relying on post-hoc calibration may perform well on i.i.d. test sets but degrade rapidly under dataset shift, often yielding ‘confidently wrong’ predictions. Because operational forecasting environments are inherently subject to covariate shifts—such as seasonal variations and evolving weather dynamics—relying on standard calibration is insufficient. To ensure safe operational decision-making, it is imperative to utilize architectures, such as ensembles, that explicitly capture epistemic uncertainty and maintain reliable prediction bounds under distributional shift.”

title: An interpretable probabilistic model for short-term solar power forecasting using natural gradient boosting
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why Probabilistic?):

PV power is inherently stochastic due to volatile weather, which threatens grid stability and requires higher reserve capacities. Deterministic (single-point) forecasts are insufficient. Probabilistic forecasts quantify uncertainty, allowing TSOs/DSOs to estimate optimal reserve requirements and helping energy traders minimize risk in day-ahead markets.

The Motivation (Why Explainable?):

Trust & Safety: Grid operations are safety-critical, so operators cannot blindly trust black-box models. Furthermore, TSOs/DSOs have a societal duty to be transparent with the public.
Debugging & Bidding: Debugging ML models is notoriously difficult. Traders need to know when a model is uncertain or biased so they can adjust their bidding strategies.

Their claim to fame / Novelty:

They claim this is the first attempt to fully interpret a probabilistic machine learning model in the context of power systems.
They combine Natural Gradient Boosting (NGBoost) with SHAP and SHAP interaction values to peek inside the black box.

The Value Derived from Explainability (What did XAI actually do?):

Physics Verification: It proved the model didn’t just memorize data but learned actual physical relationships (e.g., PV efficiency dropping at high temperatures).
Uncertainty Interpretation: SHAP helped explain what drives predictive uncertainty (e.g., lower confidence during mid-day high radiation; high confidence during low-humidity or night hours).
Model Improvement (Feature Selection): SHAP revealed that certain weather features (precipitation, temperature, wind speed) were actually confusing the model’s uncertainty estimations. By dropping them, the model’s CRPS improved by 10%.

Their ultimate result:

NGBoost vastly outperformed Gaussian Process (GP) and LUBE in point accuracy, interval sharpness (75% narrower than LUBE), and training time (109s vs ~25 mins for LUBE).

text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

Datasets / Testbed:

1.5 years of 15-minute data from two PV parks (PVP1, PVP2) in Southern Germany. Night hours (22:00-06:00) were excluded.

Key Variables:

Lagged power (t-15, t-30, t-45), radiation, temperature, humidity, precipitation, wind speed, month (sin/cos), and hour.

Baselines Compared Against:

Persistence (point only).
Gaussian Process (GP) with a Rational Quadratic (RQ) kernel.
LUBE (Lower Upper Bound Estimation) for prediction intervals. Configured with a shallow network (20 neurons) and set to a target coverage (\(\mu\)) of 95%.

text:
4. Validation Strategy (Predictions & Explanations)

Validating the Predictions (Forecasting Quality):

Data Split: Sliding-horizon validation. Trained on 1 whole year, tested on the following month. They created 4 different train/test pairs (one for each season) to ensure robustness.
Metrics: MAE, RMSE, MBE (Point); PICP, PINAW, CRPS, and PIT histograms (Probabilistic).

Validating the Explanations (XAI Quality):

The paper relies entirely on qualitative domain-knowledge checks rather than formal XAI evaluation metrics.
Example 1 (Temperature): SHAP interaction plots showed that under high radiation, high temperatures negatively impact power output, perfectly matching the physics of PV panel efficiency loss.
Example 2 (Humidity): SHAP revealed high humidity decreases efficiency.
Example 3 (Time/Radiation): Explanations aligned with the known diurnal bell-shape curve of solar generation.

href: reviews/An interpretable probabilistic model for short-term solar power forecasting using natural gradient boosting.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
title: An interpretable probabilistic model for short-term solar power forecasting using natural gradient boosting
text:
5. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: Qualitative vs. Quantitative XAI Validation:

While their domain-knowledge validation is persuasive and reads well, it is strictly qualitative. They do not use any rigorous XAI evaluation metrics (e.g., explanation fidelity, robustness, stability). If the model contained subtle biases, qualitative “sanity checks” might easily miss them.

Criticism 2: The “Non-Parametric” Contradiction & Gaussian Assumption:

The authors frame NGBoost as highly flexible, but it is essentially semi-parametric. While the trees don’t assume a rigid functional form for features, the model strictly assumes the output uncertainty follows a Gaussian distribution. It forces predictive uncertainty into a parametric box, failing to capture complex, asymmetric empirical distributions.

Criticism 3: A Strawman Baseline for Neural Networks (LUBE):

Their LUBE baseline looks incredibly outdated and weak by current standards. Because the standard CWC loss function is a non-differentiable step function, they used a shallow network trained via simulated annealing. This perfectly explains why LUBE took 25 minutes to train and performed so poorly—sacrificing sharpness (terrible PINAW) just to achieve ~100% PICP.

Criticism 4: Apples-to-Oranges Comparison:

They compared a distributional model (NGBoost optimizing a log score) against an interval-bound model (LUBE optimizing CWC via metaheuristics). They completely omitted stronger, modern baselines, such as Quantile Regression Neural Networks (QRNN) or deep neural networks trained with differentiable CWC-style losses (e.g., Expanded Interval Minimization or Tube Loss).

Observation on Dimensionality:

The model struggled with high dimensionality. Removing variables actually improved performance, indicating the algorithm easily falls into suboptimal solutions if fed too much data.

Ensure my validation metrics explicitly include both PICP (Coverage) and PINAW (Width) to directly prove my model achieves better sharpness than their NGBoost while maintaining proper ~95% coverage.

Add a note in my literature review regarding the limitations of rigid parametric assumptions for distributions (NGBoost) and computationally heavy, non-differentiable baselines (LUBE), clearly positioning my approach as the solution.

text:
Authors & Year: Elias Isaac Huai-En Lim and Nicholas Heng Loong Wong (2025)
Venue (Journal/Conference): 2025 Asia Pacific Signal and Information Processing Association Annual Summit and Conference (APSIPA ASC)
DOI: 10.1109/APSIPAASC65261.2025.11249263
Primary Topic/Concept: Integrating explainable AI (XAI) and uncertainty quantification (UQ) into deep neural network based battery state of health (SOH) estimation
Application Domain: Lithium-ion battery diagnostics for electric vehicles and battery management systems
Datasets Used: McMaster Battery Aging Dataset and Oxford Battery Degradation Dataset
Code/Data Available?: Public datasets are referenced; no dedicated code repository is explicitly provided in the paper
Proximity/Threat Level: Medium to High / Relevant methodological reference for trustworthy regression in energy systems

href: reviews/A Unified Framework for Interpretable and Uncertainty-Aware Battery State of Health Estimation.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: A Unified Framework for Interpretable and Uncertainty-Aware Battery State of Health Estimation Using Deep Neural Networks
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why SOH Estimation Matters)

Accurate battery state of health estimation is critical for electric vehicles and renewable energy systems because it directly affects safety, reliability, performance, and battery longevity.
Poor SOH estimation can lead to premature battery replacement, degraded operation, poor maintenance decisions, and in extreme cases, battery safety hazards such as thermal runaway.
Deep neural networks are increasingly attractive for SOH estimation because they can model nonlinear degradation behavior from sensor data, but they are difficult to trust in deployment because they are black-box models.



The Motivation (Why Explainability and Uncertainty?)

The authors argue that accurate predictions alone are not enough in safety-critical systems.
A practical battery diagnostic model should answer two questions:

Why did the model predict this SOH value?
How certain is the model about that prediction?

XAI is introduced to make model behavior interpretable, while UQ is introduced to provide confidence intervals around predictions so that operators can assess risk and act more cautiously when the model is uncertain.



Their Claim to Fame / Novelty

The paper proposes a unified framework that combines:

SHAP
LIME
Integrated Gradients (IG)
Counterfactual explanations
Adaptive Confidence Intervals (ACI)
MC dropout
Deep ensembles

The novelty is not a brand-new backbone model, but rather the integration of interpretability and predictive uncertainty into a single SOH estimation pipeline.
They position the work as filling a gap in the literature, namely the lack of frameworks that jointly address interpretability + uncertainty for regression-based, time-series, multivariate tabular battery data.



The Value Derived from Explainability

The explainability toolkit is used to identify which features drive SOH predictions globally and locally.
It also allows layer-wise inspection of how feature importance changes through the depth of the network.
The paper claims explainability improves transparency, helps interpret edge cases, and enables actionable analysis via counterfactuals.



The Value Derived from Uncertainty Quantification

Their UQ framework tries to capture both:

Epistemic uncertainty: uncertainty due to model limitations or lack of knowledge
Aleatoric uncertainty: uncertainty due to measurement noise and inherent data variability

Confidence intervals are used to communicate prediction reliability, which is especially important for deployment in battery management systems.



Their Ultimate Result

The framework achieves:

RMSE = 0.01175 on McMaster
RMSE = 0.01432 on Oxford
PICP = 91.2% on McMaster
PICP = 89.8% on Oxford
MPIW = 0.2311 on McMaster
MPIW = 0.2457 on Oxford

The authors interpret these results as evidence that the framework provides both accurate and informative SOH predictions.

title: A Unified Framework for Interpretable and Uncertainty-Aware Battery State of Health Estimation Using Deep Neural Networks
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

Datasets / Testbed
The study uses two public lithium-ion battery datasets:

McMaster Battery Aging Dataset
Oxford Battery Degradation Dataset

Both datasets contain time-series battery measurements over multiple charge-discharge cycles, including: - voltage - current - temperature - capacity


Preprocessing
The paper applies fairly standard preprocessing: - moving average smoothing for noisy readings - cycle-based feature extraction such as: - maximum voltage - mean temperature - z-score normalization - stratified 80:20 train:test split across cells and cycles


Model Architectures
They replicate two previously published models:

CNN architecture

Uses stacked 1D convolutional layers and global pooling
Applied primarily to the McMaster dataset
This appears to be the main model of focus

Bi-LSTM with attention

Uses interpolated time-series features
Includes dropout and batch normalization
Applied to the Oxford dataset
Used more as a validation model than the central focus




Training Setup

Implemented in TensorFlow
Optimizer: Adam
Learning rate: 0.001
Batch size: 128
Early stopping patience: 5
Loss function: Mean Squared Error (MSE)



Explainability Framework
The interpretability component includes four methods:

1. SHAP

Used to estimate feature contributions to predicted SOH
Applied globally and locally
Also used layer-wise



2. LIME

Used to fit local surrogate explanations around individual predictions
Particularly emphasized for understanding edge cases



3. Integrated Gradients (IG)

Used to attribute importance via gradients accumulated from a baseline input to the actual input
Intended to provide a more path-aware notion of feature influence



4. Counterfactual Explanations

Used to identify minimal input perturbations required to significantly change the predicted SOH
Intended to provide actionable what-if style explanations




Adaptive Confidence Interval (ACI)
This is the main UQ contribution.
The ACI combines: - Epistemic uncertainty - estimated using MC dropout - and deep ensembles - Aleatoric uncertainty - estimated by injecting Gaussian noise into the input data - and examining predictive variability
The total uncertainty is then combined into a confidence interval using pooled estimates of means and variances:
[ CI = {n_{model} + n_{data}} z ]
Where: - model terms represent epistemic uncertainty - data terms represent aleatoric uncertainty - (z) corresponds to the desired confidence level - they use: - (n_{model} = 50) - (n_{data} = 50) - 95% confidence level


Evaluation Metrics
They evaluate both predictive accuracy and interval quality.

Predictive accuracy

RMSE



Uncertainty quality

PICP: Prediction Interval Coverage Probability
MPIW: Mean Prediction Interval Width

This is a sensible start, although still limited for a full UQ evaluation.

text:
4. Validation Strategy (Predictions & Explanations)

Validating the Predictions
The predictive side is evaluated using: - RMSE for point prediction error - PICP for coverage reliability - MPIW for interval compactness
The framework is tested on both McMaster and Oxford datasets, and the paper claims consistent performance across both despite operating condition shifts.


Validating the Explanations
The explanation validation is mostly qualitative. The authors argue that: - SHAP and IG consistently identify SOC and voltage as the most influential features - LIME helps explain atypical degradation cases - layer-wise analysis shows different features becoming more or less important across network depth - counterfactual changes are broadly consistent with the attribution results
In other words, the paper treats agreement across multiple XAI methods as a kind of internal consistency check.


Layer-Wise Findings
A particularly interesting point is that: - SOC dominates deeper convolutional layers - Current and voltage are more important in earlier layers
This suggests a hierarchical representation: - early layers extract more direct electrical signatures - deeper layers may encode more abstract health-related structure centered around SOC
This is one of the more interesting interpretability observations in the paper.

text:
5. Main Results

Explainability Results

SHAP and IG consistently rank SOC and voltage as the dominant features
LIME is helpful for local edge-case interpretation
Counterfactuals identify minimal changes that alter SOH predictions in ways broadly aligned with SHAP and IG
Layer-wise SHAP shows the representation of importance shifts across the network depth



Uncertainty Results
On the McMaster dataset: - RMSE: 0.01175 - PICP: 91.2% - MPIW: 0.2311
On the Oxford dataset: - RMSE: 0.01432 - PICP: 89.8% - MPIW: 0.2457


Interpretation of the Results
The paper argues that these results indicate: - low prediction error - reasonably high coverage - compact enough intervals to remain informative - some degree of generalizability across datasets

text:
6. Strengths of the Study

Strength 1: Joint Treatment of Two Real Problems
A major strength is that the paper does not treat explainability and uncertainty as separate optional add-ons. It directly addresses two deployment bottlenecks of black-box SOH models: - lack of interpretability - lack of calibrated confidence
That is valuable because most papers address only one of the two.


Strength 2: Multi-Method Explainability
Using SHAP, LIME, IG, and counterfactuals together gives the framework some triangulation value. Even if no formal faithfulness tests are used, comparing multiple explanation methods is still more convincing than relying on only one.


Strength 3: Distinction Between Epistemic and Aleatoric Uncertainty
The paper explicitly acknowledges that not all uncertainty is the same. That conceptual distinction is important and often missing in applied engineering papers.


Strength 4: Cross-Dataset Evaluation
Using both McMaster and Oxford datasets is a good design choice. It provides at least some evidence that the framework is not tied to a single dataset.


Strength 5: Practical Framing
The paper keeps the discussion tied to battery management relevance: - safety - real-time deployment - confidence-aware diagnostics - actionable outputs
That practical framing makes the paper useful even if some methodological pieces are still immature.

text:
7. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: The Paper Overstates the Strength of Its Uncertainty Results
There appears to be a serious inconsistency between the abstract and the main results table.

In the abstract, the paper reports:

PICP = 0.6288, meaning only 62.88% of ground truth values fell within the intervals

But in the results section and Table I, it reports:

PICP = 91.2% on McMaster
PICP = 89.8% on Oxford


These are drastically different conclusions. A PICP of 62.88% would indicate poor interval calibration for nominal 95% intervals. A PICP near 90% is still imperfect, but far more acceptable.
This inconsistency is not minor. It materially affects how trustworthy the uncertainty framework really is. At minimum, it suggests reporting or methodological confusion that should have been clarified.


Criticism 2: Interval Metrics Alone Are Not Enough for UQ Validation
The framework only evaluates uncertainty using: - PICP - MPIW
These are useful, but incomplete. They do not tell us whether uncertainty increases when the model is more likely to be wrong. A model can produce broad or narrow intervals with acceptable average coverage while still ranking risky predictions badly.
The paper itself partially acknowledges this and suggests future inclusion of: - Spearman correlation between uncertainty and residuals - Negative log-likelihood (NLL) - Brier score
This is a good admission, but it also means the current uncertainty evaluation is underdeveloped.


Criticism 3: The Proposed ACI Is More Engineering Heuristic Than Principled Probabilistic Modeling
The adaptive confidence interval formulation pools estimates from model and data uncertainty in a fairly ad hoc way. It is practical, but it is not the same as learning a full predictive distribution. There is no rigorous derivation showing that this pooled CI is statistically calibrated under the nonlinear dependencies of the model.
So while the framework is uncertainty-aware, it is not necessarily a fully principled uncertainty model. It is closer to an uncertainty engineering wrapper around point predictors.


Criticism 4: The Explainability Validation Is Almost Entirely Qualitative
The explainability claims are based on: - intuitive agreement with domain expectations - agreement across methods - plausible feature rankings
That is better than nothing, but it is still weak. The paper does not test: - explanation robustness - explanation stability under perturbation - explanation fidelity - sensitivity to correlated inputs - reproducibility of attributions across retraining runs
This is especially important because battery features like voltage, current, temperature, and SOC are often strongly correlated.


Criticism 5: “Model-Agnostic” Is Used a Bit Too Generously
The paper describes the framework as model-agnostic, but several components are not uniformly lightweight or architecture-independent in practice. For example: - layer-wise analysis depends on network internals - IG is gradient-based and tied to differentiable models - counterfactuals may depend heavily on optimization details and feature realism constraints
So the system is not purely model-agnostic in the strictest sense.


Criticism 6: Counterfactuals Are Underdeveloped
The paper includes counterfactual explanations, but only at the input level. That means they identify minimal feature changes, but they do not really explain internal reasoning pathways. The authors admit this and suggest future use of r-counterfactuals or internal-layer counterfactuals.
This is important because input-level counterfactuals on sensor data can easily become unrealistic or physically implausible unless constrained properly.


Criticism 7: Computational Cost Is Acknowledged but Not Quantified
The paper repeatedly mentions runtime overhead from: - MC dropout - layer-wise explainability - counterfactual generation
But it does not actually benchmark: - latency - memory - deployment cost - scalability across hardware
That weakens the claim of practical deployment readiness.


Criticism 8: Baseline Comparison Is Weak
The paper mainly demonstrates that the framework works, but it does not perform a strong comparative study against: - simpler neural baselines without XAI/UQ - probabilistic neural baselines - Bayesian deep learning baselines - conformal prediction approaches - quantile regression methods - heteroscedastic regression models
The authors state this will be future work, but without such comparisons it is difficult to isolate the val

title: A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning: An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective
text:
Authors & Year: Wenchong He, Zhe Jiang (2023; arXiv version updated 2024)
Venue (Journal/Conference): ACM Computing Surveys

Paper Type: Survey / Taxonomy paper
Primary Topic: Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) for Deep Neural Networks
Core Perspective: Categorization of UQ methods by uncertainty source
Link/DOI: ACM Computing Surveys article; arXiv preprint version noted in the paper
Code/Data Available?: No central code contribution; this is a conceptual and methodological survey
Proximity/Threat Level: Medium to High / Foundational framing paper
Date Reviewed: 2026-03-13

objectID: reviews/A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning: An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why this survey matters):

Deep neural networks often achieve excellent predictive accuracy, but they can still make incorrect predictions with unjustifiably high confidence. This is dangerous in high-stakes domains such as medical diagnosis, autonomous driving, disaster response, and other safety-critical systems. The paper argues that predictive accuracy alone is insufficient; models also need to know when they do not know. :contentReferenceoaicite:1
The authors position uncertainty quantification (UQ) as the mechanism for assigning confidence to predictions beyond conventional accuracy metrics. They emphasize that uncertainty is not monolithic: it arises from different sources, and understanding those sources is essential for selecting the right method. :contentReferenceoaicite:2

Their claim to fame / Novelty:

The central novelty is not a new UQ algorithm, but a new taxonomy. Existing surveys, according to the authors, mainly categorize UQ methods either:

by neural network architecture, or
by Bayesian vs non-Bayesian viewpoint.

This survey instead organizes methods by uncertainty source, specifically:

Data uncertainty,
Model uncertainty, and
Combined data + model uncertainty.


The authors argue this is practically more useful, because in real problems one type of uncertainty may dominate, and method selection should be driven by that reality rather than by model family labels alone. :contentReferenceoaicite:3

The conceptual contribution:

The paper clearly distinguishes:

Data uncertainty (aleatoric) as randomness/noise intrinsic to the data and often irreducible,
Model uncertainty (epistemic) as lack of knowledge due to limited data, suboptimal architecture/parameters, or distribution shift, which is often reducible. :contentReferenceoaicite:4

It then maps major UQ approaches to these uncertainty types, creating a more decision-oriented view of the literature. :contentReferenceoaicite:5

The practical value of the survey:

The taxonomy is linked to real deployment contexts such as:

out-of-distribution detection,
active learning,
robustness,
reinforcement learning,
medical applications,
geoscience,
transportation,
biochemical engineering.


This makes the survey more than a catalog; it acts as a method-selection framework.

Their ultimate message:

No single UQ method is universally best.
The right UQ choice depends on:

what kind of uncertainty dominates,
whether calibration, interpretability, computational tractability, or OOD awareness matters most,
and what deployment environment the model must survive in.

objectID: reviews/A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective.html#methodology-technical-framing
href: reviews/A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective.html#methodology-technical-framing
title: A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning: An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Framing

Problem formulation:

The survey defines a learning setup where a model predicts both:

the target, and
an associated uncertainty score.

The paper frames UQ as optimizing not only empirical prediction loss, but also calibration-related behaviour through expected calibration error (ECE). In other words, a good UQ model should not merely be accurate; its confidence should align with its actual error rate. :contentReferenceoaicite:8

Two-source uncertainty formulation:

Data uncertainty arises from noisy measurement, ambiguity in labels, overlap in class distributions, imperfect sampling, transmission errors, representation limitations, and heterogeneous noise levels. The paper emphasizes that for classification this can be understood through conditional entropy, while for regression it is tied to observation noise, especially heteroscedastic noise. :contentReferenceoaicite:9
Model uncertainty arises from imperfect parameter estimation, architecture misspecification, and training/test distribution mismatch, including OOD cases. The paper stresses that this is often the type of uncertainty you hope to reduce with more data or better modelling choices. :contentReferenceoaicite:10

Their master taxonomy:

The survey groups UQ methods into three main branches:

Model uncertainty methods
Data uncertainty methods
Combined model + data uncertainty methods


This top-level taxonomy is arguably the main intellectual contribution of the paper. :contentReferenceoaicite:11
crumbs: A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning: An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective

objectID: reviews/A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective.html#detailed-taxonomy-of-uq-methods
href: reviews/A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective.html#detailed-taxonomy-of-uq-methods
title: A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning: An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective
text:
4. Detailed Taxonomy of UQ Methods

4.1 Model Uncertainty Methods
The survey divides model uncertainty methods into three main subfamilies.

A. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs)

The Bayesian view places a prior over network parameters and seeks a posterior distribution over weights instead of a single point estimate. Uncertainty is then reflected in the predictive distribution obtained by integrating over parameter uncertainty. :contentReferenceoaicite:12
The paper reviews several approximations because exact posterior inference is intractable in modern DNNs:

Variational Inference (VI):

Approximates the posterior with a tractable family, often Gaussian.
Advantage: principled and flexible.
Limitation: capturing full covariance is computationally expensive, and simplifying covariance structure can reduce fidelity. :contentReferenceoaicite:13

Laplace Approximation:

Approximates the posterior locally around the MAP estimate using a Gaussian based on the Hessian.
Advantage: can be applied post hoc to a trained model.
Limitation: local approximation, difficulty handling multimodal posteriors, Hessian inversion issues, and calibration challenges. :contentReferenceoaicite:14

MCMC-based approximations:

Theoretically attractive because they can converge to the exact posterior with enough samples.
Limitation: prohibitively expensive and often slow to converge in high-dimensional DNN settings. :contentReferenceoaicite:15

MC Dropout:

Included as a practical approximation to BNN-style uncertainty.
Advantage: easy to implement with minimal architecture changes.
Limitation: often less calibrated than stronger baselines, despite its popularity. :contentReferenceoaicite:16





B. Ensemble Methods

Ensembles estimate uncertainty from variation across multiple independently trained models. The survey treats them as capturing uncertainty from architecture choice, parameter initialization, data sampling, and training hyperparameters. :contentReferenceoaicite:17
Variants include:

Bootstrap ensembles
Architecture ensembles
Hyperensembles


Strengths:

Simple idea,
Scalable conceptually,
Can capture several dimensions of model uncertainty.


Weaknesses:

High computation and memory cost,
Dependence on model diversity; if ensemble members collapse to similar solutions, uncertainty estimates weaken. :contentReferenceoaicite:18




C. Sample-density-aware Methods

The survey argues that BNNs and ensembles do not automatically solve uncertainty under low sample density or dataset shift. A model can still be overconfident far from the training support. :contentReferenceoaicite:19
This leads to:

Gaussian Process (GP) hybrids
Deep kernel learning
Deep Gaussian processes
Distance-aware neural networks


The central intuition is that uncertainty should increase when a test point lies far from known training regions. GP-inspired approaches naturally express this, but classical GP methods struggle with computational scaling and kernel design in high-dimensional settings. Hybrid methods try to combine DNN representation learning with GP uncertainty behaviour. :contentReferenceoaicite:20
Distance-aware DNNs try to enforce meaningful latent distances so that OOD points do not collapse into in-distribution-looking representations. This is appealing for robust uncertainty estimation, but the paper notes these methods are difficult to enforce properly, especially when using Lipschitz-style constraints. :contentReferenceoaicite:21





4.2 Data Uncertainty Methods
The survey next reviews methods aimed at capturing irreducible or observation-related uncertainty.

A. Deep Discriminative Models
These directly model predictive uncertainty in supervised learning.

Parametric predictive distributions

For classification, output distributions are often categorical.
For regression, models frequently assume Gaussian noise with mean and variance predicted by the network, giving heteroscedastic regression.
Mixture density networks extend this to multimodal outputs.


Strength:

Direct and intuitive.
Naturally suited to heteroscedastic regression problems.

Limitation:

Requires choosing a parametric family, which may not match the true data-generating uncertainty.
The survey is careful to note that distribution choice matters greatly. :contentReferenceoaicite:22

Non-parametric prediction interval methods

These avoid committing to an explicit distributional form and instead estimate intervals directly.
The survey discusses methods such as lower-upper bound estimation and constrained optimization views of interval learning, including the trade-off between interval width and coverage probability. :contentReferenceoaicite:23

Strength:

More flexible when the true distribution is hard to specify.

Limitation:

Often harder to optimize well, and interval-based uncertainty may provide less full information than a full predictive density. :contentReferenceoaicite:24




B. Deep Generative Models

The survey then covers deep generative approaches that learn complex predictive distributions in high-dimensional spaces, especially via conditional deep generative models. :contentReferenceoaicite:25
These methods use latent variables to represent predictive variability and can generate multiple outputs for the same input, from which uncertainty can be derived.
Broadly, the survey positions them as attractive when:

the predictive distribution is highly complex,
a simple Gaussian or interval assumption is too restrictive,
and one wants richer uncertainty structure.

But these methods also bring their own practical burdens:

training complexity,
stability concerns,
and more difficult interpretation. :contentReferenceoaicite:26






4.3 Combined Model + Data Uncertainty

The survey emphasizes that many real-world problems require capturing both data and model uncertainty simultaneously. :contentReferenceoaicite:27
One route is simply to combine a model-uncertainty method with a data-uncertainty method, but this increases computation and storage demands.
Another route is evidential deep learning, which the paper highlights as a more efficient single-network framework for representing total uncertainty. :contentReferenceoaicite:28
This part of the survey is important conceptually because it recognizes that real deployment does not neatly separate aleatoric and epistemic effects.

title: A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning: An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective
text:
5. Application Domains & Why They Matter
A strong feature of the paper is that it does not stay purely abstract. It grounds the taxonomy in application domains.

Medical diagnosis

Both uncertainty types are critical.
Data uncertainty appears through ambiguous labels, noisy measurements, and registration errors.
Model uncertainty appears when patient populations are not well represented in training data.
The survey also points out that interpretability of uncertainty is especially important here. :contentReferenceoaicite:29

Geoscience

Spatiotemporal data bring sensor noise, registration uncertainty, heterogeneous distributions across space and time, and sparse observations.
This domain strongly illustrates why dataset shift and sample density matter. :contentReferenceoaicite:30

Transportation

Traffic and autonomous driving problems contain temporal dynamics, measurement loss, environmental perturbations, and safety-critical decisions.
This domain nicely motivates both stochastic uncertainty and robustness under unusual events. :contentReferenceoaicite:31

Biochemical engineering

Here the survey highlights partial scientific knowledge, biological heterogeneity, and uncertain mechanistic relationships.
This is relevant to your kind of research mindset, because it shows UQ is not only about model performance but about supporting scientific decision-making where domain knowledge is incomplete. :contentReferenceoaicite:32

Deep reinforcement learning

The paper later shows how both data uncertainty and model uncertainty matter in RL:

stochastic rewards/transitions imply data uncertainty,
limited state-space coverage implies model uncertainty.

This matters for exploration, policy learning, and safe decision-making. :contentReferenceoaicite:33

title: A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning: An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective
section: 6. Validation Strategy / How the Survey Judges Methods
text:
6. Validation Strategy / How the Survey Judges Methods

This is a survey, not a benchmark paper.

It does not perform one unified empirical benchmark across all methods.
Instead, its “validation” is conceptual and comparative:

defining uncertainty sources,
mapping methods to those sources,
listing strengths and weaknesses,
and discussing how these methods relate to application needs.


What it does well:

It provides a clear framework for method selection.
It avoids treating all UQ techniques as interchangeable.
It makes the literature easier to reason about from a deployment perspective. :contentReferenceoaicite:35

What it does not do:

It does not empirically establish which family is best under standardized tasks.
It does not provide a unified quantitative benchmark of calibration, sharpness, OOD detection, or computational burden across all methods.
So its value is primarily taxonomic and interpretive, not experimental.

objectID: reviews/A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective.html#thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
href: reviews/A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective.html#thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
title: A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning: An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective
text:
7. Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1 (AI): Strong conceptual framing, but not a comparative benchmark

The taxonomy is genuinely useful, but the paper stops short of giving a rigorous cross-method empirical benchmark. That means a reader still has to do substantial downstream work to decide which UQ method is best for a given forecasting problem.

Criticism 2 (AI): The survey is broad, but less deep on forecasting-specific metrics

Since this is a general DNN UQ survey, it does not deeply specialize in forecasting metrics such as CRPS, interval score decomposition, coverage-width trade-offs in operational forecasting, calibration under temporal dependence, or multi-horizon uncertainty quality.
For your work in probabilistic forecasting, this paper is better as a conceptual scaffold than as a forecasting-methods playbook.

Criticism 3 (AI): Some sections prioritize categorization over deployment nuance

The taxonomy is clean, but in practice many methods blur boundaries.
For example, ensembles can partially reflect data effects indirectly, and some generative approaches can capture both uncertainty families depending on training design.
The categories are useful, but reality is messier than the diagram.

Criticism 4 (AI): Limited treatment of explanation-quality evaluation

The future directions note that combining UQ and explainability is important, which is excellent, but the survey does not yet give a concrete framework for evaluating that interaction.
This is especially relevant if one wants not just calibrated uncertainty, but interpretable uncertainty attribution. :contentReferenceoaicite:36

Criticism 5 (AI): Computational practicality remains a central unresolved problem

The survey repeatedly acknowledges that many theoretically attractive methods, especially BNNs, MCMC, GP hybrids, and combinations of model and data uncertainty, are computationally expensive or difficult to scale. :contentReferenceoaicite:37
This is important because the “best” UQ method on paper may still be unusable in large operational settings.

section: 8. Relevance to My Research / Why This Paper Matters for Me
text:
8. Relevance to My Research / Why This Paper Matters for Me

Why this paper is useful for probabilistic energy forecasting:

It gives a strong theoretical basis for distinguishing:

irreducible uncertainty in the data generating process,
from reducible uncertainty caused by limited coverage, model misspecification, or distribution shift.

That distinction is extremely relevant in electricity, load, and renewable forecasting, where weather-driven stochasticity and OOD operating regimes coexist.

How I can use it in my literature review:

I can cite this paper to justify why uncertainty should not be treated as one scalar concept.
I can use its taxonomy to structure my review section:

data uncertainty methods,
model uncertainty methods,
joint methods,
application-driven method choice.


How it helps position my work:

If I am developing a forecasting model for real-world deployment, this paper supports the argument that:

calibration alone is not enough,
model family alone is not enough,
and uncertainty-method choice must align with the dominant uncertainty source in the operational setting.


Why it matters for OOD and shift-aware forecasting:

The survey explicitly recognizes dataset shift and low sample density as sources of model uncertainty.
That directly supports research directions involving:

OOD detection,
epistemic uncertainty,
ensemble disagreement,
density-aware representations,
and robustness under temporal or climatic regime shift. :contentReferenceoaicite:39

text:
9. Future Directions Highlighted by the Paper
One of the most useful parts of the survey is that it explicitly identifies open gaps.

Combine UQ with DNN explainability

The paper argues that uncertainty quantification and explanation are both central to trustworthy AI, but are still mostly treated separately.
It suggests that combining them could produce more robust and trustworthy systems. This is a particularly important insight for XAI-driven forecasting research. :contentReferenceoaicite:40

Methodological gaps

Although not all future directions are fully elaborated in the snippets retrieved, the paper clearly frames open issues around:

calibration,
scalability,
trustworthy deployment,
handling multiple uncertainty sources coherently,
and application-specific method selection.


My interpretation of the most important unresolved challenge:

The field still lacks a clean, scalable, interpretable, and empirically robust framework that simultaneously:

separates aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty,
handles OOD data well,
scales to modern deep learning,
and is understandable enough for operators in high-stakes domains.

text:
Authors & Year: Pei Du, Xuankai Zhang, Tingting Chen, and Wendong Yang (2025)
Venue (Journal/Conference): Systems (MDPI)
DOI: 10.3390/systems13111011
Primary Topic/Concept: Hybrid deep learning for carbon price forecasting with feature selection, interpretability, and interval prediction
Core Methods: Boruta, BiTCN, Informer, SHAP, Monte Carlo Dropout
Markets Studied: Guangdong and Shanghai carbon markets, with additional robustness tests on EU carbon prices and U.S. Henry Hub natural gas
Date Reviewed: 2026-03-13
Proximity/Threat Level: Moderate to High, especially if your work also combines multivariate hybrid forecasting with explainability and uncertainty quantification

objectID: reviews/An Interpretable Hybrid System Using Temporal Convolutional Network and Informer Model for Carbon Price Prediction.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/An Interpretable Hybrid System Using Temporal Convolutional Network and Informer Model for Carbon Price Prediction.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: An Interpretable Hybrid System Using Temporal Convolutional Network and Informer Model for Carbon Price Prediction
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why this problem matters)
Carbon price forecasting matters because carbon prices sit at the center of emissions trading systems and affect both policy design and enterprise compliance decisions. The authors argue that the carbon market is nonlinear, complex, and influenced by many external drivers, so simple historical or deterministic forecasting approaches are inadequate.


The Motivation (Why a hybrid model?)
The paper argues that a single model is often not flexible enough to capture all the components of carbon price dynamics. Carbon prices are influenced by multiple heterogeneous drivers, and different architectures may be better at extracting different structures in the data. Their proposed solution is therefore a staged hybrid architecture: - BiTCN for local spatio-temporal dependence and bidirectional feature extraction - Informer for long-sequence global dependency modeling using sparse attention


The Motivation (Why explainability?)
The paper is explicitly positioned against the black-box nature of many deep forecasting systems. The authors want not only better prediction accuracy, but also: - insight into which drivers matter most, - understanding of regional heterogeneity across markets, - and a more decision-useful model for governments and firms.


The Motivation (Why interval prediction?)
The authors make the very sensible point that point predictions alone are often insufficient in real decision settings. Decision-makers need uncertainty bounds, not just a single predicted value. They therefore add Monte Carlo dropout to obtain prediction intervals.


Their claim to fame / novelty
The paper’s novelty is not a single new algorithm, but rather the integration of several components into one interpretable system: 1. Multi-source feature integration, including structured and unstructured variables, 2. Boruta-based feature selection over 21 candidate factors, 3. BiTCN-Informer hybridization for staged feature extraction, 4. SHAP-based interpretability for both global and local driver analysis, 5. Monte Carlo dropout for interval prediction, 6. Cross-market validation beyond the two core Chinese datasets.


What the XAI actually did
SHAP was used not just decoratively, but to produce market-specific driver rankings and regional comparisons: - In Guangdong, the EU-ETS carbon price was the most influential driver. - In Shanghai, energy and financial variables such as crude oil, natural gas, and USD/CNY were more dominant.
This is important because the explainability output is tied directly to an economic interpretation rather than presented as generic feature-importance plots.
