objectID: reviews/Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values.html#methodology-technical-details
href: reviews/Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values.html#methodology-technical-details
title: Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

Starting Point: Standard SHAP Limitation

Conventional Shapley values usually use a payoff like
v0(S, x) = E[f(x) | X_S = x_S],
which is fundamentally tied to explaining a prediction or expected outcome.
This ignores higher moments of the predictive distribution, especially variance or entropy. :contentReferenceoaicite:6

Their Core Idea: Change the Value Function

Instead of only explaining the mean prediction, they define alternative cooperative games whose payoffs depend on uncertainty-relevant quantities.
The paper studies several value functions:

KL-based game: v_KL(S, x) = -D_KL(p(Y|x) || p(Y|x_S))
Cross-entropy game: v_CE(S, x) = -H(p(Y|x), p(Y|x_S))
Information-gain game: v_IG(S, x) = -H(Y|x_S)
Entropy game: v_H(S, x) = H(Y|x_S)
Modified entropy game: v_H*(S, x) = E[H(p(Y|x)) | X_S = x_S] :contentReferenceoaicite:7


Important Theoretical Result:

Under these alternative games, a feature’s marginal contribution gets a clear information-theoretic meaning.
For example, under the information-gain game, the marginal contribution equals local conditional mutual information: Δ_IG(S, j, x) = I(Y; x_j | x_S). :contentReferenceoaicite:8

Why this is powerful:

The attributions are no longer just “how much this feature changed a prediction.”
They become “how much this feature reduced or increased uncertainty, in bits, at this instance.”

Connection to Conditional Independence:

A major theoretical strength is the link to conditional independence and context-specific independence.
The paper proves that, for the information-theoretic games, zero marginal payout corresponds closely to conditional independence structure, except for measure-zero pathologies. :contentReferenceoaicite:9

How Uncertainty is Estimated in Practice:

They introduce a generic uncertainty estimator h(x).
For classification, total predictive entropy is estimated from class probabilities.
They decompose uncertainty into:

Total entropy
Aleatoric uncertainty
Epistemic uncertainty

The decomposition is done using ensembles such as random forests or MC dropout style basis functions. :contentReferenceoaicite:10

Reference Distribution / Sampling Choices:

The framework is deliberately modular regarding how out-of-coalition features are imputed.
They do not insist on a single “correct” reference distribution, and acknowledge the long-standing debate around marginal vs conditional vs structurally informed sampling.
They also note the usual caveat that Shapley methods can become unreliable if imputations force the model far off the data manifold. :contentReferenceoaicite:11

Computational Strategy:

Exact Shapley computation is combinatorial and quickly infeasible.
They therefore use coalition sampling, noting that most total weight lies near extreme coalition sizes.
They also use paired sampling to reduce variance and improve convergence. :contentReferenceoaicite:12
crumbs: Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values

objectID: reviews/Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values.html#validation-strategy-predictions-explanations-and-inference
href: reviews/Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values.html#validation-strategy-predictions-explanations-and-inference
title: Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values
text:
4. Validation Strategy (Predictions, Explanations, and Inference)

What they validate:

They validate not only whether the uncertainty explanations “look sensible,” but also whether the framework behaves coherently under known statistical structure and under real ML tasks like shift detection and feature selection.

Formal Statistical Validation:

One of the most important additions is a split conformal inference procedure for Shapley variables.
They split data into one part for model fitting and one part for Shapley computation, then estimate empirical quantile bounds for the Shapley distribution of a feature.
This gives finite-sample coverage guarantees for whether the Shapley value of a feature tends to stay near zero. :contentReferenceoaicite:13

Interpretation of This Inference Step:

This lets them ask a more statistically grounded question:

Is this feature’s uncertainty attribution typically close to zero?

That is especially useful for feature selection and for distinguishing relevant from irrelevant predictors.

Limitations of the Guarantee:

The guarantee is not conditional on all covariates, so it is not a fully local confidence interval in the strongest possible sense.
It is more of a PAC-style population guarantee for the distribution of Shapley values of a feature. :contentReferenceoaicite:14
crumbs: Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values

objectID: reviews/Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values.html#experiments-empirical-results
href: reviews/Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values.html#experiments-empirical-results
title: Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values
text:
5. Experiments & Empirical Results

5.1 Supervised Learning Proof-of-Concept

Image Data (MNIST):

They train binary CNN classifiers on hard-to-distinguish digit pairs: 1 vs 7, 3 vs 8, and 4 vs 9.
Using a DeepSHAP-style pipeline with MC dropout, they visualize pixel contributions to predictive entropy.
They show that epistemic uncertainty explanations highlight image regions that genuinely make the model more or less uncertain.
Aleatoric uncertainty appears more diffuse, consistent with irreducible noise. :contentReferenceoaicite:15

Text Data (IMDB sentiment):

They apply the method to a transformer sentiment model on IMDB reviews.
Token-level attributions indicate which words or phrases increase predictive ambiguity.
The examples show that the model’s uncertainty rises around semantically mixed or contradictory expressions. :contentReferenceoaicite:16

Tabular Simulation:

They design a Gaussian simulation where Shapley values under the entropy game have a closed-form solution.
This allows them to compare multiple imputation methods for out-of-coalition features:

KernelSHAP
maximum likelihood
copula
empirical samplers
ctree

Result: no single sampler dominates universally, but methods that respect conditional dependencies generally perform better when features are correlated.
Most methods converge toward the true value with increasing sample size. :contentReferenceoaicite:17




5.2 Covariate Shift and Active Learning

Datasets Used:

BreastCancer, Diabetes, Ionosphere, and Sonar from the UCI repository.

Setup:

XGBoost with 50 trees estimates class probabilities and predictive uncertainty.
They perturb one random feature in the test set by adding Gaussian noise, creating a subtle covariate shift.

Main Result:

The information-theoretic Shapley values correctly identify the perturbed feature as the driver of excess uncertainty.
Importantly, the perturbations are subtle and often remain within the observed support of training values, so this is not a trivial outlier-detection case.

Interpretation:

The method can be paired with shift-detection or active-learning systems to explain why a sample has been marked as uncertain or exploratory. :contentReferenceoaicite:18




5.3 Feature Selection

Benchmark Design:

They modify the Friedman benchmark so that:

the conditional mean depends on one group of features,
the conditional variance depends on a different group.


Purpose:

This is a very clean test of whether the method can separate “features that matter for the mean” from “features that matter for uncertainty.”

Main Result:

It succeeds: Shapley values for the mean cluster around zero for irrelevant mean features, and Shapley values for the variance cluster around zero for irrelevant variance features.
This supports the claim that the method can distinguish different modes of predictive information rather than collapsing everything into a single importance notion. :contentReferenceoaicite:19




5.4 Active Feature-Value Acquisition

Setup:

Using the same modified Friedman setup, they randomly delete entries in the design matrix to simulate missing data or costly feature acquisition.

Goal:

Rank which missing feature values are most useful to query next.

Main Result:

Absolute Shapley values provide informative feature rankings.
Performance degrades as missingness increases, as expected, but remains useful.
Even at 50% missingness, they report an AUC of 0.682, which is still substantially above random. :contentReferenceoaicite:20

objectID: reviews/Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
href: reviews/Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
title: Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values
text:
6. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: Strong Theory, but Less of a Head-to-Head with Modern Uncertainty-XAI Alternatives

The paper is theoretically elegant, but the empirical section is more proof-of-concept than benchmark-heavy.
It demonstrates usefulness across tasks, but does not present a broad, modern comparison against a rich set of competing uncertainty explanation methods.
Since the authors themselves note that very little prior work exists, this is understandable, but it still means the empirical dominance claim is modest rather than overwhelming.

Criticism 2: Modularity is a Strength, but also a Source of Ambiguity

The method is deliberately agnostic about uncertainty estimator choice, reference distribution, and imputation strategy.
That makes the framework flexible and broadly applicable.
But it also means practical performance can vary a lot depending on implementation choices. In other words, the “method” is partly a family of methods, not a single locked-down pipeline.

Criticism 3: Computational Burden is Still a Serious Issue

The paper openly acknowledges that Shapley computation is hard, and that dependency-aware imputations are statistically and computationally expensive.
So while the theoretical framing is strong, scaling this cleanly to large, high-dimensional forecasting problems could still be painful.

Criticism 4: Local Information-Theoretic Meaning Does Not Fully Rescue Shapley Averaging

One of the strongest parts of the paper is that marginal payouts Δv(S, j, x) have a clean interpretation as local dependence measures.
But the authors themselves note that once these quantities are averaged over coalitions into Shapley values, interpretability becomes murkier again.
So the framework improves the semantics of local contributions, but does not completely solve all classic SHAP interpretability concerns.

Criticism 5: The Conformal Inference Result is Useful, but Not Fully Local

The coverage guarantee is over the distribution of Shapley values for a feature, not fully conditioned on the local feature context.
So it gives population-style control, not the strongest possible instance-conditional uncertainty statement.

Observation on Relevance to Forecasting Research:

This paper is especially valuable conceptually for your area because it separates prediction importance from uncertainty importance.
For probabilistic load, solar, or wind forecasting, that is a major distinction:

a feature may improve the conditional mean forecast,
a different feature may tighten or widen the predictive distribution.

That makes this work highly relevant if your research is trying to explain not only point forecasts but also predictive intervals, quantiles, CRPS behaviour, or uncertainty calibration.

title: Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values
section: 7. Why This Paper Matters for My Research Context
text:
7. Why This Paper Matters for My Research Context

If I work on probabilistic forecasting:

This paper gives a principled way to explain why uncertainty changes across the input space, not just why the expected forecast changes.

If I work on SHAP-based feature selection:

It suggests that feature selection should perhaps be task-specific:

one subset for point prediction,
another subset for uncertainty estimation.


If I care about trust and robustness:

The connection to covariate shift detection is especially important.
It is not just “the model is uncertain,” but “this feature is making the model uncertain here.”

If I care about rigorous XAI:

The information-theoretic grounding and conditional independence results are much stronger than many purely heuristic attribution stories.

href: reviews/Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values.html#action-items-integration
title: Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values
text:
8. Action Items & Integration

Read the GitHub repository (facebookresearch/infoshap) and inspect how they implement entropy-based SHAP in practice.
Consider whether my own work should distinguish explanations for point forecasts from explanations for predictive uncertainty.
When using SHAP in probabilistic forecasting, explicitly state whether I am explaining the conditional mean, quantiles, interval width, entropy, variance, or another uncertainty functional.
Explore whether a similar framework can be adapted to probabilistic energy forecasting models, especially where CRPS, coverage, or interval sharpness are important.
In my literature review, position this paper as a foundational bridge between uncertainty quantification and local feature attribution.
Note its practical limitation: the usefulness of the framework depends heavily on the quality of the uncertainty estimator and the chosen feature imputation/reference distribution.
Consider citing this work when motivating why classic SHAP on point predictions is insufficient for uncertainty-aware forecasting research.

href: reviews/Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values.html#bottom-line-takeaway
title: Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values
text:
9. Bottom-Line Takeaway

One-sentence summary:

This paper is important because it upgrades Shapley explanations from “what changed the prediction?” to “what changed the model’s uncertainty, and by how much in information-theoretic terms?”

My overall assessment:

This is a strong conceptual and methodological contribution rather than a paper that wins by brute-force benchmarking.
Its biggest value lies in the framing, theory, and transferability of the idea.
For any uncertainty-aware ML or forecasting project, it is a very useful reference for justifying why XAI should move beyond point predictions alone. :contentReferenceoaicite:21

text:
Authors & Year: Stephan Rabanser, Stephan Günnemann, Zachary C. Lipton (2019)
Venue (Journal/Conference): NeurIPS 2019 (Highly reputable, Tier 1 conference in ML)

objectID: reviews/Failing Loudly An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/Failing Loudly An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why “Fail Loudly”?):

Standard software systems rely on explicit tests and type-checks to throw exceptions (“fail loudly”) when inputs violate assumptions. Machine learning systems, however, generally assume test data is drawn i.i.d. from the training distribution. When this assumption is violated (dataset shift), ML models fail silently, outputting highly confident but incorrect predictions without alerting the operator.

The Core Problem:

High-dimensional data (like images) makes traditional statistical two-sample testing incredibly weak due to the curse of dimensionality. There are no established best practices for detecting shift in complex real-world ML pipelines.

Their Claim to Fame / Novelty:

The paper provides a comprehensive empirical framework for achieving three distinct goals during deployment:

Detect shift using as few examples as possible.
Characterize shift by identifying the samples most representative of the change.
Determine Malignancy, separating shifts that safely preserve model accuracy from those that actively destroy it.


The Value Derived from the Pipeline (What did they actually find?):

BBSDs Reigns Supreme: Using the soft predictions (softmax outputs) of the black-box classifier itself as a dimensionality reduction technique (BBSDs), followed by simple univariate testing, works astonishingly well across a massive variety of shifts—even when the underlying label-shift assumption is violated.
Univariate \(\approx\) Multivariate: Surprisingly, running multiple univariate Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) tests across latent dimensions (with a heavy Bonferroni correction) performs comparably to complex, computationally heavy multivariate kernel tests like MMD.
The MNIST Bombshell: By applying their framework to standard datasets, they discovered that the widely used, supposedly i.i.d. original MNIST train/test split actually contains a statistically significant distribution shift (specifically, the digit ‘6’ is drawn at a different rotation/openness in the test set).
crumbs: Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift

objectID: reviews/Failing Loudly An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift.html#methodology-technical-details
href: reviews/Failing Loudly An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift.html#methodology-technical-details
title: Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

The Pipeline Design:

Step 1: Dimensionality Reduction (DR). Reduce raw high-dimensional inputs to a lower-dimensional latent space \(K\).
Step 2: Two-Sample Testing (TST). Run statistical tests comparing the source (training) latent representations against the target (deployment) latent representations.

Dimensionality Reduction Methods Compared:

No Reduction (Raw pixels)
PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
SRP (Sparse Random Projection)
UAE / TAE (Untrained and Trained Autoencoders)
BBSDs / BBSDh (Black-Box Shift Detection using the classifier’s own Softmax or Hard predictions)
Domain Classifier (A model explicitly trained to distinguish source vs. target data).

Statistical Tests Used:

Multivariate: Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) with a permutation test.
Univariate: Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test aggregated via Bonferroni correction.
Categorical/Binomial: Chi-Squared (for hard labels) and Binomial test (for domain classifiers).

Datasets & Simulated Shifts:

Tested on MNIST, CIFAR-10, USPS, and COIL-100.
Perturbations included: Adversarial (FGSM), Knock-out (class imbalance), Gaussian noise, and Image transforms (rotation, translation, zoom). Shifts were varied by intensity and fraction of affected data (10% to 100%).
crumbs: Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift

objectID: reviews/Failing Loudly An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift.html#validation-strategy-detection-characterization-malignancy
href: reviews/Failing Loudly An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift.html#validation-strategy-detection-characterization-malignancy
title: Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift
text:
4. Validation Strategy (Detection, Characterization, & Malignancy)

Validating Shift Detection:

The authors evaluated the p-value evolution and detection accuracy across varying target sample sizes (\(s \in \{10, \dots, 10000\}\)). BBSDs could reliably detect large shifts with just 20 samples, vastly outperforming methods like PCA or untrained autoencoders.

Validating Shift Characterization (Most Anomalous Samples):

Instead of standard anomaly detection, they used the output probabilities of the Domain Classifier to rank samples. The items the domain classifier most confidently placed in the “target” bucket were presented as exemplars of the shift.

Validating Shift Malignancy:

The Heuristic: To figure out if a shift actually hurts the primary task classifier, they took the “most anomalous” samples identified by the domain classifier and obtained their true labels via an external labeling function. They then checked the black-box model’s accuracy on just those anomalous samples. If accuracy drops significantly compared to the source baseline, the shift is flagged as malignant.
crumbs: Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift

objectID: reviews/Failing Loudly An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
href: reviews/Failing Loudly An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
title: Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift
text:
5. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1 (AI): The Malignancy “Catch-22” (Label Requirement):

The framework’s method for determining if a shift is harmful requires passing the most anomalous target samples to an “external labeling function.” In real-world unsupervised deployment—where distribution shift detection is most critical precisely because we lack labels—this is a massive, often prohibitive assumption. While they argue you only need to label a tiny fraction of data, waiting for human-in-the-loop labeling defeats the purpose of an automated, real-time “loud failure.”

Criticism 2 (AI): Batch vs. Streaming Evaluation:

The methodology relies on classical two-sample testing (p vs q), which inherently assumes we are comparing two static batches of data. Real-world ML pipelines face continuous, time-correlated data streams. Standard KS or MMD tests assume i.i.d. samples within the target window; if the incoming stream has temporal auto-correlation, these tests will throw massive false-positive alarms. The authors briefly acknowledge this in their conclusion, but it remains a critical barrier to out-of-the-box deployment.

Criticism 3 (AI): Image-Centric Bias & Softmax Geometries:

The finding that BBSDs (Softmax outputs) is the ultimate DR technique is highly specific to the geometry of neural networks trained on image classification (ResNet-18). Does this hold up in tabular environments using Gradient Boosted Trees? Does it hold in LLMs? Softmax calibration degrades terribly under shift; while this makes it great for detecting that a shift occurred, it might be overly sensitive to entirely benign shifts in strictly bounded tabular domains.

Criticism 4 (AI): The Danger of the Bonferroni Correction:

Using multiple univariate KS tests combined with a Bonferroni correction worked well here because the latent dimension \(K\) was small (\(K=10\) for BBSDs on CIFAR/MNIST). However, Bonferroni scales terribly. If applied to an ImageNet classifier (\(K=1000\)), the threshold \(\alpha/K\) becomes so conservative that the statistical power of the test would likely vanish, rendering the model blind to subtle shifts.
crumbs: Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift

href: reviews/Failing Loudly An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift.html#action-items-integration-into-my-work
title: Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift
section: 6. Action Items & Integration into My Work
text:
6. Action Items & Integration into My Work

Adopt BBSDs as a Core Baseline: Any framework I build for monitoring ML models in production must benchmark against BBSDs + KS Test. It is computationally virtually free (since the model is already computing softmax anyway) and serves as the gold-standard baseline.
Address the Malignancy Gap: Position my own research as solving the exact limitation this paper introduces: How do we determine shift malignancy entirely unsupervised, without requiring an external labeling oracle? (e.g., via predictive variance, entropy tracking, or self-consistency metrics).
Incorporate the “Domain Classifier” concept for Explainability: Use their method of ranking anomalies via Domain Classifier confidence to explain what shifted in my own datasets, rather than just firing a binary alarm.
Quote the “Failing Loudly” paradigm: This is an excellent philosophical framing for the introduction of my thesis. ML should not fail silently; MLOps pipelines must be designed with explicit statistical circuit-breakers.

title: High-resolution energy consumption forecasting of a university campus power plant based on advanced machine learning techniques
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation
The study is motivated by the operational difficulty of forecasting energy demand in large university campuses, which behave like miniature cities. Their consumption is driven by a mix of weather, academic schedules, building functions, and unusual disruptions such as COVID-19. The authors argue that traditional linear statistical models struggle with such irregular, nonlinear demand patterns, especially for long-horizon forecasting.


Why this matters
Accurate long-term energy forecasts are important for: - balancing production and consumption, - improving operational efficiency of campus energy systems, - reducing costs, - improving sustainability planning, and - supporting better strategic decisions for large institutions.


Their claimed contribution
The paper’s main contribution is not a fundamentally new algorithm, but rather an applied forecasting framework that combines: - a long historical dataset, - multiple classical machine learning baselines, - a strong tabular learner (XGBoost), - SHAP for interpretability, and - a likelihood-style metric (NLL) to supplement deterministic error measures.


What is actually novel here
The practical novelty lies in the combination of: 1. six years of hourly campus demand data, 2. long-term forecasting emphasis, rather than only short-term day-ahead prediction, 3. real-world deployment to forecast the full year 2023, and 4. a lightweight modeling philosophy, explicitly positioned against more computationally heavy deep learning methods.


Their main result
XGBoost was the best-performing model on the testing set, with: - MAE = 0.8680 - RMSE = 1.2078 - MAPE = 3.1292% - R² = 0.94 - NLL = 1.5924
It also outperformed the naïve mean baseline by about 46% in NLL, and the model’s 2023 deployment forecasts remained close to actual campus demand statistics.

href: reviews/High-resolution energy consumption forecasting of a university campus power plant.html#methodology-technical-details
title: High-resolution energy consumption forecasting of a university campus power plant based on advanced machine learning techniques
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

Dataset / Testbed

System studied: University of Missouri campus power plant
Forecasting target: Campus energy demand
Resolution: Hourly
Historical period: 2017 to 2022
Training corpus size: 52,637 hours
Deployment period: Full year 2023, 8,760 hours



Raw inputs
The original dataset contains demand plus key weather parameters: - air temperature, - relative humidity, - wind speed, - wind direction, - atmospheric pressure, - solar intensity.


Feature engineering
The paper expands the feature space through: - Fourier features for seasonality, - lag features based on past demand, - time-series index features for hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, seasonal, holiday, and annual structure.
The authors note that the engineered dataset expanded from 7 original features to 22 features, though they also refer elsewhere to 25 diverse features, which introduces some ambiguity in the exact final feature count.


Preprocessing
The paper reports: - K-Best feature selection, - mode imputation for missing values, - outlier removal, - scaling using Standard Scaler and Min-Max Scaler.


Models compared
Five models were benchmarked: - Decision Tree - Random Forest - Support Vector Regressor - K-Nearest Neighbors - XGBoost


Validation strategy
The paper uses a temporal split, with: - 84% training data covering five years, - 16% testing data covering the most recent year.
Within the training process, they also apply a five-fold time-series cross-validation procedure.


Metrics
The evaluation is broader than many applied campus-energy papers: - MAE - RMSE - MAPE - R² - NMAE - NRMSE - Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL)


Probabilistic framing
The probabilistic component is relatively modest. They do not train a full probabilistic model in the same sense as quantile regression, mixture density models, or NGBoost. Instead, they compute NLL assuming Gaussian residuals on the test set. So the probabilistic evaluation is essentially a post-hoc likelihood check under a residual normality assumption.

title: High-resolution energy consumption forecasting of a university campus power plant based on advanced machine learning techniques
text:
4. Key Empirical Findings

Overall model ranking
The paper shows a clear ordering in test performance: 1. XGBoost 2. Decision Tree 3. KNN 4. Random Forest 5. SVR


Testing-phase performance

SVR: MAE 1.5285, RMSE 2.1426, MAPE 5.3841%, R² 0.78
RF: MAE 1.0470, RMSE 1.7117, MAPE 3.7490%, R² 0.86
KNN: MAE 1.1383, RMSE 1.5998, MAPE 4.0500%, R² 0.88
DT: MAE 0.9252, RMSE 1.3275, MAPE 3.2600%, R² 0.91
XGBoost: MAE 0.8680, RMSE 1.2078, MAPE 3.1292%, R² 0.94



Likelihood-based performance
Their NLL comparison is: - Baseline mean predictor: 2.9586 - SVR: 2.1816 - RF: 2.3314 - KNN: 1.9634 - DT: 1.7235 - XGBoost: 1.5924
This strengthens the case that XGBoost was not merely best in point error, but also best under their Gaussian-residual likelihood criterion.


Sensitivity analysis
The paper does a genuinely useful robustness check: - With 1%, 5%, and 10% random missingness, XGBoost remains fairly stable. - Under a simulated COVID-style demand reduction scenario, the model still keeps R² above 0.92.
This is one of the stronger practical sections of the paper because it moves beyond ordinary train/test reporting.


Real-world deployment
The model was used to forecast the entire year 2023. Reported descriptive statistics show that the forecasted distribution was very close to the actual one: - forecasted mean: 27.53 MWh - actual mean: 27.31 MWh - mean error: 0.22 MWh
They also report: - actual 2023 total campus demand: 239,217 MW - forecasted total: 241,236 MW
This real deployment element makes the paper more valuable than a purely retrospective benchmark.

text:
5. Explainability / SHAP Analysis

Why SHAP was used
The paper uses SHAP to make the XGBoost model more transparent and to identify which variables drive long-term campus demand predictions.


What SHAP found
According to the authors, the most important features were: 1. Air temperature 2. Hour of day 3. Day of week 4. Year index 5. Fourier seasonal terms 6. Relative humidity 7. Solar intensity 8. Lagged demand values


Interpretation of the explanations
This ranking is intuitive and plausible: - Temperature reflects HVAC-driven demand. - Hour of day captures diurnal operating cycles. - Day of week captures weekday/weekend differences. - Seasonal Fourier terms encode broader annual structure. - Lagged demand helps preserve recurrent campus patterns.


What the SHAP section adds
The SHAP analysis supports the claim that the model is not purely opportunistic. It appears to be using physically meaningful and calendar-driven signals rather than only arbitrary correlations.


What the SHAP section does not do
The paper does not use SHAP for: - rigorous feature selection, - causal interpretation, - explanation stability analysis, - robustness analysis of explanations, - comparison of explanations across model classes, or - uncertainty explanation in a richer probabilistic sense.
So SHAP is used primarily as a post-hoc interpretability layer, not as an integrated scientific validation framework.

objectID: reviews/High-resolution energy consumption forecasting of a university campus power plant.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
href: reviews/High-resolution energy consumption forecasting of a university campus power plant.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
title: High-resolution energy consumption forecasting of a university campus power plant based on advanced machine learning techniques
text:
6. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: The “probabilistic forecasting” claim is weaker than it sounds
The paper presents NLL and speaks about uncertainty quantification, but this should be interpreted carefully. The model is still fundamentally a point forecasting model. The probabilistic component comes from assuming Gaussian residuals on the test set, not from learning a full predictive distribution directly. That is a much weaker notion of probabilistic forecasting than: - quantile regression, - conformal prediction, - NGBoost, - Bayesian neural networks, - Gaussian mixture models, or - direct interval/distributional forecasting.
So while the paper does include a probabilistic evaluation metric, it is more accurate to say it offers a likelihood-based post-hoc uncertainty check than a full probabilistic forecasting framework.


Criticism 2: Baseline selection is practical, but not ambitious
The baselines are reasonable classical ML comparators, but they are not especially strong relative to the current state of the art in forecasting research. There is no comparison against: - LSTM/GRU sequence models in this specific benchmark, - Temporal Fusion Transformer, - N-BEATS, - direct quantile boosting, - LightGBM/CatBoost, - conformalized models, - probabilistic deep learning baselines.
The paper explicitly justifies this by emphasizing computational efficiency and long-term practicality, but the tradeoff is that the study proves XGBoost is best among a restricted benchmark set, not necessarily among the strongest modern forecasting methods.


Criticism 3: The probabilistic evaluation assumes Gaussian residuals without deeply justifying it
Their NLL framework depends on a Gaussian residual assumption. Yet campus demand data can be heteroscedastic, regime-dependent, calendar-sensitive, and affected by structural changes. A single Gaussian residual model may not describe that complexity well. This matters because a good NLL under the wrong distributional assumption may still overstate calibration quality.


Criticism 4: Some methodological details are a bit muddy
There are a few places where the exposition feels slightly inconsistent or under-specified: - They mention 25 features in one place and 22 engineered features in another. - They discuss both training/validation/testing and a split where 84% is training and 16% is validation/test in a way that is not always perfectly clean conceptually. - They mention pre-validation and grid search, but the exact tuned hyperparameters are not clearly foregrounded in the parts shown. - The notation around the likelihood section and some metric equations is not especially polished.
These are not fatal flaws, but they reduce reproducibility clarity.


Criticism 5: SHAP is descriptive, not deeply validated
The SHAP results are sensible, but they are mostly used to confirm expected domain relationships. That is useful, but limited. The paper does not ask deeper questions such as: - Are the SHAP rankings stable over time? - Are explanations robust across folds? - Do explanations drift pre-, during-, and post-COVID? - Are the same drivers important in extreme demand events? - Does explanation stability align with forecast stability?
For a paper that highlights explainability, there is room for much stronger XAI analysis.


Criticism 6: Context specificity may limit external generalization
The authors do acknowledge this. The University of Missouri campus has unusual demand drivers, especially lab, research, and animal facilities. That means the demand structure may differ substantially from: - residential districts, - ordinary office campuses, - industrial microgrids, - campuses with electric heating, - campuses in different climates.
So the paper is a strong case study, but not yet a general proof that the same modeling choice will dominate elsewhere.


Criticism 7: The deployment section is a major strength, but still not a full operations study
Forecasting 2023 with post-hoc comparison is excellent and far better than many papers stop at. But the study still does not quantify downstream operational benefit such as: - cost savings, - improved dispatch, - reduced reserve margins, - peak shaving benefit, - emissions reduction, - optimization performance when forecasts are embedded in an EMS.
So the paper demonstrates predictive quality, but not yet full economic or control-system value.

text:
7. What This Paper Gets Right

Strong points

Uses a real operational dataset over a long period.
Includes COVID-era disruption, which is useful for realism.
Chooses a practical and computationally efficient modeling family.
Compares multiple classical models rather than only presenting one.
Adds SHAP, which improves interpretability.
Includes likelihood-based evaluation, even if limited.
Performs sensitivity analysis on missingness and demand shocks.
Most importantly, it includes real-world 2023 deployment, which greatly strengthens credibility.



Why it matters
This paper is valuable because it is operationally grounded. It is not trying to be the most theoretically sophisticated forecasting paper ever written. Instead, it shows how a robust tabular learner can work well in a real campus energy setting, at a one-year horizon, with interpretable drivers and reasonable resilience to data issues.

Why it is relevant
This paper is relevant if I am working on: - energy demand forecasting, - feature importance and XAI, - lightweight forecasting systems, - campus or institutional energy systems, - long-horizon forecasting under real operational constraints.


Where my work can go further
If I want to position my own study beyond this one, I can improve on it by: 1. using true probabilistic forecasting rather than Gaussian residual NLL only, 2. adding stronger modern baselines, 3. evaluating calibration explicitly, 4. validating explanations quantitatively, and 5. connecting forecast quality to actual operational decisions such as dispatch, storage scheduling, or demand response.

text:
10. Bottom-Line Summary
This is a strong applied forecasting paper rather than a methodological breakthrough. Its main achievement is showing that XGBoost, paired with engineered temporal and weather features, can deliver accurate, interpretable, and operationally credible long-term campus energy forecasts. The study is especially strong in its deployment-minded framing and sensitivity analysis. Its main weaknesses are that its probabilistic framing is fairly shallow, its baseline set is limited, and its SHAP analysis remains descriptive rather than rigorously validated. Even so, it is a useful and credible benchmark for real-world institutional energy forecasting.

title: How to evaluate uncertainty estimates in machine learning for regression?
text:
Authors & Year: Laurens Sluijterman, Eric Cator, Tom Heskes (2024 journal article; arXiv v2 in 2023)
Venue: Neural Networks, volume 173, article 106203
DOI: 10.1016/j.neunet.2024.106203
arXiv: 2106.03395
Primary Topic: How uncertainty estimates for regression should be evaluated
Contribution Type: Methodological critique and simulation-based evaluation framework
Methods Used in Demonstrations: Naive bootstrap and concrete dropout
Core Metrics Discussed: Log-likelihood, RMSE, PICP, CICP, PICF, CICF, Brier score, interval width
Proximity / Threat Level: High relevance / methodological foundation for evaluating probabilistic forecasting and interval reliability
Date Reviewed: 2026-06-07

objectID: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: How to evaluate uncertainty estimates in machine learning for regression?
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

What problem are they solving?
The paper argues that common ways of evaluating uncertainty estimates in regression can make an uncertainty method look reliable even when its intervals behave poorly in important regions of the input space.
The authors focus on two dominant evaluation habits:

Log-likelihood testing, where models that output predictive densities are compared using test-set log-likelihood.
Prediction interval coverage probability (PICP), where interval methods are judged by the fraction of test observations falling inside their intervals.

Both seem reasonable at first glance. If a predictive distribution assigns high likelihood to held-out observations, it sounds like the uncertainty is good. If a 90% interval contains about 90% of held-out observations, it sounds calibrated. The paper’s main point is that this reasoning is incomplete.


Main argument
The central claim is that aggregate predictive metrics do not prove that uncertainty estimates are locally reliable.
A method can:

achieve good PICP while being overconfident in one region and underconfident in another;
achieve better log-likelihood because its mean prediction is better, not because its uncertainty estimate is better;
produce acceptable predictive uncertainty while estimating model uncertainty and data noise variance incorrectly;
fail to widen confidence intervals in sparse or poorly sampled regions even though such widening is exactly what epistemic uncertainty should do.



What is novel?
The novelty is not a new forecasting model. The contribution is an evaluation framework.
The authors propose testing uncertainty estimates through controlled simulations where:

the data-generating function is known;
training data can be resampled repeatedly;
prediction and confidence intervals can be evaluated across repeated experiments;
coverage can be checked point by point rather than only on average.

This lets them evaluate pointwise coverage, not merely marginal or average coverage.


Why this matters
For probabilistic forecasting, it is tempting to report one coverage number and one sharpness number. This paper is useful because it explains why that is not enough. A model can have the right global PICP and still be unreliable in the operating regimes where uncertainty matters most.
For energy, load, solar, wind, or other operational forecasting problems, this is especially important because data are not uniformly informative across the system. Some regions may be well sampled, while others may be sparse, seasonal, shifted, or operationally rare. Those are precisely the regions where uncertainty estimates must behave cautiously.

objectID: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#uncertainty-framework-key-definitions
href: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#uncertainty-framework-key-definitions
title: How to evaluate uncertainty estimates in machine learning for regression?
text:
3. Uncertainty Framework & Key Definitions

Regression setup
The paper works in a regression setting where observations are represented as:
[ Y X = x N(f(x), ^2(x)) ]
or equivalently:
[ y_i = f(x_i) + _i ]
Here:

(f(x)) is the true regression function;
(^2(x)) is the data noise variance;
((x)) is the learned model estimate.

The authors distinguish two uncertainty components:

Model uncertainty: uncertainty about the learned estimate ((x)). This corresponds closely to epistemic uncertainty and should be high where the model has limited knowledge.
Data noise variance: irreducible noise in the observation process. This corresponds closely to aleatoric uncertainty.

The predictive uncertainty combines both components. That is part of the problem: a good total predictive uncertainty estimate can hide a bad decomposition into model uncertainty and data noise variance.


Prediction intervals vs confidence intervals
The paper is careful about the difference between prediction intervals and confidence intervals.
Prediction interval (PI):

aims to contain a future observation (Y);
includes both model uncertainty and data noise;
can be checked in real data by asking whether held-out observations fall inside the interval.

Confidence interval (CI):

aims to contain the true function value (f(x));
is about the uncertainty in the estimated function, not the noise in individual future observations;
cannot normally be checked directly in real-world data because (f(x)) is unknown.

This distinction is important. In ordinary applied modelling, if we check whether observed test values fall inside intervals, we are evaluating prediction interval coverage, not confidence interval coverage. Confidence interval coverage can only be evaluated directly when the true function is known, such as in simulation.


Pointwise vs marginal coverage
The most important distinction in the paper is between pointwise and marginal coverage.
Marginal coverage means the interval has the correct coverage on average over the input distribution.
Example: a 90% prediction interval covers 90% of test observations overall.
Pointwise coverage means the interval has the correct coverage at each input location (x).
Example: for each specific operating condition (x), the 90% interval covers the target 90% of the time across repeated experiments.
Pointwise coverage is stronger and more useful. Marginal coverage can hide local failures. A model can be too narrow in some regions and too wide in others, while still averaging to the right global PICP.


Important wording clarification
The paper often talks about testing coverage on a “single data set.” That wording can be confusing in applied system modelling.
The more useful interpretation is:

A single collected sample or single train/test split gives only one realization of the system’s data-generating process. It may not reveal whether intervals behave correctly across repeated samples or across all operating regimes of the system.

For a real physical or operational system, the concern is not just “one dataset” in the abstract. The concern is uneven system coverage. If some part of the operating space has little data, a model should express higher epistemic uncertainty there. A global PICP score can miss exactly that failure.

objectID: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#existing-evaluation-strategies-critiqued
href: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#existing-evaluation-strategies-critiqued
title: How to evaluate uncertainty estimates in machine learning for regression?
text:
4. Existing Evaluation Strategies Critiqued

PICP-based interval testing
PICP is defined as the fraction of test observations that fall inside their prediction intervals:
[ PICP = _i 1{y_i PI(x_i)} ]
This is widely used because it is simple and intuitive. If we construct 90% intervals, we hope PICP is close to 0.9.
The paper’s criticism is that PICP estimates coverage averaged over the test distribution. It does not guarantee that intervals are reliable at each individual value of (x).


CICP-based confidence interval testing
The analogous confidence interval measure is CICP:
[ CICP = _i 1{f(x_i) CI(x_i)} ]
But this requires knowing the true function (f(x)). In normal real-world applications, we do not know this. That is why CICP is mainly available in simulation studies.
This is one of the key practical frustrations with the paper: the strongest evaluation target is not directly observable in ordinary applied modelling.


Log-likelihood testing
The log-likelihood procedure applies when a model outputs a full predictive density (p(y x)), often a normal distribution with estimated mean and variance. The method is then evaluated using average test-set log-likelihood.
This paper is not about a formal likelihood ratio test. It is about using log-likelihood as a predictive scoring metric to compare probabilistic models.
The authors acknowledge that log-likelihood is sensible if the goal is to estimate the full predictive density. However, they argue that if the practical goal is to construct good prediction intervals, a better log-likelihood does not necessarily imply better intervals.


Standard benchmark habit
The paper traces much of the benchmark culture to the probabilistic backpropagation evaluation setup, where methods are tested on regression datasets such as:

Boston Housing
Concrete Compression Strength
Energy Efficiency
Kin8nm
Naval Propulsion
Combined Cycle Power Plant
Protein Structure
Wine Quality Red
Yacht Hydrodynamics
Year Prediction MSD

The authors argue that these benchmarks are useful for comparison, but the usual metrics do not isolate uncertainty quality well enough.

objectID: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#major-criticisms-of-existing-evaluation
href: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#major-criticisms-of-existing-evaluation
title: How to evaluate uncertainty estimates in machine learning for regression?
text:
5. Major Criticisms of Existing Evaluation

Criticism 1: Predictive performance does not prove correct uncertainty decomposition
Predictive uncertainty combines model uncertainty and data noise variance.
A method might get a good overall predictive uncertainty score because:

its model uncertainty estimate is good;
its data noise estimate is good;
one bad estimate compensates for another bad estimate;
the mean prediction is better, even though uncertainty is not.

Therefore, PICP and log-likelihood do not tell us whether epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty have been estimated correctly.
This matters for out-of-distribution detection. If model uncertainty is supposed to rise in unfamiliar regions, we need to know whether the model uncertainty component itself is behaving correctly. A good predictive score may not answer that.


Criticism 2: Coverage cannot be properly tested from one realization
Intervals are random because they depend on:

which training data were sampled;
which targets were observed;
random effects in model training, such as initialization and stochastic optimization.

To test whether an interval procedure has the desired coverage, the whole experiment should be repeated: sample data, train model, construct intervals, evaluate coverage.
The authors demonstrate this with a simple linear example. Even when the interval procedure is correctly calibrated, a single evaluation can look misleading. In one simulation, CICP may be 0; in another, it may be 1. This does not mean the interval procedure is useless. It means one realization cannot establish coverage.
Practical translation: cross-validation, bootstrapping, blocked resampling, repeated train/test splits, or simulation-based stress tests are attempts to approximate this repeated-experiment logic. They still do not give true CICP unless (f(x)) is known, but they are better than relying on one split.


Criticism 3: Good PICP does not guarantee pointwise coverage
PICP measures average coverage across the test set. It does not show where coverage succeeds or fails.
A model can achieve near-perfect PICP by:

over-covering easy or well-sampled regions;
under-covering difficult, sparse, shifted, or high-risk regions;
averaging those failures into a respectable global number.

This is one of the most important ideas to carry into forecasting work. The right question is not only:

Do the 90% intervals cover 90% of observations overall?

It is also:

Do the 90% intervals cover approximately 90% of observations in the operating regimes where decisions will be made?



Criticism 4: Better log-likelihood does not imply better prediction intervals
Log-likelihood rewards the whole predictive density. A model can improve log-likelihood because its mean predictions are better, even if its uncertainty estimate is worse.
The paper gives a small example where one method has slightly better log-likelihood, about -3.109 versus -3.110, but much worse 68% interval coverage, about 0.57 versus 0.67.
The takeaway is simple: if the final use of the model is interval construction, interval behaviour must be evaluated directly. Log-likelihood alone is not enough.

objectID: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#proposed-solution-simulation-based-testing
href: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#proposed-solution-simulation-based-testing
title: How to evaluate uncertainty estimates in machine learning for regression?
text:
6. Proposed Solution: Simulation-Based Testing

Main idea
The authors propose controlled simulation-based evaluation.
Instead of relying on one real train/test split, the evaluator defines a data-generating process where the true function and noise process are known. Then the full modelling procedure is repeated many times.
This allows the evaluator to ask:

Do prediction intervals cover future observations at each (x)?
Do confidence intervals cover the true function (f(x)) at each (x)?
Do intervals widen where data are sparse?
Do methods trade off width and coverage sensibly?
Are local failures hidden by global averages?



Procedure
The proposed testing process is:

Choose a distribution (P_{X,Y}) for simulating datasets.
Simulate a fixed test set so methods can be compared on the same inputs.
Simulate a training set.
Train the uncertainty estimation method.
Construct prediction intervals and confidence intervals at chosen levels.
Repeat the training-set simulation and model-fitting process many times.
Compute coverage for each test input across simulations.
Compare methods using Brier score and average interval width.



New metrics
The paper introduces pointwise coverage fractions:

PICF: Prediction Interval Coverage Fraction, the pointwise coverage of prediction intervals across repeated simulations.
CICF: Confidence Interval Coverage Fraction, the pointwise coverage of confidence intervals across repeated simulations.

The authors then use a Brier-style score to penalize deviations from the desired coverage level:
[ BS = _i (PICF(x_i) - (1-))^2 ]
A low Brier score means the intervals are close to the intended coverage level across the input space, not just on average.


Simulation options proposed
The authors suggest three broad ways to build simulations:

Use known toy functions with controlled noise.
Build simulations from real datasets, such as the standard regression benchmark datasets.
Use a very large dataset split into one test set and many distinct training sets.

The third option is practically useful but limited: it can test prediction intervals, but not confidence intervals, because the true function is still unknown.

objectID: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#experiments-figure-level-interpretation
href: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#experiments-figure-level-interpretation
title: How to evaluate uncertainty estimates in machine learning for regression?
text:
7. Experiments & Figure-Level Interpretation

Methods compared
The paper uses two methods mainly for demonstration:

Naive bootstrap: repeatedly resample the training data, train multiple neural networks, and use variation across the resulting models to construct confidence intervals.
Concrete dropout: train a neural network with dropout and keep dropout active during prediction, using repeated stochastic forward passes to estimate uncertainty.

The bootstrap method here is essentially an ensemble method with bootstrap resampling. Its uncertainty estimate comes from the spread across multiple fitted models.
Concrete dropout behaves like a stochastic ensemble at prediction time, but its interval behaviour is not guaranteed to match the intuitive epistemic uncertainty story.


Homoscedastic toy example: Figures 4, 5, and 6
The first toy simulation uses:
[ f(x) = (2x - 1)^3 ]
with constant Gaussian noise.
Figure 4: Both bootstrap and dropout achieve PICP values close to the desired 90% and 80% levels. If the evaluation stopped here, both methods would look acceptable.
Figure 5: When the authors evaluate confidence interval coverage using the true function, the CICP values are much less reassuring. Good PICP does not translate into good confidence interval behaviour.
Figure 6: The authors switch from averaging over test points to averaging over simulations at each (x). This reveals that some input regions are covered too often and others too rarely. This is the key pointwise coverage argument.


Heteroscedastic toy example: Figure 7
The second toy example uses non-constant noise:
[ (x) = 0.1 + x^2 ]
This matters because bootstrap assumes homoscedastic noise in their setup, while concrete dropout can estimate heteroscedastic noise.
Figure 7: PICP can point in the wrong direction. Bootstrap can look comparable or slightly better under global PICP, even though the pointwise evaluation shows worse local interval behaviour. The paper reports a PICF Brier score of 0.011 for bootstrap and 0.0011 for dropout, strongly favouring dropout in this case.
This is one of the clearest demonstrations that average PICP can reward the wrong method.


Sparse-data / out-of-distribution example: Figures 8 and 9
The authors then create a bimodal input distribution so that some regions have limited data.
This is the most relevant part for epistemic uncertainty.
The desired behaviour is:

intervals should be narrower where data are dense;
intervals should widen where data are sparse;
model uncertainty should reflect lack of knowledge about poorly sampled regions.

Figure 8: Bootstrap behaves more sensibly by widening confidence intervals in the sparse region. Dropout does the opposite in the example: its intervals shrink where there is less data.
This is especially important because dropout has better aggregate scores in the example:

PICP: dropout 0.83 versus bootstrap 0.75 for 80% intervals;
log-likelihood: dropout 0.14 versus bootstrap 0.12.

If the evaluator looked only at PICP or log-likelihood, dropout would appear better. But visually and conceptually, the bootstrap intervals better reflect epistemic uncertainty in the low-data region.
Figure 9: Repeating the experiment 100 times confirms the same concern. Both methods can have reasonable PICP, while their confidence interval behaviour differs substantially in the sparse region.
This figure is useful for the phrasing “a good overall uncertainty score does not guarantee sensible uncertainty behaviour in under-sampled operating regions.”


Boston Housing simulation: Figure 10
To move beyond one-dimensional toy functions, the authors build a simulation from the Boston Housing dataset.
Their procedure:

Train a random forest on the original data and treat it as the true function (f(x)).
Model squared residuals with a second random forest and treat that as (^2(x)).
Simulate new targets using the original covariates and the learned function/noise model.
Evaluate bootstrap and dropout using repeated simulated datasets.

They split the generated data into:

366 training samples;
100 test samples;
40 validation samples.

Figure 10: PICP again looks fairly close to the desired 80% level, but PICF and CICF reveal that individual points are often over-covered or under-covered. The authors report that for PICF, bootstrap has a Brier score of 0.027 and dropout has 0.032. For CICF, bootstrap has 0.147 and dropout has 0.15. Both methods show important local weaknesses.
This section supports the claim that the proposed approach can be made more realistic by using simulations based on real datasets, although it still depends heavily on how the simulator is constructed.

title: How to evaluate uncertainty estimates in machine learning for regression?
text:
9. Relevance to My Research Context

Why I would cite this paper
I would cite this paper to justify a stricter evaluation standard for probabilistic forecasting models.
It supports the claim that:

PICP alone is not enough;
log-likelihood alone is not enough;
interval width alone is not enough;
uncertainty quality must be checked locally or conditionally;
sparse regions of the input space require special attention.



How it supports uncertainty-aware forecasting
For load, solar, wind, or electricity-price forecasting, a model can have acceptable average coverage while failing under specific conditions.
Examples:

intervals may be too narrow during high ramp events;
intervals may be too wide during stable conditions;
intervals may fail in rare weather regimes;
intervals may be poorly calibrated at longer forecast horizons;
intervals may look globally correct because errors cancel across seasons.

This paper gives methodological support for analysing coverage by regime rather than only reporting one global PICP value.


How it connects to explainability
The paper is not an XAI paper, but it is highly relevant to explainable uncertainty.
If I use SHAP or another XAI method to explain interval width, uncertainty, or prediction risk, I should first ask whether those intervals are actually reliable. Explaining a bad uncertainty estimate can produce a very polished but misleading explanation.
The evaluation logic should therefore come before or alongside the explanation logic:

Validate whether the uncertainty estimate behaves sensibly.
Then explain why uncertainty is high or low in particular regions.



Most useful insight for my work
The strongest takeaway is:

A probabilistic model should not only achieve the desired coverage overall; it should express uncertainty correctly in the specific parts of the input space where decisions are made.

This is especially important for operational systems where data density varies across the operating envelope.

href: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#clarifications-from-my-notes
title: How to evaluate uncertainty estimates in machine learning for regression?
text:
10. Clarifications From My Notes

Confidence interval coverage in real life
In real-world data-driven modelling, we usually cannot calculate true confidence interval coverage for (f(x)), because we do not know (f(x)).
If we check whether held-out observed values fall inside intervals, we are checking prediction interval coverage. That is useful, but it is not the same as confidence interval coverage.
Practical alternatives include:

repeated train/test splits;
cross-validation;
blocked or time-series validation;
bootstrapping;
synthetic simulations;
simulator-based stress tests;
local coverage diagnostics on observed outcomes.

These can approximate parts of the repeated-experiment logic, but they do not magically reveal the true function.


“Coverage cannot be tested on a single data set”
This means that coverage is a property of the interval-generating procedure over repeated samples and repeated model fits.
One train/test split can estimate how many intervals covered observations in that particular split. It cannot prove that the interval procedure has the claimed coverage generally or locally.
For a real system, this should be read as:

A single sample of system operation may hide uncertainty failures in under-sampled regions of the operating space.



Good PICP but no pointwise coverage
The important idea is cancellation.
Global PICP can look correct when:

one region is underconfident and produces intervals that are too wide;
another region is overconfident and produces intervals that are too narrow;
the average coverage across both regions happens to match the desired value.

This is why conditional coverage by operating regime is more informative than one global coverage number.


Better log-likelihood is not a likelihood test
The paper talks about log-likelihood as a scoring metric, not a traditional likelihood ratio testing procedure.
The key warning is that a better log-likelihood may reflect better point predictions rather than better interval uncertainty.


Bootstrap as an ensemble
The bootstrap method in the paper is naturally understood as an ensemble:

resample the data;
train multiple models;
predict with each model;
use the spread across model predictions as an uncertainty estimate.

The “bootstrap” part describes how the ensemble members are generated.


Figure 8 and sparse operating regions
Figure 8 is especially useful because it shows the distinction between a good score and sensible uncertainty behaviour.
Dropout has better aggregate PICP and log-likelihood in that example, but its intervals shrink in the low-data region. Bootstrap has worse aggregate scores, but its intervals widen in the sparse region, which is more consistent with epistemic uncertainty.
This is the paper’s practical warning in one picture.

href: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#action-items-integration
title: How to evaluate uncertainty estimates in machine learning for regression?
text:
11. Action Items & Integration

Cite this paper when arguing that global PICP is insufficient for validating prediction intervals.
Use it to justify reporting local or conditional coverage, not only average coverage.
Distinguish carefully between prediction intervals and confidence intervals in my own writing.
Do not claim CICP in real data unless the true function is known through simulation or a trusted data-generating model.
When discussing sparse regions, avoid vague “one dataset” wording and instead refer to under-sampled operating regimes or limited system coverage.
Pair PICP with diagnostics such as coverage by feature regime, forecast horizon, season, demand level, weather state, or interval-width bin.
Use simulation-based or surrogate-based stress tests where possible, especially if comparing uncertainty methods.
When using XAI to explain uncertainty, first verify that the uncertainty estimates are meaningful in the relevant regimes.
Link this paper with Pernot’s calibration, consistency, and adaptivity framework: Sluijterman et al. provide the pointwise-coverage critique; Pernot provides a broader diagnostic vocabulary for local adaptivity.

href: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#pre-written-assets
title: How to evaluate uncertainty estimates in machine learning for regression?
text:
12. Pre-Written Assets

Literature review paragraph
Sluijterman, Cator, and Heskes argue that common evaluation practices for regression uncertainty estimates can be misleading. In particular, they show that neither test-set log-likelihood nor prediction interval coverage probability is sufficient to establish that uncertainty estimates are locally reliable. Log-likelihood can improve because of better mean prediction rather than better uncertainty estimation, while PICP only measures marginal coverage and can hide overconfident and underconfident regions that cancel on average. The authors therefore propose simulation-based testing in which the data-generating function is known and the modelling process is repeated many times, allowing pointwise prediction and confidence interval coverage to be evaluated through PICF, CICF, Brier scores, and interval width. Their results with bootstrap and dropout methods show that aggregate scores can favour methods with undesirable interval behaviour, especially in sparse regions of the input space.


Methodological caution sentence
Reporting a single PICP value is not enough to establish reliable probabilistic forecasts, because correct average coverage can mask severe local miscalibration across operating regimes.


Practical integration sentence
For operational forecasting, the paper supports evaluating interval coverage conditionally across meaningful regimes such as forecast horizon, weather state, season, demand level, or sparse regions of the input space, rather than relying only on global PICP or log-likelihood.


One-line review
This paper is a methodological warning that uncertainty estimates should be evaluated where they are used, not only averaged into a reassuring global score.
crumbs: How to evaluate uncertainty estimates in machine learning for regression?

objectID: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#bottom-line-takeaway
href: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#bottom-line-takeaway
title: How to evaluate uncertainty estimates in machine learning for regression?
text:
13. Bottom-Line Takeaway
The paper’s main value is its evaluation philosophy.
It does not say that PICP or log-likelihood are useless. It says they answer weaker questions than many researchers assume. PICP answers whether intervals cover observations on average over a test set. Log-likelihood answers how well a predictive density fits held-out data. Neither one proves that uncertainty is correct locally, that model uncertainty is separated from data noise, or that intervals behave sensibly in sparse operating regions.
For my own work, the important lesson is to treat uncertainty validation as a local and regime-aware problem. A probabilistic forecasting model should not merely be calibrated on average; it should be reliable in the parts of the system where the uncertainty will guide decisions.
