title: Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods
text:
Authors & Year: Xianzhou Dong, Weiyong Guo, Cheng Zhou, Yongqiang Luo, Zhiyong Tian, Limao Zhang, Xiaoying Wu, Baobing Liu (2024)
Venue (Journal/Conference): Energy
DOI: 10.1016/j.energy.2024.133309
Application Domain: Building electricity demand forecasting
Core Methods: Physical simulation + EMD + K-means + LSTM / TCN-GRU + SHAP + Monte Carlo + transfer learning
Case Study: Glodon Xi’an Digital Architecture R&D Building, China
Proximity/Threat Level: Medium to High / Relevant methodological inspiration
Date Reviewed: 2026-03-13
crumbs: Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods

objectID: reviews/Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why hybrid modeling?):

The paper starts from a very practical tension in building energy forecasting:

Pure physical simulation is interpretable and grounded in real building physics, but it often fails to match actual operational behavior accurately.
Pure data-driven models can fit measured demand more accurately, but they behave like black boxes and ignore explicit physical structure.

Their central argument is that building electricity demand is fundamentally governed by physical mechanisms, but actual usage also contains hidden operational patterns that only data-driven learning can uncover.

The Motivation (Why this matters specifically for buildings?):

Building electricity forecasting supports optimal control, energy management, and cost reduction.
Even small forecasting improvements can translate into meaningful operational and economic benefits.
In commercial buildings, actual demand is shaped not only by climate and HVAC physics, but also by occupancy behavior and irregular working patterns, which are difficult to represent in a purely simulation-based framework.

Their claim to fame / Novelty:

They propose a hybrid forecasting framework that explicitly combines:

Physical software simulation for heating and cooling loads,
EMD for decomposing complex demand signals,
K-means clustering for inferring work-state intensity,
Deep learning via LSTM or TCN-GRU,
SHAP + Pearson correlation for interpretability,
Monte Carlo weather-error propagation for prediction intervals,
Transfer learning for floors with limited historical data.

The novelty is not any single component alone, but the system-level integration of physical priors, data decomposition, learned representations, interpretability, uncertainty quantification, and data-efficiency strategies into one building forecasting pipeline.

The Value Derived from Explainability and Hybridization:

Physical relevance: The model does not rely purely on opaque learned correlations; it explicitly incorporates simulated heating and cooling loads.
Operational relevance: It discovers a more realistic “work” feature from the electricity data itself, rather than relying only on fixed calendar schedules.
Interpretability: SHAP and correlation analysis show which features matter most, especially work-state, lag terms, and cooling load.
Practical deployment value: The framework is extended beyond point forecasting to include uncertainty intervals and transfer learning for incomplete-data settings.

Their ultimate result:

The hybrid models achieve R² above 0.85, reaching up to about 0.9, while pure physical simulation alone only reaches about 0.3.
MAE, MSE, and RMSE remain below 0.07, and SMAPE stays around 0.2 in the main hybrid setup.
In transfer learning settings, R² remains above 0.8, with somewhat higher errors but still workable performance.
crumbs: Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods

objectID: reviews/Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand.html#methodology-technical-details
href: reviews/Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand.html#methodology-technical-details
title: Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

Dataset / Testbed:

The study uses hourly electricity demand data from the air-conditioning terminals on each floor of the Glodon Xi’an Digital Architecture R&D Building.
The building is a large office building with 12 floors above ground and 3 below, with substantial HVAC infrastructure and a central ecological atrium.
The example time span shown in the paper covers data from April 17, 2023 to November 27, 2023.

Physical Model Component:

A BIM model is constructed in Autodesk Revit and imported into the Hongye Building Performance Analysis Platform, which uses EnergyPlus, OpenFOAM, and Radiance as core engines.
The software computes annual dynamic heating and cooling loads based on building envelope, weather, HVAC design, and occupancy-related conditions.
From this simulation, the paper extracts:

Cooling load: (L_c)
Heating load: (L_h)


Deep Learning Component:

Two learning backbones are tested:

LSTM
TCN-GRU

Both models include dropout and dense layers, and use Adam optimization with MSE as validation loss.
The paper positions:

LSTM as stronger for long-range temporal dependencies and expressive sequence learning,
TCN-GRU as combining local temporal extraction through dilated convolutions with sequential memory through GRU units.


Input Features:

The hybrid model uses six main external features:

Temperature
Humidity
Holiday
Work-state
Cooling load (L_c)
Heating load (L_h)

Lagged demand features are also used in the interpretability analysis, particularly lag-1 and lag-2.

EMD Pre-processing:

They use Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) to break complex electricity demand data into simpler Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs).
The motivation is that raw electricity demand contains overlapping oscillatory structures that are difficult for deep learning models to learn directly.
The IMFs are ranked by energy, and the higher-energy modes are selected to reduce computational cost while preserving most of the informative structure.
Prediction is done IMF-by-IMF, and the final forecast is reconstructed by summing the predicted IMFs.

K-means Work-State Extraction:

A major contribution is the introduction of a learned “work” feature.
Instead of assuming that working hours are fixed by calendar, they cluster electricity demand behavior using K-means.
The electricity demand is first split into clusters, then mapped into three work-intensity classes: 0, 1, and 2.
This lets the model infer actual operational intensity from load patterns rather than imposing a rigid schedule.

Prediction Interval Method:

Instead of using residual-based prediction intervals, they use weather forecast error intervals and a Monte Carlo process.
The idea is to perturb the weather inputs, generate many temperature scenarios, run them through the model, and then derive the forecast interval from the resulting predictive distribution.
This is conceptually different from the more standard residual-distribution approach.

Transfer Learning Setup:

Transfer learning is tested between floors.
The paper uses decomposed IMFs from one floor as the source task and fine-tunes models for another floor with limited data.
Initial layers are frozen, source weights are transferred, and remaining layers are fine-tuned.
They specifically compare training with 5 IMFs versus 8 IMFs.
crumbs: Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods

objectID: reviews/Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand.html#validation-strategy-predictions-interpretability-uncertainty
href: reviews/Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand.html#validation-strategy-predictions-interpretability-uncertainty
title: Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods
text:
4. Validation Strategy (Predictions, Interpretability & Uncertainty)

Validating the Predictions (Forecasting Quality):

The paper evaluates performance using:

MAE
MSE
RMSE
SMAPE
R²

These are used both to assess the effect of pre-processing and the final hybrid forecasting models.

Validating EMD Pre-processing:

They test model performance with and without EMD.
For LSTM, adding EMD reduces errors and increases R² from 0.056 to 0.2938.
For TCN-GRU, EMD also improves performance, increasing R² from 0.2964 to 0.3588.
Their interpretation is that EMD makes hidden structure easier for the models to learn.

Validating the Work-State Feature:

Two approaches are compared:

A manually fixed work-hour schedule,
A K-means-derived work-state.

The fixed schedule gives R² = 0.3040.
The K-means-derived feature improves performance dramatically to R² = 0.8417.
Residual plots, Q-Q plots, and residual density plots all favor the K-means approach, suggesting that it captures real operational regimes more faithfully.

Validating the Final Hybrid Model:

On the 8th-floor dataset, both hybrid models achieve roughly R² ≈ 0.85.
Errors are low, with RMSE and MAE below 0.07, and SMAPE below 0.25.
The paper says TCN-GRU appears slightly better overall in the main hybrid forecasting experiment, especially from residual distribution behavior.

Validating the Explanations (XAI Quality):

They use SHAP values and Pearson correlation heatmaps.
This is not a formal XAI benchmarking framework; it is mainly a feature-importance and domain-consistency analysis.
For the third floor, the top features are:

work
(L_c)
lag-1
lag-2

For the eighth floor, the top features are:

work
lag-1
lag-2
(L_c)

The ranking shift is interpreted as a time-scale effect: lag terms dominate at shorter scales, while physically simulated cooling load becomes more influential at larger scales.

Validating Prediction Intervals:

They generate intervals using Monte Carlo propagation of weather uncertainty.
The reported PINAW is 0.7513 for the shown LSTM interval example.
The paper argues that this is more practically aligned with real forecasting conditions than intervals based only on residual assumptions.

Validating Transfer Learning:

With transfer learning, R² remains above 0.8.
Increasing IMF count from 5 to 8 improves R², for example from 0.83 to 0.88 in the LSTM setup.
Errors remain below 0.2, while SMAPE stays around 0.4.
The paper concludes that LSTM performs slightly better than TCN-GRU in the transfer learning setting, especially in residual normality and generalization.
crumbs: Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods

objectID: reviews/Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
href: reviews/Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
title: Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods
text:
5. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: The “hybrid” idea is strong, but causality is still limited.

The paper is better than a purely black-box demand model because it injects physically simulated cooling and heating loads.
However, the final predictive mechanism is still primarily correlational rather than causal.
The physical model provides useful priors, but the deep model does not explicitly enforce thermodynamic consistency or energy-balance constraints during learning.

Criticism 2: The XAI is useful, but still shallow.

SHAP and Pearson correlation are helpful for identifying influential features, but this is still a relatively lightweight form of interpretability.
The paper does not evaluate:

explanation stability,
sensitivity to perturbations,
faithfulness/fidelity,
robustness across retraining runs.

So the interpretability story is persuasive, but not especially rigorous.

Criticism 3: Their strongest gain may come from feature engineering, not necessarily architecture.

A big jump in performance comes from the K-means-derived work-state feature.
That suggests the paper’s real contribution may be less about LSTM vs TCN-GRU and more about constructing better operational features.
In that sense, the “hybrid” framework is partly a feature-engineering framework disguised as a forecasting architecture.

Criticism 4: The comparison against pure physical simulation is somewhat easy to win.

The paper emphasizes that pure physical simulation only reaches R² ≈ 0.3.
That result is believable, but it is also not surprising.
Whole-building or floor-level electricity demand includes many operational irregularities, occupancy deviations, and control behaviors that calibrated simulation alone often misses.
So the comparison is valid, but not especially demanding as a benchmark.

Criticism 5: The uncertainty modeling is interesting, but incomplete.

Their Monte Carlo interval method based on weather forecast error is novel in context and practically meaningful.
But it only propagates uncertainty from weather forecasts, mainly temperature and humidity.
It does not fully capture:

model uncertainty,
occupancy uncertainty,
control-system uncertainty,
sensor noise,
structural misspecification.

So the interval is not a full predictive uncertainty distribution, but rather a partial uncertainty analysis.

Criticism 6: The transfer learning claim is promising, but narrow.

Transfer learning is only demonstrated across floors within the same building.
This is useful, but still a relatively favorable transfer setting because the floors share infrastructure, climate, schedule patterns, and building envelope assumptions.
True generalization to different buildings, HVAC systems, climates, or usage types is not shown.

Criticism 7: The weather feature set is thin.

The authors themselves acknowledge that only temperature and humidity are used from weather data.
For building electricity demand, especially cooling-dominated operation, omitted variables such as:

solar radiation,
wind speed,
cloud cover,
occupancy proxies,
internal equipment gains, could materially affect performance and feature interpretation.


Criticism 8: Residual normality is slightly overused as a quality signal.

The paper repeatedly treats approximately normal residuals as evidence of good generalization and model validity.
That is not completely wrong, but it is a weak standard on its own.
A model can still have operationally important biases, heteroscedasticity, or poor tail behavior even if residual plots look roughly normal.

section: 6. Why This Paper Matters for My Research
text:
6. Why This Paper Matters for My Research

What is genuinely useful here:

It offers a strong example of how to combine:

physical priors,
decomposed time-series structure,
learned operational states,
explainability,
interval forecasting,
and data-efficiency techniques.

This is especially valuable if I want to argue that interpretable forecasting should not be framed as purely “post-hoc XAI on black-box models,” but can also come from hybridization with domain structure.

What I would borrow:

The idea of using derived operational-state features instead of relying only on calendar variables.
The use of simulation outputs as explanatory auxiliary features rather than as standalone forecasts.
The framing that interpretability can also be about verifying whether physically meaningful variables rise in importance.

What I would improve:

Add stronger baselines.
Add formal explanation-quality tests.
Compare residual-based vs weather-error-based intervals more directly.
Use richer exogenous features.
Test transfer learning across more diverse domains, not just neighboring floors.

title: Hybrid model for robust and accurate forecasting building electricity demand combining physical and data-driven methods
text:
7. Action Items & Integration

Cite this paper in the part of my literature review dealing with hybrid physical + ML forecasting frameworks for energy systems.
Use it as an example of interpretable hybrid forecasting, but note that its XAI evaluation remains largely descriptive rather than rigorous.
Reference its K-means work-state feature engineering idea when discussing operational-state extraction from electricity demand.
Mention its weather-error-driven Monte Carlo interval approach as an alternative to residual-based uncertainty estimation.
Position my own work as extending beyond this by using stronger uncertainty modeling, more formal XAI validation, richer feature sets, or broader transfer tests.
Note that this paper shows an important principle: physical simulation is often most valuable as a structured input to ML, rather than as a standalone forecasting engine.

This paper is a strong example of a practically motivated hybrid forecasting framework: it shows that physically simulated HVAC loads, data-driven decomposition, learned work-state features, and post-hoc interpretability can be combined to produce accurate and operationally meaningful building electricity forecasts, but its claims about interpretability, uncertainty, and transferability remain more promising than fully proven.

title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
Authors & Year: Sinem Guler Kangalli Uyar, Bilge Kagan Ozbay, Berker Dal (2025)
Venue (Journal/Conference): Energy & Buildings
DOI: 10.1016/j.enbuild.2025.115815
Primary Topic: Building Energy Performance Ratio (BEPR) prediction using interpretable machine learning
Core Methods: XGBoost, SHAP, XGBoost Quantile Regression (XGBoost-QR)
Study Region: Istanbul, Türkiye
Dataset Size: 3,594 residential buildings
Threat / Relevance Level: High relevance for interpretable building-energy modeling, especially for studies combining prediction with explanation and heterogeneous-effects analysis
crumbs: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression

objectID: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation
The paper is motivated by the need to improve building energy efficiency using data-driven methods that can both predict performance accurately and explain what drives it. Buildings account for a large share of global energy consumption and emissions, so identifying the determinants of poor energy performance is directly relevant for energy policy, retrofit prioritization, and sustainable building design.
The authors focus on the Building Energy Performance Ratio (BEPR), which is a relative measure comparing a building’s annual energy consumption per square meter against a reference building. In this formulation: - BEPR > 100 means higher energy consumption than the reference building, hence lower efficiency. - BEPR < 100 means lower energy consumption than the reference building, hence higher efficiency.


Why standard mean prediction is not enough
A key argument in the paper is that mean-based regression hides important heterogeneity. Two buildings can have similar average predicted performance while being driven by very different underlying factors. This is especially important in energy datasets with extremes, such as very efficient buildings or very inefficient, older, poorly insulated buildings.


Why interpretability matters
The authors explicitly position interpretability as a requirement rather than an optional extra. Their argument is that black-box models may predict well, but without explanation they are less useful for: - identifying actionable retrofit priorities, - understanding the physical drivers of inefficiency, - supporting fair and transparent policy design, - distinguishing which variables matter most for low- versus high-performance buildings.


Main novelty / claim to fame
The main novelty is not simply that they use XGBoost. Rather, it is the combination of: 1. XGBoost for high-accuracy prediction, 2. SHAP for interpretability, and 3. XGBoost Quantile Regression for analyzing how feature effects change across different parts of the BEPR distribution.
Their central contribution is that they do not stop at predicting BEPR. They ask: - Which variables matter most overall? - Do these variables change in importance across low-, medium-, and high-BEPR buildings? - Can this heterogeneity support more targeted energy-efficiency interventions?


What the paper ultimately contributes
The study contributes three things: - a comparative benchmarking of multiple machine learning models for BEPR prediction, - an interpretable explanation of the best-performing model using SHAP, - a quantile-based framework that reveals heterogeneous feature effects across different energy-performance levels.

objectID: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#problem-setup-study-design
href: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#problem-setup-study-design
title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
3. Problem Setup & Study Design

Target variable
The prediction target is Building Energy Performance Ratio (BEPR).
The paper defines it as:
[ BEPR = 100 () ]
where: - (EP_a) = annual energy consumption per square meter of the actual building, - (EP_r) = annual energy consumption per square meter of the reference building.
This makes BEPR a regulatory and comparative efficiency indicator rather than a direct raw load value.


Research questions
The study is structured around three main questions: 1. What building characteristics most strongly influence BEPR? 2. Do the determinants differ between buildings with low BEPR and high BEPR? 3. How can those differences support better residential energy-efficiency policy?


Workflow
The research design combines: - building data, - meteorological data, - socioeconomic data, - preprocessing and standardization, - train/test split, - model training and hyperparameter optimization, - model evaluation, - selection of best model, - interpretability analysis via SHAP, - heterogeneous-effects analysis via quantile regression.

objectID: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#dataset-variables-context
href: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#dataset-variables-context
title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
4. Dataset, Variables & Context

Dataset
The study uses 3,594 residential buildings in Istanbul. All buildings are reinforced concrete structures and the sample is derived from Energy Performance Certificates (EPCs). Because EPCs are not continuously updated, the dataset is essentially cross-sectional rather than longitudinal.


Building context
Istanbul is a strong case study because it has: - a very large residential building stock, - substantial variation in age and building form, - many multi-storey buildings, - a large share of older buildings, - strong policy relevance in the Turkish energy-efficiency context.


Input features
The model uses 20 variables, including: - wall U-value, - window U-value, - roof U-value, - column U-value, - beam U-value, - slab-related U-values, - door U-value, - building age, - average floor height, - number of floors, - heating power, - cooling power, - hot water power, - lighting power, - average wind speed, - average temperature, - quality-of-life index, - market value.
These variables span: - building envelope quality, - mechanical system capacity, - local weather, - socioeconomic proxies.


Important note about missing data dimensions
A major limitation is already visible at the data level: the study does not include occupant behavior, schedules, thermostat habits, appliance usage, or maintenance data. It also lacks temporal operational data such as hourly or seasonal smart-meter readings. This becomes important later when interpreting both the strengths and the limitations of the findings.

title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
5.1 Compared algorithms
The paper compares a broad set of regression algorithms: - Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) - Decision Tree (DT) - K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) - Support Vector Regression (SVR) - Artificial Neural Network (ANN) - Random Forest (RF) - Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)
It then separately applies: - XGBoost Quantile Regression (XGBoost-QR)

Why this comparison matters
This comparison is useful because it spans: - simple linear models, - local / distance-based models, - non-linear kernel methods, - neural networks, - ensemble tree methods.
This lets the authors assess whether gains come merely from nonlinearity, or specifically from the boosted-tree structure.

title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
5.2 Training and validation strategy

Train/test split: 80/20
Cross-validation: 5-fold cross-validation
Hyperparameter tuning: grid search
Feature processing: z-score standardization for continuous variables


Evaluation metrics
The paper evaluates models using metrics such as: - (R^2) - adjusted (R^2) - RMSE
The paper also checks model behavior using Bland-Altman plots, which is a useful diagnostic addition because it goes beyond aggregate performance metrics and reveals error structure.

href: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#why-xgboost-won
title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
5.3 Why XGBoost won
The paper reports that XGBoost achieved the best test performance while keeping overfitting within an acceptable range relative to the training set. The authors note that its superiority is consistent with prior building-energy literature that finds boosted trees effective for complex, heterogeneous, high-dimensional problems.
This makes sense methodologically: - XGBoost handles nonlinearity well, - captures interactions without explicit manual feature engineering, - includes regularization, - is robust in heterogeneous tabular datasets, - often performs especially well when feature effects are mixed, non-additive, and not smoothly linear.

objectID: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#why-they-moved-from-xgboost-to-xgboost-qr
href: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#why-they-moved-from-xgboost-to-xgboost-qr
title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
section: 5.4 Why they moved from XGBoost to XGBoost-QR
text:
5.4 Why they moved from XGBoost to XGBoost-QR
The authors do not treat quantile regression as just another probabilistic add-on. They motivate it from the heteroscedasticity seen in the model errors.
From the Bland-Altman analysis, prediction errors widen as mean energy consumption increases. That means the model is less uniform in accuracy across the response range. In other words, the problem is not just “predict the average BEPR,” but “understand the conditional distribution of BEPR across different building profiles.”
That is why they use XGBoost-QR: - to model different quantiles of BEPR, - to analyze different performance regimes, - to reduce the masking effect of average-based models.
crumbs: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression

objectID: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#technical-note-on-xgboost-qr
href: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#technical-note-on-xgboost-qr
title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
5.5 Technical note on XGBoost-QR
A technically interesting part of the paper is the discussion of why ordinary pinball loss is awkward inside standard XGBoost. Since XGBoost relies on second-order optimization, the standard pinball loss is problematic because it is non-differentiable and has zero second derivative in the needed sense.
To address this, the study uses Arctan Pinball Loss, a smooth approximation that: - is differentiable, - has a non-zero second derivative, - allows quantile regression inside the XGBoost framework.
The paper also notes an advantage of multi-quantile prediction in a shared model: quantiles share tree splits, which helps reduce the risk of quantile crossing.
This is one of the stronger technical contributions of the paper.

title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
6. Interpretability Strategy

Why SHAP was chosen
Although XGBoost has built-in feature importance measures such as gain, weight, and cover, the authors argue that these can produce inconsistent rankings. They therefore use SHAP for a more stable and theoretically grounded explanation framework.


Scope of interpretability
The paper uses SHAP in a mainly global-to-local way: - global feature importance rankings, - dependence plots for top variables, - interaction-style visual interpretation using color-coded feature overlays.
This is a good design choice because it does not stop at ranking variables; it also explores how the variables behave across their value ranges.

href: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#best-performing-predictive-model
title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
7.1 Best-performing predictive model
The headline result is straightforward:

XGBoost was the strongest overall predictive model among the tested algorithms.
It outperformed the benchmark models on test performance.
It also maintained an acceptable train-test gap, which the authors interpret as acceptable overfitting control.

The paper therefore justifies using XGBoost as the main predictive engine and SHAP / XGBoost-QR as the explanatory layers around it.

objectID: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#global-shap-feature-importance
href: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#global-shap-feature-importance
title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
7.2 Global SHAP feature importance
The SHAP analysis identifies the following variables as the most important BEPR drivers: 1. wall_U 2. roof_U 3. window_U 4. building_age
This is a highly intuitive and physically plausible result.

Why this matters
These variables are all directly linked to heat transfer and building fabric quality: - poor wall insulation increases thermal losses, - poor roof insulation increases envelope losses, - poor window insulation increases thermal leakage, - older buildings often reflect outdated materials, weaker insulation standards, or aging envelopes.
This is exactly the kind of result that strengthens trust in the model: the most important variables are not arbitrary high-dimensional artifacts, but core building-physics variables.
crumbs: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression

objectID: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#shap-dependence-findings
href: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#shap-dependence-findings
title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
7.3 SHAP dependence findings
The dependence plots show the following patterns:

wall_U

Strong positive relationship with BEPR contribution.
As wall U-value increases, SHAP values rise.
Poor wall insulation strongly worsens predicted energy performance.
The effect becomes steeper at higher wall_U values.



window_U

Also positively related to BEPR contribution.
The relationship is more nonlinear than wall_U.
There are hints of plateauing or fluctuation at higher values.
Outliers with very poor window insulation can have disproportionately large impact.



roof_U

Positive relationship with BEPR contribution.
Poor roof insulation increasingly worsens energy performance.
The effect strengthens further at high roof_U values.



building_age

Older buildings tend to push BEPR upward.
The effect is positive overall but more dispersed at higher ages.
This suggests heterogeneity among old buildings: some may have been retrofitted, while others remain highly inefficient.



Interaction insight
The paper also shows that the impact of insulation variables is often stronger in older buildings, especially for wall and roof insulation. This is a useful interaction insight because it links fabric quality to building vintage, which is highly actionable for retrofit strategy.
crumbs: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression

objectID: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#quantile-based-findings
href: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#quantile-based-findings
title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
7.4 Quantile-based findings
The quantile analysis is one of the strongest parts of the paper.
The authors examine effects across quantiles such as: - 0.10 - 0.25 - 0.50 - 0.75 - 0.90

General pattern
The impact of the top variables becomes stronger at higher quantiles. That means: - in buildings with worse energy performance, - wall, roof, window insulation, and building age matter even more.


Specific qualitative pattern

At lower quantiles, envelope features such as wall_U and window_U are especially influential.
At higher quantiles, building_age and roof_U become more prominent.
By the 0.90 quantile, the ranking shifts, showing that the determinants of very poor energy performance are not exactly the same as those of average or highly efficient buildings.



Why this is important
This means the paper does not just say “insulation matters.” It says: - which insulation-related variables matter, and - for which types of buildings they matter most.
That is much more useful for policy and retrofit triage.
crumbs: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression

objectID: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#policy-and-practical-significance
href: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#policy-and-practical-significance
title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
8. Policy and Practical Significance
The practical value of the paper is that it turns a predictive model into a decision-support tool.

What decision-makers gain
Policymakers or planners could use findings like these to: - target older buildings with poor wall and roof insulation, - prioritize retrofit schemes by energy-performance segment, - design different interventions for different BEPR strata, - identify vulnerable, high-consumption buildings in lower-income contexts, - avoid one-size-fits-all retrofit policy.


Social and equity relevance
One especially strong idea in the discussion is that quantile-based modeling can help identify vulnerable buildings that might sit in the upper consumption quantiles due to age, poor insulation, and socioeconomic disadvantage. That makes the framework useful not just for efficiency, but also for equity-oriented energy policy.
crumbs: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression

objectID: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#strengths-of-the-study
href: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#strengths-of-the-study
title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
9. Strengths of the Study

Strength 1: Good problem framing
The paper is very clear about the difference between: - average prediction, - interpretable prediction, - distribution-aware prediction.
That conceptual layering is well done.


Strength 2: Sensible choice of methods
Using XGBoost for accuracy, SHAP for interpretability, and quantile regression for heterogeneity is a coherent and methodologically defensible combination.


Strength 3: Physically plausible explanations
The main explanatory variables align well with domain knowledge, which increases trust in the model.


Strength 4: Heterogeneity is treated seriously
Many papers stop at global feature importance. This one goes further by asking how effects differ across performance regimes.


Strength 5: Useful diagnostic thinking
The inclusion of Bland-Altman analysis and explicit discussion of heteroscedasticity is a valuable methodological step.


Strength 6: Strong policy relevance
The results are highly actionable for retrofit targeting and building-energy policy design.

section: Criticism 1: The interpretability is still mainly correlational
text:
Criticism 1: The interpretability is still mainly correlational
Even though the paper is more interpretable than a standard black-box study, SHAP still explains the model, not the true causal system. The paper occasionally reads as though feature importance directly reveals causal leverage. That should be treated more carefully.
A high SHAP value means a variable was important to the prediction, not necessarily that changing it alone would produce the exact same real-world improvement in BEPR.

title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
section: Criticism 2: Missing occupant behavior is a major limitation
text:
Criticism 2: Missing occupant behavior is a major limitation
The omission of occupant behavior is not minor. It is one of the biggest constraints in residential energy modeling.
Without data on: - occupancy schedules, - thermostat behavior, - appliance usage, - maintenance quality, - operational habits,
the model is heavily weighted toward envelope and proxy socioeconomic variables. That likely biases interpretability toward what is observable in certificates rather than everything that truly drives energy use.
This is especially important in the upper quantiles, where user behavior and operational irregularities may dominate.

section: Criticism 3: Cross-sectional EPC data limits dynamic realism
text:
Criticism 3: Cross-sectional EPC data limits dynamic realism
Because the EPC data are not temporal, the model cannot capture: - seasonal dynamics, - daily operation, - degradation over time, - behavior changes, - post-retrofit evolution.
That makes the paper stronger as a structural benchmarking study than as a dynamic building-operations study.

href: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#criticism-4-single-region-scope-limits-generalizability
title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
Criticism 4: Single-region scope limits generalizability
The Istanbul-only focus is understandable and useful, but it limits external validity. The model may not transfer cleanly to: - different climates, - different regulatory baselines, - different construction traditions, - different socioeconomic contexts.
A model that performs well in Istanbul may behave differently in colder continental climates, tropical climates, or regions with different building codes.

section: Criticism 5: Comparison is broad, but not necessarily deepest in every direction
text:
Criticism 5: Comparison is broad, but not necessarily deepest in every direction
The authors compare many algorithms, which is good for breadth. But the paper is still largely a tabular ML comparison, and it does not deeply explore: - uncertainty calibration quality, - alternative interpretable boosting frameworks, - causal feature analysis, - counterfactual retrofit analysis, - advanced distributional models beyond quantile regression.
So the study is strong in practical ML benchmarking, but less strong as a broader uncertainty-modeling study.

title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
section: Criticism 6: SHAP validation remains mostly plausibility-based
text:
Criticism 6: SHAP validation remains mostly plausibility-based
The SHAP findings are physically intuitive, but the paper does not rigorously validate explanation quality using: - stability tests, - perturbation consistency, - explanation sensitivity analysis, - fidelity stress tests, - causal sanity checks.
So although the explanations look credible, they are still largely accepted because they align with engineering common sense.

href: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#my-overall-interpretation
title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
11. My Overall Interpretation
This is a strong applied paper with a very sensible structure:

compare models,
select the best predictor,
interpret it with SHAP,
extend it with quantile regression,
convert the outputs into policy-relevant insight.

Its biggest strength is not any single technique, but the fact that the paper does not stop at predictive accuracy. It explicitly asks what the model has learned and whether those learned patterns differ across performance levels.
In that sense, it is a good example of moving from: prediction → interpretation → heterogeneity-aware policy insight.
If I were positioning my own work relative to this paper, I would say this study is a strong benchmark for interpretable tabular building-energy modeling, but it still leaves room for improvement in: - temporal realism, - behavioral data integration, - causal interpretation, - explanation validation, - cross-region generalization.

objectID: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#one-paragraph-summary
href: reviews/Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression.html#one-paragraph-summary
title: Interpretable building energy performance prediction using XGBoost Quantile Regression
text:
12. One-Paragraph Summary
This paper presents a strong applied machine-learning framework for predicting and interpreting the Building Energy Performance Ratio of residential buildings in Istanbul. Among several algorithms, XGBoost performed best, and SHAP showed that wall U-value, roof U-value, window U-value, and building age were the dominant drivers of BEPR. The most valuable contribution is the use of XGBoost Quantile Regression, which reveals that the relative importance of these factors changes across low-, medium-, and high-performance buildings. This makes the study more useful than a standard mean-regression paper because it captures heterogeneous effects that are directly relevant for targeted retrofit policy. Its main limitations are the lack of behavioral variables, lack of temporal dynamics, and limited geographic generalizability, but overall it is a very solid benchmark in interpretable building-energy modeling.

text:
Authors & Year: Giulia Vilone and Luca Longo (2021)
Venue: Information Fusion, 76, 89-106
DOI: 10.1016/j.inffus.2021.05.009
Article Type: Systematic review / conceptual taxonomy
Primary Topic/Concept: Notions of explainability and evaluation approaches for explainable artificial intelligence
Application Domain: General AI and machine learning; useful as a methodology foundation rather than as a domain-specific forecasting paper
Evidence Base: 406 peer-reviewed articles from 1975 to 2020, filtered around XAI notions and explanation-evaluation approaches
Code/Data Available?: No code; the value is the taxonomy of explanation goals, attributes, and validation approaches
Proximity/Threat Level: High / Foundational support for defining what my XAI component should achieve and how I should judge whether it works
Date Reviewed: 2026-06-18

objectID: reviews/Notions of explainability and evaluation approaches for explainable artificial intelligence.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/Notions of explainability and evaluation approaches for explainable artificial intelligence.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: Notions of explainability and evaluation approaches for explainable artificial intelligence
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

Why This Paper Matters

This is not a direct competitor paper. It is a methodology foundation paper.
The useful contribution is that it asks the prior question before selecting an XAI method: what is an explanation supposed to do?
For my work, this matters because an XAI layer should not be justified only by saying that SHAP, feature importance, saliency, or another explainer was applied.
The explanation must have a purpose: it should improve understanding, support decision-making, expose model behaviour, reveal failure modes, or help users decide when to trust the model.



The Problem It Addresses

Machine learning models, especially deep learning models, can be accurate but difficult for users to understand.
This creates practical problems around transparency, user interaction, trust, liability, and the ability to challenge automated decisions.
XAI research has produced many explanation methods, but the field does not have a single agreed definition of what makes an explanation valid, reliable, useful, or understandable.



What the Paper Contributes

The paper organises the XAI literature into a hierarchy of concepts.
The two branches most relevant to my work are:

notions of explainability: the qualities an explanation should have
evaluation approaches: the ways explanation quality can be assessed

The paper separates explanation quality into both technical and human-facing dimensions.
This is important because an explanation can be technically impressive but still fail if users cannot understand it or cannot use it to make better decisions.

objectID: reviews/Notions of explainability and evaluation approaches for explainable artificial intelligence.html#what-xai-is-supposed-to-achieve
href: reviews/Notions of explainability and evaluation approaches for explainable artificial intelligence.html#what-xai-is-supposed-to-achieve
title: Notions of explainability and evaluation approaches for explainable artificial intelligence
section: 3. What XAI Is Supposed To Achieve
text:
3. What XAI Is Supposed To Achieve

XAI as Human-Agent Interaction

A central framing in the paper is that explainability is not only a property of a model.
It is also an interaction between an explainer, an explanation, and an end-user.
This means the quality of an explanation depends on the user’s task, prior knowledge, domain context, and decision needs.



Four Purposes of Explanation
The paper highlights four broad reasons for explaining a model:

Explain to justify

The explanation should support the legitimacy of a prediction or decision.
In my work, this means explaining why a forecast, interval, or uncertainty estimate is defensible.

Explain to control

The explanation should expose model behaviour enough to debug, monitor, or identify failures.
In my work, this supports checking whether uncertainty explanations reveal data leakage, unrealistic drivers, or unreliable operating regions.

Explain to improve

The explanation should help improve the model or the modelling process.
In my work, this could mean using explanation patterns to refine features, diagnose poor interval behaviour, or identify conditions where the model needs more data.

Explain to discover

The explanation should help users learn relationships and patterns that were not obvious before.
In my work, this is relevant when using XAI to discover which conditions drive uncertainty, interval widening, or asymmetric risk.




Explanation Quality Criteria
The paper collects many notions that can be used as criteria for explanation quality. The most useful ones for my methodology are:







Criterion
Meaning for my research




Actionability
The explanation should help the user decide what to do next, not just describe the model.


Causality / causal plausibility
The explanation should be interpreted carefully: model associations are not automatically causal, but explanations should still be checked against domain logic.


Completeness
The explanation should describe enough of the model behaviour to be useful.


Comprehensibility
The explanation should be understandable to the intended audience.


Effectiveness
The explanation should support better decisions.


Efficiency
The explanation should help users make decisions faster or with less unnecessary effort.


Faithfulness
The explanation should reflect the actual model behaviour, not an attractive but misleading story.


Informativeness
The explanation should provide information that is relevant to the user’s question.


Justifiability
The explanation should be assessable against domain knowledge.


Robustness / stability
Similar inputs or small irrelevant perturbations should not produce wildly different explanations.


Sensitivity
The explanation should reflect meaningful changes in the model output when inputs change.


Understandability
The user should be able to form a useful mental model of the system.





Important Distinction

The paper is useful because it prevents a shallow version of XAI.
XAI is not simply “generate a plot”.
XAI should answer a user-relevant question such as:

Why did the model make this prediction?
Why is this prediction uncertain?
Why is the interval wide here?
Which inputs are driving the upper and lower risk bounds?
Is this explanation stable enough to trust?
Does this explanation change the decision I should make?
crumbs: Notions of explainability and evaluation approaches for explainable artificial intelligence

objectID: reviews/Notions of explainability and evaluation approaches for explainable artificial intelligence.html#evaluation-strategy
href: reviews/Notions of explainability and evaluation approaches for explainable artificial intelligence.html#evaluation-strategy
title: Notions of explainability and evaluation approaches for explainable artificial intelligence
text:
4. Evaluation Strategy

Two Main Evaluation Families
The paper groups evaluation approaches into two broad families:

Objective evaluations

These use formal, automated, or quantitative metrics.
They are useful for checking whether an explanation behaves consistently with the model.

Human-centred evaluations

These involve users, domain experts, or human judgement.
They are useful for checking whether the explanation is understandable, useful, trustworthy, and decision-relevant.


This split is important for my research because a good XAI evaluation should ideally include both.


Objective Evaluation Ideas
Objective evaluation can include:

Sensitivity to input perturbation

Change, remove, mask, or perturb input features and check whether explanations respond in a sensible way.

Sensitivity to model parameter randomisation

Compare explanations from a trained model with explanations from a randomised or partially randomised model.
If the explanation barely changes when the model is randomised, the explainer may not be faithful to the trained model.

Explanation completeness

Check how much of the model’s inferential process the explanation captures.

Robustness and stability

Similar observations should produce similar explanations when the model prediction is similar.

Faithfulness checks

Features identified as important should actually affect the model output when perturbed.

Counterfactual validity

Counterfactual examples should remain feasible and logically connected to the data domain.


For my work, the most relevant objective checks are likely faithfulness, perturbation sensitivity, stability across nearby inputs, and consistency across retraining or resampling.


Human-Centred Evaluation Ideas
Human-centred evaluation can include:

asking users or domain experts whether explanations are understandable
asking whether the explanation agrees with domain knowledge
measuring task accuracy with and without explanations
measuring decision time or cognitive load
collecting confidence, trust, usefulness, or satisfaction ratings
using open-ended feedback to identify confusion or missing information
asking whether the explanation would change a user’s decision

The important point is that explanations are ultimately consumed by humans. Therefore, a technically faithful explanation can still be incomplete if it does not help the intended user build a useful mental model or make a better decision.


Useful Validation Map for My Research








XAI objective
Validation question
Possible validation approach




Explain forecast behaviour
Do important features actually affect the forecast?
Perturbation tests, feature removal, retraining checks


Explain uncertainty or interval width
Do the highlighted drivers change the uncertainty estimate or prediction interval?
Perturb upper/lower quantile drivers and observe interval response


Build appropriate trust
Does the explanation help users identify reliable vs risky predictions?
Expert review, decision task, trust calibration survey


Support actionability
Does the explanation change what the user would do?
Scenario-based evaluation with domain users


Support debugging
Does the explanation reveal unrealistic feature reliance or data issues?
Domain audit of high-impact explanations


Support stability
Are explanations consistent across similar cases?
Neighbourhood stability and repeated-training checks


Support comprehensibility
Can the target user explain back the model behaviour?
Interview, questionnaire, or short interpretation task

text:
5. Methodology Support for My Research

How I Should Use This Paper
This paper gives me language for the methodology chapter. It supports the claim that an XAI component must be designed around:

the intended user
the decision context
the explanation question
the desired explanation qualities
the validation method used to judge the explanation

This is especially useful because my work is not only about producing forecasts or uncertainty estimates. It is about making those uncertainty estimates interpretable and useful.


Direct Implications for My XAI Design

I should explicitly state what my explanations are meant to achieve.
I should avoid treating feature attribution as automatically equivalent to explanation.
I should connect the explanation target to the actual decision problem.
If I explain uncertainty, I should explain the uncertainty object itself, such as interval width, quantile spread, prediction risk, or epistemic/aleatoric contribution.
I should evaluate explanations using both technical checks and human/domain reasoning where possible.
I should be careful with causal language. XAI can reveal model dependence, but that is not automatically the same as real-world causation.



Methodological Principle I Can Reuse

An XAI method is useful only if it produces explanations that are faithful enough to the model, understandable enough for the target user, and actionable enough to support the relevant decision.

This principle is the main reason the paper belongs in the methodology foundation of my review.

6. How This Connects To My Literature Review

Position in the Review

This paper should be cited before or during the section where I define what I mean by XAI.
It is also useful in the evaluation section, where I justify why explanation quality must be assessed rather than assumed.
It can support a paragraph arguing that explanation methods should be selected and validated according to the user-facing purpose of the explanation.



Suggested Use in My Argument
I can use this paper to support three methodological claims:

XAI must be purpose-driven.

The explanation should be linked to justification, control, improvement, discovery, decision support, or trust calibration.

XAI quality is multidimensional.

A useful explanation must balance faithfulness, stability, comprehensibility, informativeness, actionability, and domain plausibility.

XAI must be evaluated.

Evaluation should not stop at visual inspection. It should include objective checks and, where possible, human-centred or expert-centred validation.

text:
7. Final Takeaway
This paper is a foundation for deciding whether I am “doing XAI correctly”.
The central lesson is that XAI is not the act of attaching an explainer to a model. XAI is the design and validation of explanations that help a specific user understand, question, trust, debug, or act on a model’s output.
For my research, this means the XAI component should be evaluated against explanation quality criteria such as faithfulness, stability, understandability, domain plausibility, and actionability. This is especially important when the explanation target is not only the point forecast, but also the uncertainty around that forecast.

title: Postprocessing of point predictions for probabilistic forecasting of day-ahead electricity prices: The benefits of using isotonic distributional regression
text:
Authors & Year: Arkadiusz Lipiecki, Bartosz Uniejewski, Rafał Weron (2024)
Venue (Journal/Conference): Energy Economics
DOI: 10.1016/j.eneco.2024.107934
Core Topic: Postprocessing point forecasts into full probabilistic forecasts for day-ahead electricity prices
Main Methods Studied: Quantile Regression Averaging (QRA), Conformal Prediction (CP), and Isotonic Distributional Regression (IDR)
Markets Studied: Germany and Spain
Test Horizon: Two 4.5-year out-of-sample periods spanning COVID and the war in Ukraine
Code/Data Availability: They mention using public data and an open-source Julia package, PostForecasts.jl, for postprocessing
Proximity/Threat Level: High / Directly relevant if I work on probabilistic forecasting, postprocessing, calibration, or distributional evaluation
Why this paper matters: It shows that strong probabilistic forecasts do not necessarily require end-to-end distributional deep learning; carefully designed postprocessing on top of strong point forecasts can outperform more complex neural distribution models

href: reviews/Postprocessing of point predictions for probabilistic forecasting of day-ahead electricity prices.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: Postprocessing of point predictions for probabilistic forecasting of day-ahead electricity prices: The benefits of using isotonic distributional regression
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why probabilistic electricity price forecasting?)

The paper starts from a practical market argument: decisions based on predictive distributions of day-ahead electricity prices can yield substantially higher profits than decisions based only on point forecasts.
This is especially relevant in electricity markets because prices are volatile, spiky, and regime-dependent, particularly during shocks such as COVID, fuel crises, and the war in Ukraine.
In a trading or risk management setting, a point forecast gives only a central guess, while a predictive distribution gives information about tail risk, asymmetry, and forecast confidence.



The Motivation (Why postprocess point forecasts instead of building a probabilistic model from scratch?)

The authors argue that most models used in practice and in the literature still generate point predictions only.
Rather than discarding that large ecosystem, they propose a practical route: take already strong point forecasts and convert them into probabilistic forecasts through postprocessing.
This is attractive because it leverages progress in point forecasting while avoiding the full complexity of bespoke probabilistic model design.



Their claim to fame / novelty

This is, according to the authors, the first study to consider Isotonic Distributional Regression (IDR) for electricity price forecasting.
It is also one of the first to use Conformal Prediction (CP) in this domain.
They do not merely compare methods individually; they also study forecast combination, and use Shapley values to quantify how much each postprocessing component contributes to the final ensemble.
Their combined model, LEAR-Ave, beats a state-of-the-art Distributional Deep Neural Network with Johnson SU output (DDNN-JSU) over long and difficult test periods.



The actual scientific value

The paper makes a strong case that distributional quality can be improved substantially by intelligent postprocessing, not just by increasingly complex end-to-end deep architectures.
It also shows that diversity among probabilistic components matters: the best overall results come not from a single postprocessor, but from combining QRA, CP, and IDR.
Shapley analysis reveals that IDR contributes the most to the ensemble, even though its standalone performance is less uniformly stable than QRA.

href: reviews/Postprocessing of point predictions for probabilistic forecasting of day-ahead electricity prices.html#methodology-technical-details
title: Postprocessing of point predictions for probabilistic forecasting of day-ahead electricity prices: The benefits of using isotonic distributional regression
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

Datasets / testbed

The authors use publicly available data from:

ENTSO-E for day-ahead prices, load forecasts, and renewable generation forecasts
Investing.com for carbon emission, natural gas, crude oil, and coal prices

Markets:

Germany: BZN|DE-LU, historically BZN|DE-AT-LU before 30.09.2018
Spain: BZN|ES

Time span:

01.01.2015 to 31.12.2023

Test period:

Starts on 27.06.2019
Gives a 4.5-year out-of-sample evaluation

Data engineering details:

Some ENTSO-E series had 15-minute resolution and were aggregated to hourly
DST transitions were explicitly handled by averaging missing/duplicate hours




Point forecasting backbone
The paper is not about inventing a new point forecasting model. Instead, it uses point predictions as inputs to postprocessing.

Main point model: LEAR

They use a variant of the LASSO-Estimated AutoRegressive (LEAR) model.
Inputs include:

lagged electricity prices
day-ahead load forecasts
day-ahead renewable generation forecasts
macro variables: carbon emission prices, natural gas, Brent crude, and coal prices
weekday dummies

Important implementation choices:

They apply an asinh variance-stabilizing transformation to prices
They use coordinate descent LASSO
They use 7-fold cross-validation
They repeat the LEAR estimation 5 times per training window and average the results to reduce randomness




Benchmark point model: naive

They also include a simple similar-day naive benchmark
Monday, Saturday, and Sunday use the price from the same day last week
Other weekdays use yesterday’s price




Forecast generation setup

Rolling window estimation
Forecasts are generated daily for all 24 hours of the next day
LEAR uses four training window lengths:

56, 84, 1092, and 1456 days

Postprocessing is trained separately by hour using calibration windows:

28, 56, 91, and 182 days

href: reviews/Postprocessing of point predictions for probabilistic forecasting of day-ahead electricity prices.html#postprocessing-methods-compared
title: Postprocessing of point predictions for probabilistic forecasting of day-ahead electricity prices: The benefits of using isotonic distributional regression
text:
4. Postprocessing Methods Compared

4.1 Quantile Regression Averaging (QRA / QRM variant)

QRA estimates quantiles directly using quantile regression.
The authors test several variants and retain the best-performing one:

a Quantile Regression Machine (QRM)-style formulation using the average point forecast as the regressor

Strengths:

Direct quantile estimation
Flexible and well-established in energy forecasting
Generally strong and stable overall performer

Weaknesses:

Computationally the heaviest of the postprocessors in the paper because a separate optimization is needed for each quantile




4.2 Conformal Prediction (CP)

CP constructs prediction intervals using recent absolute forecast errors.
It is attractive because it provides valid intervals under weak assumptions and requires no parametric distributional assumption.
In this paper, CP is centered around the average point forecast.
Limitation:

Quantiles are derived under an implicit symmetry assumption around the point forecast
This can be restrictive in electricity prices, where distributions are often asymmetric and heavy-tailed




4.3 Isotonic Distributional Regression (IDR)

IDR is the most novel method here.
It is a nonparametric distributional learning method under a stochastic order / isotonicity constraint.
Intuition:

If one point forecast is higher than another, the corresponding predicted distribution should shift in an orderly way

Why it fits this problem:

Point forecasts are natural ordering variables for subsequent conditional distributions

Implementation:

The authors fit separate IDR distributions for each of the four point forecast models
Then they combine them by vertical averaging

Key property:

IDR directly minimizes CRPS under isotonic constraints

Important empirical finding:

IDR is the most behaviorally varied of the three methods
That variation appears to be exactly why it adds the most value in the ensemble




4.4 Ensemble of predictive distributions: LEAR-Ave

Final ensemble = average of:

LEAR-QRM
LEAR-CP
LEAR-IDR

The paper’s strongest message is that the combination beats all standalone methods, including the sophisticated DDNN benchmark



4.5 Additional probabilistic benchmarks
They also compare against simpler Gaussian-error-based probabilistic benchmarks: - Naive-1N - Naive-N - LEAR-N
These assume prediction errors are normally distributed with estimated standard deviation.


4.6 Distributional deep learning benchmark

The main modern benchmark is DDNN-JSU
It is a Distributional Deep Neural Network outputting the parameters of a Johnson SU distribution
This is the “complex neural competitor” that the postprocessing approaches are tested against

text:
5. Validation Strategy

Forecast evaluation
The paper is strong in evaluation design.

Test setting

Two large markets
4.5-year test periods
Includes highly nonstationary and crisis-heavy conditions



Main metric

CRPS (Continuous Ranked Probability Score)
This is the central metric for probabilistic forecast quality



Secondary analysis

APS20 for the extreme 20 percentiles, targeting tail/risk performance
Conditional Predictive Ability (CPA) test to assess whether forecast differences are statistically significant
Rolling 182-day skill scores to inspect temporal stability and regime sensitivity
Shapley values to assess contribution of each ensemble component




Why this validation is strong

They do not stop at average performance
They check:

overall distribution quality
temporal robustness
tail performance
statistical significance
component contribution in the ensemble


That is a real strength of the paper.

objectID: reviews/Postprocessing of point predictions for probabilistic forecasting of day-ahead electricity prices.html#main-results
href: reviews/Postprocessing of point predictions for probabilistic forecasting of day-ahead electricity prices.html#main-results
title: Postprocessing of point predictions for probabilistic forecasting of day-ahead electricity prices: The benefits of using isotonic distributional regression
text:
6. Main Results

Overall CRPS performance

LEAR-Ave is the best model overall across both Germany and Spain and across all four subperiods.
The simple Gaussian and naive baselines perform worst, as expected.
The LEAR-based postprocessing family consistently outperforms the deep distributional benchmark in most settings.



The most important headline result

The combined postprocessed forecast outperforms DDNN-JSU, despite the latter being a much more complex model.



Relative behavior of the three postprocessors

QRA / LEAR-QRM:

Strong all-rounder
Stable
Often the best standalone method

CP / LEAR-CP:

Stable but usually the weakest contributor of the three
Useful in the ensemble, but not the star

IDR / LEAR-IDR:

Most uneven over time
Sometimes weaker in volatile transition periods
But in certain regimes, especially calmer periods after volatile ones, it becomes very strong
Contributes the most to the ensemble according to Shapley values




Tail-risk results

In the tails, the story becomes more nuanced.
LEAR-Ave still performs best overall across the full test sets.
However, DDNN-JSU shows strength in some tail-focused settings, especially right after hyperparameter optimization.
The authors therefore do not dismiss DDNN-JSU entirely; instead, they argue it may have tail-performance potential, but at very high tuning cost.



Computational findings

Postprocessing is far cheaper than frequent deep model hyperparameter tuning.
Approximate timing reported:

LEAR: around 2.5 to 3 hours
QRA: 10 to 15 minutes
CP: 10 to 15 seconds
IDR: 15 to 20 seconds
LEAR-Ave: around 2.75 to 3.25 hours total
DDNN-JSU: around 6 to 6.5 hours for forecasting, while hyperparameter optimization could take weeks

This makes the postprocessing route extremely attractive in practice

href: reviews/Postprocessing of point predictions for probabilistic forecasting of day-ahead electricity prices.html#what-shapley-analysis-revealed
title: Postprocessing of point predictions for probabilistic forecasting of day-ahead electricity prices: The benefits of using isotonic distributional regression
text:
7. What Shapley Analysis Revealed
One of the most interesting parts of the paper is that Shapley values are not used for feature importance, but for ensemble-component importance.

What they found

Across both Germany and Spain, IDR contributes the most to LEAR-Ave
CP contributes the least
In 2023, IDR’s contribution exceeds 75% in both markets



Why this matters

IDR is not necessarily the most stable standalone model
But it brings the most diversity and the most marginal value when combined with QRA and CP
This is a really important lesson: the most valuable component in an ensemble is not always the one with the most stable standalone average score

objectID: reviews/Postprocessing of point predictions for probabilistic forecasting of day-ahead electricity prices.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
href: reviews/Postprocessing of point predictions for probabilistic forecasting of day-ahead electricity prices.html#my-thoughts-criticisms-unstated-limitations
title: Postprocessing of point predictions for probabilistic forecasting of day-ahead electricity prices: The benefits of using isotonic distributional regression
text:
8. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: Strong paper, but still heavily tied to a strong point forecasting backbone

The postprocessing works well partly because the base point forecasts are already strong.
That means some of the gains may reflect the strength of the improved LEAR implementation, not only the postprocessing scheme itself.
In other words, this is not a “pure postprocessing comparison in isolation”; it is a postprocessing comparison on top of a carefully optimized point forecasting pipeline.



Criticism 2: IDR’s success is real, but also regime-dependent

The authors are honest that IDR is the most uneven method over time.
That means IDR may not be a universal winner.
Its strongest value seems to come from complementing other methods, not necessarily replacing them.



Criticism 3: CP is somewhat handicapped by symmetry

Conformal Prediction is attractive for validity, but in this setup it is transformed into quantiles via a symmetry-centered construction.
Electricity price distributions are often not symmetric, especially during crisis periods and spikes.
So the paper’s CP implementation may understate how competitive more advanced conformalized or asymmetric conformal methods could be.



Criticism 4: Benchmark fairness versus DDNN-JSU

The paper compares against DDNN-JSU using a fixed hyperparameter set optimized earlier.
That is practical and defensible, but it does mean the deep benchmark may be under-optimized relative to what is theoretically possible.
The authors acknowledge this themselves.
So the paper proves that postprocessing can beat realistically deployed deep distributional models, but not necessarily the best imaginable re-tuned version of them.



Criticism 5: Distributional assumptions are not equally stressed

The Gaussian baselines are obviously simplistic and mostly serve as weak references.
That is fine, but it means the main real contest is QRA vs CP vs IDR vs DDNN-JSU.
I would have liked to see stronger modern alternatives too, for example:

direct quantile neural networks
conformalized quantile regression
mixture density models
nonparametric distributional learners beyond isotonicity




Criticism 6: Interpretability is only lightly touched

Shapley values here are used to interpret ensemble contribution, not the economics or drivers of price formation.
That is useful, but different from explaining the market itself.
So this is not really an XAI paper in the broad electricity-price sense; it is more a paper about performance attribution inside an ensemble.



Criticism 7: Heavy dependence on calibration design

The success of the method depends on:

window lengths
rolling recalibration
averaging scheme
market regime

Those are practical strengths, but also tuning levers.
This raises a portability question: how much of the reported advantage would remain under different calibration schedules or other markets outside Germany and Spain?

It is practical, not just methodological

10. Positioning Relative to My Own Work
This paper is highly relevant if I am working on: - probabilistic forecasting - calibration/postprocessing of point forecasts - ensemble distributions - uncertainty quantification in energy systems - risk-sensitive forecasting

What I can borrow

The idea of treating probabilistic forecasting as a postprocessing problem
The use of CRPS + tail metrics + CPA tests
The notion that diversity among probabilistic components matters
Shapley-value attribution at the ensemble component level



What I can improve on

Add stronger modern probabilistic baselines
Explore asymmetric or adaptive conformal methods
Test whether IDR-style gains persist in:

other power systems
renewable forecasting
load forecasting
highly nonstationary non-price time series

Separate the effect of:

base point model quality
postprocessor quality
ensemble diversity

text:
11. Action Items & Integration

Read up on Isotonic Distributional Regression in the original Henzi et al. papers, since this paper shows it is not just theoretically elegant, but practically useful.
Consider whether my own forecasting pipeline could benefit from a postprocessing layer rather than only end-to-end probabilistic modeling.
Use CRPS, tail-only pinball metrics, and CPA tests together when benchmarking probabilistic models.
Explore ensemble-component Shapley values as a way to explain why a combination works.
Treat model diversity as a design objective, not merely an accidental property.
Be cautious about concluding that a sophisticated deep distributional model is superior just because it is more expressive; this paper is a strong counterexample.
If I compare against neural distributional methods, document how much hyperparameter tuning they actually receive, since fairness depends heavily on that choice.

title: Postprocessing of point predictions for probabilistic forecasting of day-ahead electricity prices: The benefits of using isotonic distributional regression
text:
12. Final Takeaway
This paper is a strong argument for postprocessing as a serious probabilistic forecasting strategy, not just a lightweight add-on. Its central message is not merely that IDR works, but that a diverse ensemble of simple, well-designed postprocessors on top of strong point forecasts can outperform more complicated end-to-end distributional deep learning systems.
If I had to summarize the paper in one line:

Do not assume the best probabilistic forecast must come from the most complex probabilistic model; in hard electricity markets, smart postprocessing and forecast combination can win.
