title: Probabilistic load forecasting for buildings considering weather forecasting uncertainty and uncertain peak load
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why probabilistic load forecasting?):

The paper argues that deterministic building load forecasting is inadequate when both supply-side and demand-side uncertainties are growing.
In modern grids, uncertainty comes not only from variable generation but also from building-side behaviour, operating schedules, and sudden abnormal peak loads.
For practical decision-making, especially demand-side management and peak demand limiting, operators need distributions, intervals, or quantiles rather than a single point estimate.

The Motivation (Why buildings specifically?):

Much of the earlier probabilistic load forecasting literature focused on aggregate or system-level load.
Individual buildings are much more volatile and are therefore harder to forecast.
For non-residential buildings, especially those with HVAC-driven demand, load uncertainty depends strongly on both weather forecasting uncertainty and abnormal peak events.

The Motivation (Why model peak load separately?):

The authors identify a gap: previous work either ignored building-level abnormal peak load or relied on deterministic peak forecasting approaches that are poorly suited to large fluctuations and weak weather correlation.
They argue that abnormal peaks are fundamentally different from normal weather-driven demand and should not simply be absorbed into a single forecasting model.

Their claim to fame / Novelty:

They propose a two-component probabilistic forecasting architecture:

a probabilistic normal load forecasting model, and
a probabilistic peak abnormal differential (PAD) load forecasting model.

They explicitly integrate real probabilistic weather forecasts, rather than synthetic temperature scenarios based only on historical climate data.
They introduce a hybrid decomposition method combining linear regression (LR) and local outlier factor (LOF) to separate normal load from abnormal load.
They separately model the occurrence and magnitude of abnormal peaks.

What is actually new here conceptually?

The paper’s real contribution is not merely “ANN + probability.”
It is the decomposition of total building load uncertainty into:

uncertainty in the normal operational load, mainly weather-driven, and
uncertainty in the abnormal peak component, which is rarer, less weather-dependent, and statistically irregular.

That decomposition is the key modelling idea.

text:
3. Problem Formulation & Modelling Philosophy

Main forecasting view:

The total building load is treated as the combination of:

a normal load process, and
a positive abnormal differential component representing peak abnormalities.


Key definitions:

Normal load: load with no significant deviation from neighbouring load values.
Abnormal load: load with significant deviation from neighbouring values.
Abnormal peak load: abnormal load with significant positive deviation.
Peak abnormal differential (PAD) load: the difference between abnormal peak load and the corresponding normal load at that same time step.

Overall forecasting logic:

At any time, the probabilistic forecast can be thought of as:

either the normal load forecast alone, or
the normal load forecast plus the PAD forecast if an abnormal peak occurs.


Why this matters:

This is a more physically and statistically structured way to represent building load uncertainty than forcing one monolithic model to explain both everyday consumption and rare spikes.

text:
4. Methodology & Technical Details

4.1 Overall Model Architecture
The proposed framework has two basis-function-style components:

Probabilistic normal load forecasting model

Built using an ANN
Inputs: weather variables + calendar information
Weather uncertainty enters through probabilistic temperature forecasts

Probabilistic PAD load forecasting model

Built using statistical methods
Models:

probability of PAD occurrence
probability distribution of PAD magnitude

Inputs mainly depend on calendar information rather than weather


This separation is sensible because the authors assume normal load is weather-sensitive, while PAD events are less weather-dependent and more schedule/event related.



4.2 Probabilistic Normal Load Forecasting

Model type: Three-layer backpropagation ANN
Learning algorithm: Levenberg-Marquardt (LM)
Why ANN?:

The authors argue ANN is suitable because the relationship between building load, weather, and occupancy-related calendar effects is nonlinear and difficult to formulate analytically.
Calendar variables are used as proxies for occupancy and operational schedules.

Inputs to the ANN:

Outdoor dry-bulb temperature
Relative humidity
Hour of day
Day of week
Month of year

Output:

Hourly deterministic normal load

Training setup:

Historical data split into training and testing samples in a 7/8 : 1/8 ratio
Implemented in MATLAB using the Neural Network Toolbox
Hidden neurons set to 12 using empirical guidance plus trial and error
Mean square error target: 0.001
Learning rate: 0.5
Iterations: 1000

How probabilistic forecasts are generated from this ANN:

The ANN itself is first trained as a deterministic normal-load model.
Then deterministic temperature input is replaced with hourly probabilistic temperature quantiles.
Running the ANN over these temperature quantiles yields corresponding quantiles of the normal load forecast.

Important modelling choice:

They treat temperature as the dominant uncertain weather input and use its probabilistic forecast to induce the load forecast distribution.
Relative humidity remains deterministic in the case studies.





4.3 Construction of Probabilistic Temperature Forecasts

Weather source: Hong Kong Observatory (HKO)
Available weather information:

probabilistic daily minimum temperature forecasts
probabilistic daily maximum temperature forecasts
deterministic hourly temperature forecasts
deterministic hourly relative humidity forecasts

Their method:

Convert the HKO minimum/maximum temperature probability plots into usable time series data
Transform these into cumulative distribution functions
Interpolate 1%–99% quantiles of daily minimum and maximum temperature
Use those quantiles together with deterministic hourly forecasts to derive hourly probabilistic temperature forecasts

Why this is noteworthy:

Many earlier studies used historical temperature scenarios rather than actual forecast distributions.
This paper explicitly uses updated forecast uncertainty from an operational weather service, which makes the method more realistic for real-time deployment.





4.4 Probabilistic PAD Load Forecasting
The PAD model has two submodels:

A. Probabilistic Occurrence Model

PAD occurrence is assumed to depend mainly on:

hour of day
month of year

The model forecasts the probability that PAD occurs at hour h in month m
It is based on empirical occurrence probabilities from historical data
Underlying assumption:

PAD load occurs with the same probability at a given office hour across work days within a month

What this means practically:

This is a calendar-conditioned empirical probability model, not a highly flexible machine learning classifier




B. Probabilistic Magnitude Model

The magnitude of PAD load is modelled by fitting candidate probability density functions
The four candidates are:

Normal
Gamma
Weibull
Lognormal

Parameter estimation: maximum likelihood
Selection criterion: Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) error
Best fit found:

Lognormal distribution
Training K-S error: 0.0398

Interpretation:

The abnormal peak magnitudes are positively skewed and better captured by a lognormal-type distribution than by a symmetric normal distribution

text:
5. Data Processing & Decomposition Strategy
One of the most interesting parts of the paper is the preprocessing framework used to separate normal and abnormal load.

5.1 Why decomposition is necessary

A single training dataset containing both ordinary demand behaviour and irregular spikes may distort the ANN’s learning process
The authors therefore try to remove abnormal loads before training the normal-load ANN



5.2 Hybrid decomposition method
They combine two methods:

A. Linear Regression (LR) method

Used to identify abnormal loads that deviate from the weather-sensitive trend
Steps:

Perform sensitivity analysis between load and weather variables
Cluster by hour of day
Build LR between load and weather variable within each cluster
Analyse residuals with kernel density estimation (KDE)
Mark loads outside the 95% KDE confidence region as abnormal

Interesting result:

Enthalpy in second order had the strongest Pearson correlation with load (0.914), stronger than temperature or humidity alone
This supports the idea that combined thermal effects matter more than any single weather variable




B. Local Outlier Factor (LOF) method

Used to detect local anomalies in the time series
Useful where local discontinuities exist
Weakness: may fail when abnormal loads persist continuously over multiple time points



C. Why hybridise LR and LOF?

LR catches globally weather-inconsistent points
LOF catches locally unusual points
Their union gives a more robust abnormal-load detector




5.3 Hybrid method performance

Ratio of abnormal loads detected:

LR: 0.036
LOF: 0.035
Hybrid: 0.068

Interpretation:

The hybrid method is much more sensitive than either individual method
This is presented as evidence that it better captures abnormal behaviour




5.4 After decomposition

Abnormal loads are removed
Gaps are filled by linear interpolation to recover a “normal load” dataset
PAD load is then defined as the positive deviation between abnormal load and recovered normal load

6. Experimental Setup & Testbed

Building: Phase 7, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
Building type: educational / commercial-style building
Facilities: laboratories, classrooms, lecture theatres, conference rooms, staff offices
Climate: subtropical Hong Kong climate
Sampling interval: hourly
Historical window: Jan 2009 to Dec 2016
Operating hours considered: 09:00–20:00 on workdays
Excluded periods:

Sundays
public holidays
morning chiller-start spikes before 08:00

Why exclude these?

The authors argue the focus is on on-peak operating periods that matter most for demand limiting and monthly electricity costs
They also note that chiller start spikes are not the practical cause of actual monthly peak demand in their building

7. Validation Strategy

7.1 Deterministic normal-load model evaluation

Metrics:

MAPE
MAE
RMSE




7.2 PAD magnitude model evaluation

Metric:

Kolmogorov-Smirnov error between predicted and observed magnitude distribution




7.3 Probabilistic normal-load case-study evaluation

Metrics:

MAE
MAPE
RMSE
Pinball score
Quantile bandwidth / interval width
Visual inspection of whether actual loads lie within prediction intervals




7.4 What is missing

They discuss sharpness, resolution, and reliability conceptually
But they do not use a broader probabilistic metrics suite such as:

CRPS
Winkler score
calibration curves
PIT histograms for final building-load distributions

So the probabilistic evaluation is useful but not especially deep by today’s standards

text:
8. Main Results

8.1 Deterministic normal-load forecasting

Average MAPE = 5.0%
Average MAE = 77.8 kVA
Average RMSE = 108 kVA
Best month:

minimum MAPE = 2.9% in July

Worst months tend to occur during more volatile transition-season conditions such as December
Interpretation:

The ANN captures normal building behaviour reasonably well once abnormal peaks have been removed





8.2 PAD occurrence forecasting

The PAD occurrence model matched observed hourly relative frequencies fairly well
Larger deviations occurred around:

09:00
19:00
20:00

Interpretation:

The simple calendar-based occurrence model is workable, but performance is limited by the rarity of PAD events and the amount of historical PAD data available





8.3 PAD magnitude forecasting

Best-fitting distribution: Lognormal
Training fit:

K-S error = 0.0398

Validation on 2016:

K-S error = 0.09

Interpretation:

The model gives a reasonably good statistical description of abnormal peak magnitudes
This is a solid result, though not a perfect one





8.4 Real-time probabilistic normal-load case studies
The authors compare three ways of using weather forecasts:

Case 1: October, weather reported on four days

MAPE = 8.4%
MAE = 147 kVA
RMSE = 170 kVA
Pinball score = 58.9



Case 2: December, one-day-ahead weather forecasts updated daily

MAPE = 4.7%
MAE = 64 kVA
RMSE = 80 kVA
Pinball score = 27.6
Best-performing case



Case 3: December, nine-day-ahead weather forecasts

MAPE = 6.7%
MAE = 65 kVA
RMSE = 82 kVA
Pinball score = 27.8




8.5 Key empirical takeaway

One-day-ahead probabilistic weather forecasts produced the best probabilistic load forecasts
The paper therefore shows that forecast quality is strongly affected by the quality and recency of the weather forecast input

9. What the Paper Proves

It proves that building-level probabilistic forecasting improves when weather forecast uncertainty is represented explicitly
It proves that abnormal peak load should be modelled separately rather than treated as ordinary noise
It shows that updated weather forecast information matters materially
It demonstrates that a decomposed modelling strategy can work well in practice for real building data

This is a practically grounded paper rather than a purely methodological one. Its value is in operational realism.

Strong practical framing

The paper is very application-oriented and addresses a real problem in building energy management

Weather forecast uncertainty
Abnormal peak load uncertainty

Separating normal and abnormal demand is an intuitively strong modelling move

text:
11. Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: The “probabilistic” framework is partly induced rather than fully learned

The normal-load probabilistic forecast is not produced by a truly probabilistic ANN.
Instead, a deterministic ANN is driven by probabilistic temperature inputs.
That means the uncertainty is propagated primarily from one input source rather than learned jointly as an output distribution conditioned on all inputs.

Why this matters:
This may underestimate uncertainty arising from occupancy, equipment usage, operational changes, or model error.



Criticism 2: Relative humidity is treated deterministically while temperature gets the probabilistic treatment

The method assumes temperature is the dominant uncertain weather variable.
That is probably reasonable, but it is still a simplification.
For buildings with humidity-sensitive HVAC behaviour, this could underrepresent uncertainty.




Criticism 3: The occurrence model for abnormal peaks is fairly simple

PAD occurrence is modelled using empirical probabilities based mainly on month and hour.
This is interpretable and data-efficient, but also restrictive.
It ignores richer explanatory factors such as:

event schedules
examinations
operational anomalies
special building-use patterns
maintenance events


Why this matters:
The model may work well on average while still missing the real causal drivers of abnormal peaks.



Criticism 4: The magnitude model is statistically neat but not dynamically rich

Fitting a single lognormal distribution to PAD magnitude is elegant, but it may hide heterogeneity.
Different kinds of abnormal peaks may arise from different mechanisms and therefore different distributions.
A mixture model or context-conditioned model might capture this better.




Criticism 5: Probabilistic evaluation is not especially modern

The paper uses pinball score and interval-width style reasoning, which is useful.
But the evaluation could be much stronger with:

CRPS
calibration diagnostics
coverage deviation analysis
reliability diagrams
formal decomposition of sharpness vs calibration





Criticism 6: Single-site validation limits generalisability

The whole study is based on one educational building in Hong Kong.
The method may transfer, but the evidence for transferability is limited.
Buildings with different schedules, climates, or end-use structures may behave quite differently.




Criticism 7: Excluding certain spikes and off-peak periods simplifies the problem

The authors deliberately narrow the forecasting domain to office-hour on-peak periods.
This makes sense operationally, but it also means the framework is not validated for full 24-hour building demand forecasting.
The most difficult transient phenomena may therefore be partly avoided.




Criticism 8: Comparison baseline scope is narrow

The paper demonstrates internal effectiveness, but it does not compare against stronger modern probabilistic baselines such as:

quantile regression forests
gradient boosting for quantiles
probabilistic LSTMs
deep ensembles
NGBoost-style distributional learning
conformal forecasting approaches


Why this matters:
The study shows the proposed framework works, but not necessarily whether it is the best available approach.

12. Deeper Interpretation for My Research Context

What I can take from this paper:

Separate structurally distinct uncertainty sources instead of forcing one model to explain everything
Treat forecast-input uncertainty explicitly
Use domain-informed decomposition before forecasting
Benchmark not just point error but also probabilistic sharpness and quality

What this paper does not yet solve:

End-to-end probabilistic forecasting of full load distributions from all uncertain drivers
dynamic modelling of rare-event occurrence using richer covariates
rigorous probabilistic calibration analysis
multi-building or multi-climate generalisation

How I would position it in a literature review:

As an important applied study showing that probabilistic building load forecasting benefits from explicit weather uncertainty modelling and abnormal peak decomposition
But also as a transitional paper: stronger than purely deterministic building forecasting, yet not as advanced as modern end-to-end probabilistic learning frameworks

text:
13. Suggested Literature Review Positioning Paragraph
This study is important because it moves beyond conventional deterministic building load forecasting by explicitly separating ordinary weather-driven demand from rare abnormal peak behaviour. Its main contribution is a hybrid probabilistic architecture in which an ANN forecasts normal load under probabilistic temperature inputs, while abnormal peak differential load is modelled through separate occurrence and magnitude components. The framework is practically valuable because it uses real probabilistic weather forecasts rather than synthetic historical scenarios, and because it acknowledges that abnormal peak load is statistically different from normal operational demand. However, the resulting probabilistic system remains partly modular and heuristic: uncertainty is propagated mainly through temperature quantiles, abnormal peak occurrence is driven by simple empirical calendar probabilities, and the evaluation of predictive uncertainty is not as comprehensive as in more recent probabilistic forecasting literature. Thus, the paper stands as a strong applied contribution in building-level probabilistic forecasting, while still leaving room for more integrated, better-calibrated, and more generalisable probabilistic learning methods.

Core Topic: Predictive uncertainty estimation for deep neural networks using non-Bayesian ensembles

title: Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why Uncertainty?):

Deep neural networks often achieve high predictive accuracy, but they are notoriously poor at expressing when they are unsure.
This is dangerous in real-world systems because models can produce overconfident wrong predictions, especially under dataset shift or on unfamiliar inputs.
The authors position uncertainty not as an optional extra, but as a practical requirement for reliable deployment in high-stakes settings such as weather forecasting, medical diagnosis, and other safety-relevant tasks.

The Motivation (Why This Matters for Trust and Explainability?):

A model that communicates its uncertainty provides an interpretable signal about the reliability of its own prediction.
In this sense, uncertainty becomes a form of model-level explainability: it helps users understand not only what the model predicts, but also how much confidence should be placed in that prediction.
This supports trust calibration, meaning users are less likely to blindly accept unreliable predictions and less likely to reject reliable ones simply because the model is a black box.

Their Claim to Fame / Novelty:

They propose a very simple alternative to Bayesian neural networks for uncertainty estimation: train multiple neural networks independently and average their predictive distributions.
Their method combines:

proper scoring rules for probabilistic training,
ensembling to capture variation across plausible models,
optional adversarial training to smooth predictive distributions.

The key novelty is showing that this simple, scalable, non-Bayesian approach can match or outperform approximate Bayesian uncertainty methods such as MC-dropout and probabilistic backpropagation.

Why This Paper Matters for XAI:

Although the paper is not framed as a classical XAI paper, it is extremely relevant to XAI because it shows that uncertainty itself is explanatory.
Instead of explaining predictions through feature attributions such as SHAP, the paper explains model behavior through:

calibration,
confidence quality,
entropy on unfamiliar inputs,
and graceful failure under uncertainty.

This is especially important in operational settings, where a useful explanation is often not only “which features mattered,” but also “should this prediction be trusted enough to act on?”

title: Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

Overall Recipe Proposed by the Paper:

Train neural networks to predict probabilistic outputs rather than only point predictions.
Use a proper scoring rule as the optimization criterion.
Train an ensemble of independently initialized networks.
Optionally use adversarial training to improve smoothness and robustness.

Proper Scoring Rules:

The paper emphasizes that the training loss should reward calibrated predictive distributions.
For classification, this includes:

softmax cross-entropy / log-likelihood,
Brier score.

For regression, the network predicts:

a mean,
and a variance, allowing the model to represent heteroscedastic uncertainty.


Regression Setup:

Instead of minimizing only mean squared error, the regression network outputs both:

predicted mean ((x)),
predicted variance (^2(x)).

This allows the model to learn how uncertainty varies across the input space.

Adversarial Training:

The paper investigates adversarial training as a way to encourage smoother predictive distributions.
Their interpretation is important: adversarial training is not only a robustness trick, but also a way of locally smoothing uncertainty estimates around observed data.

Ensembling Strategy:

Multiple networks are trained independently with:

different random initializations,
shuffled data order,
the full training dataset.

The final predictive distribution is obtained by averaging predictions across ensemble members.
For regression, this gives a mixture distribution, approximated using the ensemble mean and variance.

Important Practical Point:

The authors deliberately avoid complex Bayesian approximations and instead propose a method that:

is easy to implement,
parallelizes naturally,
requires minimal hyperparameter tuning,
and scales to large datasets such as ImageNet.

text:
4. Validation Strategy (Predictions, Reliability & Explainability)

Validating the Predictions (Forecasting / Classification Quality):

The paper evaluates both predictive performance and uncertainty quality.
Main metrics include:

Negative Log Likelihood (NLL),
Brier Score,
classification accuracy,
RMSE for regression.


Validating the Uncertainty (Reliability Quality):

The authors focus on two major uncertainty properties:

Calibration
Whether reported probabilities align with empirical frequencies.
Robustness to distribution shift / out-of-distribution inputs
Whether the model becomes more uncertain on unfamiliar data.


OOD / Domain Shift Experiments:

They explicitly test whether the model “knows what it does not know.”
Examples include:

training on MNIST and testing on NotMNIST,
training on SVHN and testing on CIFAR-10,
ImageNet experiments separating known and unknown categories.

They analyze predictive entropy and confidence distributions on known versus unknown classes.

Actionability-Oriented Evaluation:

One of the most important experiments in the paper is accuracy as a function of confidence threshold.
This directly connects uncertainty to decision-making:

if confidence is high, predictions may be trusted,
if confidence is low, the system can defer to a human or another fallback policy.

This is one of the strongest actionability contributions of the paper.

section: 5. How the Paper Uses Uncertainty as Explainability, Trust, and Actionability
text:
5. How the Paper Uses Uncertainty as Explainability, Trust, and Actionability

5.1 Uncertainty as Explainability

The paper treats uncertainty as more than a numerical by-product; it functions as an explanation of model reliability.
A prediction accompanied by high uncertainty effectively tells the user:

this input may be unfamiliar,
the model may be extrapolating,
the output should be handled with caution.

In this way, predictive uncertainty serves as a decision-relevant explanation, even without feature-level attribution methods.



5.2 Uncertainty as a Mechanism for Trust

The paper strongly supports the idea that trust in machine learning systems should not come from accuracy alone.
A model that is accurate but systematically overconfident is dangerous because it encourages:

automation bias: blindly trusting wrong predictions,
and poor human oversight.

By producing better-calibrated uncertainty estimates, deep ensembles support appropriate trust rather than blind trust.
This aligns closely with modern XAI arguments that trustworthy AI should help users understand when to rely on the model and when not to.



5.3 Uncertainty as Actionability

This is the most useful angle for your paper.
The authors do not stop at saying uncertainty is “nice to have.” They show how uncertainty can be used to guide action.
Their confidence-threshold experiments demonstrate a very practical workflow:

accept predictions above a confidence threshold,
reject, defer, or escalate predictions below that threshold.

This converts uncertainty into an operational signal for:

human-in-the-loop intervention,
safe abstention,
fallback to simpler models,
or more cautious downstream control actions.




5.4 The Outcome of Using Uncertainty for Actionability

The outcome is that the system can fail more gracefully.
In particular, compared with MC-dropout, deep ensembles produce:

fewer overconfident errors,
better uncertainty on unseen classes,
and higher effective accuracy when filtering by confidence.

In practical terms, this means uncertainty is not merely descriptive; it improves the usefulness of the system in deployment.
The paper therefore provides a strong example of how uncertainty can increase the operational value of AI by supporting selective trust and selective action.

section: 6. Key Experimental Findings Relevant to Your Literature Review
text:
6. Key Experimental Findings Relevant to Your Literature Review

Deep ensembles outperform or match approximate Bayesian methods on several regression and classification benchmarks.
They provide better calibrated uncertainty than MC-dropout in many cases.
They are more robust to out-of-distribution examples, producing higher uncertainty where appropriate.
Ensemble size improves both predictive quality and uncertainty quality.
Adversarial training can further improve uncertainty behavior in some settings, though it is not uniformly necessary.
On ImageNet, the approach remains effective and scalable, which is important because many uncertainty papers only demonstrate results on small datasets.

text:
7. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: Uncertainty is treated as explainability, but not formally evaluated as XAI

The paper makes a strong practical case that uncertainty improves interpretability and trust, but it does not explicitly frame this under a formal XAI evaluation framework.
There is no direct study of how human users interpret or act on the uncertainty outputs.

Criticism 2: Limited decomposition of uncertainty

The method captures useful predictive uncertainty, but it does not provide a rigorous decomposition into epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty in the way later methods attempt.
For your paper, this is worth noting if you want to distinguish different sources of uncertainty more explicitly.

Criticism 3: Explanation remains model-level, not feature-level

The uncertainty signal explains reliability but not causation or feature contribution.
So while the paper is highly relevant to trust and actionability, it does not answer questions like:

which input variables drove the uncertainty,
why this specific sample is uncertain in terms of physical or operational drivers.


Criticism 4: OOD detection is evaluated empirically, not theoretically guaranteed

The paper shows strong practical OOD behavior, but deep ensembles are not a guaranteed solution to all distribution shifts.
Their success depends on ensemble diversity and the structure of the learned predictors.

Criticism 5: Computational cost is higher than a single model

Although simpler than Bayesian neural networks, the method still requires training multiple networks.
This creates a compute and memory cost that may matter in some large-scale or resource-constrained environments.

8. Relevance to My Paper

Why I would cite this paper:

It gives strong support for the argument that uncertainty can itself act as an explainability mechanism.
It links uncertainty directly to:

trust,
reliability assessment,
decision support,
and actionability in deployment.


How I would use it in my review:

I would cite this paper when arguing that explainable machine learning in safety-critical systems should not be limited to post hoc feature attribution methods.
I would use it to support the claim that well-calibrated predictive uncertainty is a form of actionable explanation, because it tells decision-makers when they can trust a model and when they should intervene.

Most useful angle for my article:

The strongest takeaway is not simply that deep ensembles improve NLL or Brier score.
It is that uncertainty estimates can be operationalized into better decisions through confidence-based filtering, rejection, fallback logic, or human review.
That makes uncertainty valuable not only for interpretability, but for real-world control and risk management.

How this connects to actionability:

The paper shows that uncertainty enables selective prediction.
Selective prediction is inherently actionable because it changes what a human or system should do next.
In other words, uncertainty is not only an explanation of model confidence; it is a trigger for downstream action.

href: reviews/Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers.html#core-framing
title: Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers
text:
1. Core Framing
For a deterministic reader, uncertainty is often heard as a weakness: the model is inaccurate, incomplete, or hesitant. The literature gives a better framing. Uncertainty is information about what is still unresolved after a model has made a prediction. It can describe the spread of plausible outcomes, the reliability of the model’s knowledge, or both.
A deterministic forecast answers:

What single value should we expect?

A probabilistic forecast answers:

What values are plausible, how likely are they, and when should the prediction be treated with caution?

This distinction is important because a point forecast can be accurate on average while still being unhelpful for decisions that depend on risk, extremes, or asymmetric costs. In energy forecasting, for example, under-prediction and over-prediction may have very different consequences. This is why several forecasting papers describe probabilistic forecasts as distributions, quantiles, prediction intervals, or densities rather than as one expected value.
crumbs: Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers.html#a-useful-taxonomy
href: reviews/Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers.html#a-useful-taxonomy
title: Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers
text:
2. A Useful Taxonomy










Term
Plain-language meaning
Reducible?
Typical examples
Practical implication




Aleatoric / aleatory uncertainty
Variability that is inherent in the process being measured or forecast.
Usually no, within the current measurement/model setup.
Sensor noise, weather variability, overlapping classes, noisy target values, random load fluctuation.
Better sensors or a different problem formulation may help, but simply adding more of the same data often will not remove it.


Epistemic uncertainty
Uncertainty caused by limited knowledge about the model, parameters, data coverage, or operating context.
In principle, yes.
Sparse data, poor coverage of rare operating regimes, model-form choice, parameter uncertainty, out-of-distribution inputs, dataset shift.
Can often be reduced with targeted data collection, model refinement, better features, or explicit out-of-distribution handling.


Data uncertainty
Uncertainty that comes from the data generation or observation process.
Often treated as aleatoric, but not always.
Measurement noise, label ambiguity, unresolved class overlap.
Explain whether the data are noisy because the world is variable or because the measurement process is weak.


Model uncertainty
Uncertainty about the model’s structure, parameters, or suitability for the current input.
Usually epistemic.
Neural-network architecture choice, limited training data, parameter posterior spread, distribution shift.
Useful for deciding where the model does not yet know enough.


Total predictive uncertainty
The combined uncertainty attached to a prediction.
Mixed.
Prediction variance, predictive entropy, forecast interval width, full predictive distribution.
Useful as a risk signal, but it can hide different causes unless decomposed.


Uncertainty under shift / OOD uncertainty
Uncertainty caused by applying the model outside the conditions it learned from.
Usually epistemic.
New operating regimes, unusual weather, unseen equipment states, shifted feature distributions.
High uncertainty should trigger caution, abstention, human review, or data collection.



The most helpful short version is:

Aleatoric uncertainty means the outcome is variable even if the model is well informed. Epistemic uncertainty means the model is not yet sufficiently informed.

That distinction should be presented as useful rather than absolute. Hullermeier and Waegeman emphasize that aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty depend on the modelling context. A source of uncertainty can move category when the measurement system, feature set, or modelling assumptions change. A class overlap that looks irreducible with one feature set may become reducible after adding a more informative sensor.
crumbs: Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers.html#probability-confidence-and-intervals
href: reviews/Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers.html#probability-confidence-and-intervals
title: Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers
text:
3. Probability, Confidence, and Intervals

Probability
Probability is the model’s numerical statement about possible outcomes. In classification it may be a probability assigned to each class. In regression or forecasting it is better to think in terms of a full conditional distribution:

Given the current inputs, what distribution of future outcomes does the model assign?

Quantiles, prediction intervals, densities, and scenarios with assigned probabilities are all ways of communicating this distribution. Scenarios without probabilities are not yet probabilistic forecasts; they are possible futures, but not weighted possible futures.


Confidence
Confidence is used less consistently than probability. In classification papers, confidence often means the maximum predicted class probability. In regression and forecasting papers, confidence may refer to an interval level, an observed coverage rate, or the model’s practical trustworthiness. The safest research language is therefore:

I use confidence only when I define the metric. Otherwise I use probability, coverage, calibration, entropy, variance, or interval width.

For deterministic readers, this distinction matters:

A probability can be part of the forecast. Confidence is about how much trust we should place in that probability or prediction.

A model can assign a high probability and still be overconfident if similar predictions are wrong more often than the probability implies. This is the calibration problem.


Prediction Intervals vs. Confidence Intervals
The load-forecasting literature is especially useful here because it explicitly warns that many papers misuse “confidence interval” when they mean “prediction interval.”








Interval term
What it refers to
Better wording




Prediction interval
A range intended to contain a future observation or realised outcome with a stated long-run coverage.
“A 90% prediction interval should contain about 90% of comparable future observations.”


Confidence interval
A range for an estimated parameter, fitted function, or model quantity.
“A 95% confidence interval describes uncertainty in the estimated mean/function/parameter.”



For forecasting research, the default term should usually be prediction interval, not confidence interval, because the object of interest is normally the future observed value, not only an unknown parameter.
crumbs: Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers.html#deterministic-to-probabilistic-translation
href: reviews/Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers.html#deterministic-to-probabilistic-translation
title: Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers
text:
4. Deterministic-to-Probabilistic Translation








Deterministic language
Probabilistic counterpart
Explanation for readers




Point forecast
Predictive distribution
A point forecast gives one number; a predictive distribution gives the range and relative plausibility of many numbers.


Expected value / mean
Conditional mean
The average outcome implied by the distribution, not the whole forecast.


Median forecast
P50 quantile
Half the probability mass lies below and half above.


Upper/lower forecast band
Quantile pair or prediction interval
The model is describing a plausible range, not just an error bar decoration.


Forecast error
Calibration and coverage
The question becomes whether stated uncertainty matches realised uncertainty.


Smaller error
Sharper calibrated forecast
A useful probabilistic forecast is as narrow as possible while still covering the right amount.


Model confidence
Calibrated reliability
The stated probability/interval should agree with observed correctness over comparable cases.



Three evaluation terms are worth introducing early:
Calibration / reliability: When the model says 90%, does the event occur about 90% of the time in comparable cases?
Sharpness: Among calibrated forecasts, are the intervals/distributions as concentrated as possible? A forecast that always gives a very wide interval may be calibrated but not useful.
Resolution / adaptivity: Does the uncertainty change meaningfully across inputs and operating regimes? If all cases receive the same interval width, the model may be ignoring important structure.
Pernot’s validation primer adds a useful refinement. Average calibration is not enough. An uncertainty method can look correct on average while being too narrow in one region of the input space and too wide in another. His terms are:







Validation target
Meaning




Average calibration
The uncertainty is correct on average across the validation set.


Consistency
The uncertainty is reliable across different predicted uncertainty levels.


Adaptivity
The uncertainty is reliable across the relevant input-feature space.



This is an excellent language bridge for deterministic readers because it says: “We are not asking you to trust a vague uncertainty number. We are asking whether that number behaves correctly where it is used.”
crumbs: Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers.html#how-this-supports-explainability
href: reviews/Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers.html#how-this-supports-explainability
title: Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers
text:
5. How This Supports Explainability
Most XAI methods explain the point prediction: which inputs pushed the forecast up or down. The uncertainty-explanation papers argue that this is incomplete because the uncertainty itself can vary across the feature space.
For this research, the stronger claim is:

It is not enough to explain the predicted value. We also need to explain why the prediction became more or less uncertain.

That framing supports feature-attribution work on:

the lower quantile,
the upper quantile,
the interval width,
the predictive entropy,
the predictive variance,
the difference between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty,
and the cases where high uncertainty is caused by feature interactions rather than by a single feature.

Watson et al. provide the clean theoretical bridge: explain predictive uncertainty by attributing features to conditional entropy or related information-theoretic quantities. Bley et al. provide a more applied bridge: in ensembles, uncertainty can be dominated by second-order feature and feature-interaction effects, so explaining uncertainty may require more than applying ordinary first-order SHAP-style reasoning to a point forecast.
crumbs: Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers.html#reusable-paragraphs
href: reviews/Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers.html#reusable-paragraphs
title: Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers
text:
6. Reusable Paragraphs

Short Conceptual Introduction
This study treats uncertainty as a property of the prediction, not merely as a symptom of model error. A deterministic model returns a single expected value, while a probabilistic model returns information about the range and relative plausibility of possible outcomes. This is important in operational forecasting because decisions are often affected not only by the most likely value, but also by the risk of high, low, or unusual outcomes.


Aleatoric and Epistemic Uncertainty
The uncertainty literature commonly distinguishes between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Aleatoric uncertainty refers to variability that remains even when the model is well informed, such as measurement noise, natural system variability, or overlapping outcome regions. Epistemic uncertainty refers to uncertainty caused by limited knowledge, such as sparse training data, uncertain model parameters, model-form choices, or inputs that differ from the training distribution. In practical terms, aleatoric uncertainty describes what is inherently variable, while epistemic uncertainty describes what the model has not yet learned.


Probability and Confidence
Probability and confidence should not be used as loose synonyms. Probability is the numerical statement made by the predictive model about possible outcomes. Confidence is better reserved for a defined reliability concept, such as calibrated class confidence, interval coverage, or observed confidence. A model can assign a high probability to an outcome and still be overconfident if similar predictions fail more often than the probability implies.


Prediction Intervals
In forecasting, the appropriate interval is usually a prediction interval rather than a confidence interval. A prediction interval is intended to contain future observations with a stated long-run coverage level. For example, a 90% prediction interval should contain approximately 90% of comparable realised outcomes if the forecasting system is well calibrated. This interpretation differs from a confidence interval, which describes uncertainty in an estimated parameter or fitted function.


Explaining Uncertainty
Explainability should extend beyond the point forecast. A feature can influence not only the predicted mean or median, but also the width, asymmetry, or entropy of the predictive distribution. Explaining the prediction interval therefore asks a different question from explaining the point forecast: which inputs made the outcome more or less predictable? This distinction is central when the goal is to understand risk, not only expected value.
crumbs: Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers.html#wording-to-avoid
href: reviews/Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers.html#wording-to-avoid
title: Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers
text:
7. Wording To Avoid







Avoid
Prefer




“The model is 90% confident the true value is inside this interval.”
“The 90% prediction interval should contain about 90% of comparable future observations if calibrated.”


“The confidence interval around the forecast.”
“The prediction interval around the forecast,” unless the interval is for a fitted parameter or function.


“Low probability means low uncertainty.”
“Low probability for one outcome may still be a confident prediction if the distribution is well specified.”


“The model is uncertain.”
“The model has high predictive entropy / wide prediction interval / high epistemic uncertainty,” depending on the metric.


“More data will reduce uncertainty.”
“More representative data can reduce epistemic uncertainty; aleatoric uncertainty may remain.”

href: reviews/Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers.html#source-map
title: Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers
text:
8. Source Map







Source
Best use in the research




Hullermeier and Waegeman, “Aleatoric and Epistemic Uncertainty in Machine Learning”
Best conceptual foundation. Use for reducible vs. irreducible uncertainty, probability vs. ignorance, and the caution that aleatoric/epistemic categories are context-dependent.


Kendall and Gal, “What Uncertainties Do We Need in Bayesian Deep Learning for Computer Vision?”
Clear practical definitions: aleatoric as observation noise; epistemic as model uncertainty reducible with enough data. Good for explaining OOD behavior and safety-critical relevance.


He and Jiang, “A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Learning: An Uncertainty Source’s Perspective”
Best source-based taxonomy: data uncertainty, model uncertainty, and methods grouped by which source they capture.


Nemani et al., “Uncertainty Quantification in Machine Learning for Engineering Design and Health Prognostics: A Tutorial”
Best engineering-facing explanation of aleatory/epistemic sources, total predictive uncertainty, confidence communication, and decomposition by total variance.


Hong and Fan, “Probabilistic Electric Load Forecasting: A Tutorial Review”
Best forecasting terminology source. Use for quantiles, intervals, densities, scenarios with probabilities, and the distinction between prediction intervals and confidence intervals.


Wen et al., “A Multi-Horizon Quantile Recurrent Forecaster”
Clean deterministic-vs-probabilistic contrast: probabilistic forecast as a conditional distribution versus point forecast as conditional mean. Good for quantile forecasting language.


Van Beers and De Visser, “How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression”
Best caution on interval evaluation. Use for confidence vs. prediction intervals, pointwise vs. marginal coverage, and why PICP can be misleading.


Pernot, “Validation of Uncertainty Quantification Metrics”
Best validation language: calibration, consistency, adaptivity, and why average calibration alone does not guarantee reliable uncertainty for individual predictions.


Ovadia et al., “Can You Trust Your Model’s Uncertainty?”
Best cautionary evidence that calibration can degrade under dataset shift and that confidence must align with accuracy in deployment conditions.


Watson et al., “Explaining Predictive Uncertainty with Information Theoretic Shapley Values”
Best theoretical bridge from UQ to XAI: explain conditional entropy and uncertainty components, not only point estimates.


Bley et al., “Explaining Predictive Uncertainty by Exposing Second-Order Effects”
Best applied bridge for explaining uncertainty with feature and feature-interaction effects, especially in ensembles and energy-price examples.


Salvi et al., “Explainability and Uncertainty: Two Sides of the Same Coin”
Useful framing that XAI alone cannot guarantee reliability and that uncertainty should be communicated alongside explanations.
crumbs: Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers

title: Uncertainty taxonomy and language for deterministic readers
text:
9. Suggested Placement In The Research
This material probably belongs early in the literature review or methodology chapter, before introducing the proposed explainable probabilistic model. The clean sequence would be:

Deterministic prediction gives a point estimate.
Probabilistic prediction gives a distribution, interval, or quantiles.
Predictive uncertainty can come from inherent variability or lack of knowledge.
Probability, confidence, and prediction intervals need precise wording.
A good uncertainty estimate must be calibrated, sharp, and adaptive.
The research contribution is to explain not only the forecast, but the uncertainty around the forecast.

Venue (Journal/Conference): Advanced Engineering Informatics
DOI: 10.1016/j.aei.2025.103730

Prediction Target: Diesel engine output power under standard operating conditions
Code/Data Available?: Not explicitly stated in the paper

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
href: reviews/Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability.html#core-contributions-novelty-motivation
title: Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability for data-driven assembly quality prediction in complex manufacturing systems
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why this problem matters):

Complex assembly systems such as diesel engines, CNC machine tools, and aircraft assembly are dynamic, multimodal, and data-imperfect environments.
Small upstream deviations accumulate across stations and eventually affect final product quality.
Traditional machine learning methods are more transparent, but struggle with multimodal complexity.
Deep learning improves accuracy, but sacrifices interpretability and trustworthy uncertainty estimation.

The Motivation (Why uncertainty-aware modeling?):

The paper argues that industrial assembly data contains three distinct uncertainty sources:

Epistemic uncertainty: due to limited knowledge, sparse data, missing conditions, or imperfect model structure.
Aleatoric uncertainty: due to inherent noise and randomness in the assembly process.
Out-of-distribution (OOD) uncertainty: due to shifts in operating conditions, environmental changes, or unseen inputs.

In an industrial setting, simply predicting a point value is not enough. Engineers need to know how reliable that prediction is, and why the model is uncertain.

The Motivation (Why explainability?):

Even though Bayesian neural networks provide some intrinsic interpretability through probabilistic parameter modeling, the authors argue that this alone is insufficient for complex assembly data.
They therefore add SHAP as a post-hoc explanatory layer to:

rank influential process variables,
support global sensitivity analysis,
support localized diagnosis of defective or risky cases,
and connect uncertainty intervals to feature-level reasoning.


Their claim to fame / Novelty:

They propose an integrated framework that combines:

a Bayesian neural network,
hierarchical priors for epistemic uncertainty,
stochastic residual modeling for aleatoric uncertainty,
feature perturbation analysis for OOD uncertainty,
and SHAP for feature attribution.

The paper’s real contribution is not merely “BNN + SHAP,” but rather the attempt to build a unified interpretable uncertainty-aware pipeline for industrial quality prediction.

The Value Derived from Explainability (What did XAI actually do?):

SHAP was used to identify the most influential assembly and test-bench variables.
It provided both:

global explanations via feature ranking, and
local explanations via interaction analysis between variables.

This allowed the model to move beyond prediction and toward practical engineering diagnosis, for example identifying which parameters to inspect or compensate when a product is likely to fail.

Their ultimate result:

The proposed UABNN outperformed ResNet, VAE, and ViT on the diesel engine dataset:

MAE: 0.3419
RMSE: 0.4466
MAPE: 0.0151
R²: 0.9831

It also showed better uncertainty behavior through narrower and more stable confidence intervals and achieved the best reported OOD AUROC in the ablation study.
crumbs: Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability for data-driven assembly quality prediction in complex manufacturing systems

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability.html#methodology-technical-details
href: reviews/Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability.html#methodology-technical-details
title: Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability for data-driven assembly quality prediction in complex manufacturing systems
text:
3. Methodology & Technical Details

Overall framing:

The paper formulates final assembly quality as the cumulative effect of process quality across multiple stations.
In the diesel engine case, deviations in variables such as protrusion heights, torque, and axial clearance propagate to downstream test outcomes such as oil pressure, fuel consumption, and torque fluctuation.

Core model architecture:

The UABNN takes a probabilistic view of network weights.
Input dimension: 39
Hidden layers: 3
Hidden units per layer: 40
Output dimension: 1
Output target: predicted diesel engine power

How uncertainty is modeled:

Epistemic uncertainty

Captured using hierarchical parameter priors over network weights.
This is meant to represent uncertainty due to incomplete knowledge or limited data.

Aleatoric uncertainty

Captured by explicitly modeling stochastic residual behavior.
This is meant to reflect irreducible randomness in the data-generating process.

OOD uncertainty

Captured through feature perturbation analysis.
Perturbed inputs are passed through sampled model configurations, and deviations are used to approximate whether the sample falls outside the training distribution.


Bayesian learning details:

A standard normal prior is imposed on weights.
The posterior is approximated with learnable mean and variance parameters.
Variational inference is used.
KL divergence regularization is used and its weight is adjusted in stages during training.
Adam optimizer is used with an initial learning rate of 0.001.

Confidence intervals:

The model outputs both a point estimate and a predictive distribution.
Confidence intervals are derived from predictive mean and variance.
The paper visualizes intervals using up to three standard deviations.

How SHAP is used:

SHAP values are computed per sample.
Global importance is obtained through average absolute SHAP values.
Local feature interactions are examined to understand coupling between process variables.
The authors position SHAP as a bridge between uncertainty outputs and interpretable engineering diagnosis.
crumbs: Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability for data-driven assembly quality prediction in complex manufacturing systems

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability.html#datasets-experimental-testbed
href: reviews/Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability.html#datasets-experimental-testbed
title: Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability for data-driven assembly quality prediction in complex manufacturing systems
text:
4. Datasets / Experimental Testbed

Industrial case study:

Real manufacturing data from 1,763 diesel engines produced by a major diesel engine enterprise.
The process includes:

sub-assembly lines 1–5,
the main diesel engine assembly line,
a diesel engine performance test line,
and a packaging line.


Raw data characteristics:

The paper mentions 172 assembly characteristic parameters in the full assembly line data.
The final UABNN uses 39 input variables and predicts power as the target.
Variables include:

cylinder liner protrusion heights,
piston protrusion heights,
torque-related measures,
axial clearance,
oil pressure,
humidity,
inlet/outlet temperatures,
fuel consumption,
intercooler variables,
and speed.


Data preprocessing:

Abnormal data points were deleted.
Duplicate data was removed.
Continuous missing data was deleted.
Small amounts of missing data were filled using mean imputation.
The authors also mention statistical preprocessing such as computing mean, standard deviation, and range.

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability.html#baselines-compared-against
href: reviews/Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability.html#baselines-compared-against
title: Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability for data-driven assembly quality prediction in complex manufacturing systems
text:
5. Baselines Compared Against

ResNet

Used as a strong nonlinear predictive baseline for structured industrial data.
Configured with three residual blocks, each with 100 hidden units, ReLU, and a fully connected layer.

VAE

Included because of its relevance to probabilistic modeling and high-dimensional structured data.
Configured with a two-layer encoder, each fully connected layer containing 100 hidden units.

ViT

Included because of its ability to model relationships in high-dimensional tabular data.
Configured with:

a linear embedding layer,
two Transformer encoder layers,
four attention heads per layer,
and a fully connected regression head.


Observation on the baseline set:

These are all deep learning baselines, but they are not necessarily the strongest uncertainty-calibrated probabilistic baselines available.
The comparison is more about predictive competitors than about a full uncertainty quantification benchmark.
crumbs: Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability for data-driven assembly quality prediction in complex manufacturing systems

objectID: reviews/Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability.html#validation-strategy-predictions-uncertainty-explanations
href: reviews/Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability.html#validation-strategy-predictions-uncertainty-explanations
title: Uncertainty-aware Bayesian neural network with SHAP interpretability for data-driven assembly quality prediction in complex manufacturing systems
text:
6. Validation Strategy (Predictions, Uncertainty & Explanations)

Train/test split:

Random split in a 3:2 ratio
60% training, 40% testing

Robustness protocol:

Experiments were repeated across five random seeds
Final metrics reported as mean ± standard deviation

Prediction metrics:

MAE
RMSE
MAPE
R²

Uncertainty stress testing:

Gaussian white noise was added to the test set at:

0 dB
3 dB
6 dB

This was used to test how confidence intervals and uncertainty distributions behave under increasingly noisy environments.

Uncertainty evaluation metrics:

ECE for calibration quality
Sharpness for concentration of predictive intervals/distributions
OOD AUROC for out-of-distribution detection capability

XAI validation strategy:

Like many SHAP papers, the validation is largely engineering-plausibility based rather than formally quantitative.
The authors validate explanations by showing that the top-ranked variables and interactions align with real production experience.

7.2 Qualitative prediction behavior

The paper shows that UABNN tracks the true power curve more closely than the baselines.
The scatter plots are tighter around the ( y=x ) line.
Error density plots are more concentrated around zero, suggesting better local accuracy.



7.3 Confidence intervals and uncertainty behavior

UABNN produced more stable confidence intervals than ResNet, VAE, and ViT.
Under increasing noise, OOD uncertainty increases noticeably.
Aleatoric uncertainty also increases with noise.
The authors interpret this as evidence that the model distinguishes different uncertainty sources rather than collapsing everything into one generic error bar.



7.4 Ablation study on uncertainty modeling

BNN

ECE = 0.231
Sharpness = 0.029
OOD AUROC = 0.51

Hierarchical priors only

ECE = 0.534
Sharpness = 0.021

ECE = 0.187
Sharpness = 0.023
OOD AUROC = 0.70

Full UABNN

ECE = 0.613
Sharpness = 0.017
OOD AUROC = 0.85

Interpretive caution:

The OOD AUROC result is easy to interpret: the full method is best.
The ECE table is less straightforward, because larger ECE is usually worse in standard calibration terminology.
The paper treats the reported values as improvements, so either:

they are using an unconventional formulation,
or the table/interpretation may contain a definitional inconsistency.

This is something worth flagging critically in a review.

8. SHAP Findings & Interpretability Results

Top global feature:

Cumulative fuel (gas) consumption dominated the SHAP rankings by a large margin.

Other important features included:

oil pressure,
fuel consumption,
inlet water temperature,
piston protrusion height 06,
cylinder liner protrusion height 02,
atmospheric humidity,
torque,
intercooler front temperature,
cylinder liner protrusion height 04.

What SHAP added:

It identified which variables most influenced predicted power.
It highlighted how some variables had linear effects and others interacted nonlinearly.
It supported diagnostic analysis for when a product is predicted to miss quality standards.

Interaction examples discussed by the authors:

cumulative fuel consumption with cylinder liner protrusion height 02,
oil pressure with cylinder liner protrusion height 05,
fuel consumption with piston protrusion height 02.

Engineering interpretation:

These interactions are framed as meaningful because geometric variables such as protrusion heights affect combustion-related behavior, which then changes how fuel and pressure influence final power output.

text:
9. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1: The uncertainty taxonomy is good, but the quantification formulas are shaky.

The conceptual split into epistemic, aleatoric, and OOD uncertainty is sensible and aligns with modern uncertainty literature.
However, the actual equations used to compute these quantities are not especially convincing.
The reported formulations look partly heuristic and partly entropy-like, rather than derived from a clearly principled probabilistic decomposition.
So while the framework is attractive conceptually, the rigor of the uncertainty definitions seems weaker than the paper’s framing suggests.

Criticism 2: The ECE interpretation is potentially problematic.

In standard calibration literature, lower ECE is better.
Yet the ablation table appears to treat larger ECE as an improvement.
That suggests either a notation issue, a reporting error, or a custom metric definition that was not explained clearly enough.
This weakens confidence in the uncertainty-validation section.

Criticism 3: The comparison set is not a full uncertainty benchmark.

ResNet, VAE, and ViT are reasonable predictive baselines, but not the strongest baselines for calibrated uncertainty estimation.
Missing comparators include:

deep ensembles,
MC dropout,
heteroscedastic regression networks,
quantile regression neural networks,
conformal prediction methods,
and stronger probabilistic transformers or evidential models.

So the paper shows superiority over generic DL baselines, but not necessarily over the state of the art in uncertainty-aware prediction.

Criticism 4: SHAP is used well for explanation, but explanation quality is not rigorously evaluated.

The paper presents plausible feature rankings and interactions.
However, it does not test explanation robustness, stability, or faithfulness.
There is no perturbation-based fidelity test, no sanity check against model randomization, and no counterfactual validation.
So the SHAP analysis is useful, but still mostly qualitative.

Criticism 5: The target seems heavily tied to test-bench variables.

Many high-importance features are closely linked to downstream performance measurements rather than purely upstream assembly factors.
That raises a practical question:

Is the model truly predicting final quality early enough to be useful for intervention,
or is it partly reconstructing quality from variables measured close to the target stage?

This affects how operationally valuable the model is for proactive quality control.

Criticism 6: The industrial realism is good, but generalization is narrow.

The paper validates on one manufacturing context: diesel engine assembly.
That is valuable, but it does not establish transferability to other complex assembly environments.
The authors acknowledge this and mention future work on antenna assembly.

Criticism 7: There is a tension between “intrinsic interpretability” and actual interpretability.

The paper sometimes overstates the intrinsic interpretability of BNNs.
Bayesian parameter distributions improve uncertainty awareness, but that does not automatically make the model human-interpretable in a meaningful operational sense.
In practice, most of the usable interpretability here still comes from SHAP, not from the BNN alone.

Observation on practical merit:

Despite the criticisms, this is a solid applied paper.
It is especially useful because it tries to combine:

industrial data realism,
uncertainty awareness,
and feature-level interpretability

into one workflow that engineers could plausibly use.

text:
10. What This Paper Contributes to the Literature

It strengthens the trend of moving from pure point prediction toward trustworthy prediction in industrial AI.
It demonstrates that uncertainty quantification and explainability can be combined in an applied manufacturing setting.
It shows that industrial quality prediction papers are starting to move beyond “best RMSE wins” and toward reliability-aware decision support.
It also highlights an important gap in the field:

many papers now claim uncertainty awareness,
but fewer papers rigorously validate whether that uncertainty is well calibrated or operationally meaningful.

11. Relevance to My Own Research / Integration Value

Why this paper is useful:

It is a strong example of how to frame uncertainty and interpretability together in an applied engineering problem.
It provides language and structure for discussing:

multiple uncertainty types,
interpretability as a practical requirement,
and the trade-off between performance and transparency.


What I would borrow:

The framing that black-box accuracy alone is insufficient in safety-critical or industrial decision systems.
The three-part uncertainty decomposition as a motivating structure.
The use of SHAP not only for ranking features but also for analyzing feature interactions and diagnosing risky samples.

What I would improve:

Use stronger probabilistic and uncertainty baselines.
Add explicit calibration plots and clearer calibration metrics.
Quantitatively validate explanations.
Distinguish more carefully between upstream process control variables and downstream proxy measurements.

text:
13. Bottom-Line Verdict
This is a strong applied interpretability-and-uncertainty paper for manufacturing quality prediction. Its biggest strength is the integrated framing: Bayesian prediction, uncertainty decomposition, confidence intervals, and SHAP-based diagnosis all live inside one industrial workflow. Its main weakness is that the uncertainty quantification and explanation validation are not as rigorous as the narrative suggests. So I would treat it as an important application paper with useful ideas and solid empirical value, but not as the final word on principled uncertainty estimation or explanation validation.

text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

Motivation: Why Uncertainty Validation Matters
Many modern machine learning models provide uncertainty estimates alongside predictions. These may come from:

Bayesian neural networks

Gaussian processes

ensemble models

quantile regression

probabilistic boosting methods

However, simply producing uncertainty estimates does not guarantee they are reliable. A model might output uncertainty values that appear reasonable but do not correspond to the actual prediction errors.
The paper argues that existing validation approaches mostly test average calibration, which checks whether uncertainties are correct on average. However, average correctness does not guarantee local reliability.
For safety-critical applications such as energy forecasting, autonomous systems, or scientific modelling, uncertainty estimates must be reliable for individual predictions and across the input space, not just globally.



Main Conceptual Contribution
The paper introduces a three-component framework for validating uncertainty quantification:

Average Calibration
Consistency
Adaptivity

These three concepts together provide a much more complete validation framework for probabilistic models.



Average Calibration
Average calibration tests whether the predicted uncertainty magnitude matches the overall error dispersion.
For variance-based uncertainty models, this typically means:
[ Var(E) u_E^2 ]
Where:

(E) = prediction error

(u_E) = predicted uncertainty

If a model is well calibrated, then the variance of the errors should match the average predicted uncertainty variance.
However, this check alone is insufficient because overestimation in some regions and underestimation in others can cancel out.



Consistency
Consistency tests whether uncertainties remain correct across different levels of predicted uncertainty.
In other words:

If the model says uncertainty is high, do we actually observe larger errors?

Mathematically this is expressed through conditional calibration:
[ Var(Z u_E = ) ]
Where
[ Z = ]
This ensures that uncertainty estimates are correctly scaled across different uncertainty magnitudes.



Adaptivity
Adaptivity is the paper’s most important conceptual contribution.
Adaptivity tests whether uncertainties remain reliable across the input space.
Instead of conditioning on predicted uncertainty, the analysis conditions on input features:
[ Var(Z X = x) ]
This evaluates whether uncertainty estimates remain valid in different regions of the data distribution.
Example:
A solar power forecasting model might produce correct uncertainty on average but fail during:

cloudy conditions

winter months

high irradiance periods

Adaptivity analysis would reveal these failures.

3. Methodology & Technical Details

Variance-Based UQ Framework
For variance-based uncertainty predictions, the paper defines the minimal validation dataset as:
[ C = {E, u_E} ]
Where:

(E = R - V)

(R) = reference value

(V) = predicted value

Total uncertainty combines prediction uncertainty and measurement uncertainty:
[ u_E = ]
Where:

(u_R) = reference uncertainty

(u_V) = predicted uncertainty




Standardised Error (Z-Score)
The standardized error is defined as:
[ Z = ]
If uncertainties are correctly estimated, then:
[ Var(Z) ]
This metric is central to many UQ validation diagnostics.



Interval-Based UQ
For prediction interval models (e.g., quantile regression or conformal prediction), the primary metric is:
Prediction Interval Coverage Probability (PICP)
This measures the proportion of observations that fall within the predicted interval.
Example:
If a model predicts 95% intervals, then approximately 95% of observations should fall inside those intervals.
However, similar to variance-based UQ, this must also be validated locally, not only globally.

text:
4. Validation Strategy
The paper validates its framework using two approaches:

Synthetic Case Studies
Six synthetic datasets are constructed to represent different failure modes.
These include cases where models are:

fully calibrated and adaptive

calibrated but inconsistent

calibrated but not adaptive

completely miscalibrated

This allows the author to demonstrate how different diagnostic tools respond to known ground truth.



Reanalysis of Existing ML Studies
The framework is also applied to previously published uncertainty quantification studies.
This reanalysis shows that many published models that appear well-calibrated actually exhibit:

local miscalibration
inconsistent uncertainty scaling
lack of adaptivity across feature space

Thus the standard validation methods used in prior literature may overestimate model reliability.

text:
5. Diagnostic Tools Evaluated
The paper evaluates several common UQ validation tools.

Calibration Curves
Calibration curves compare predicted uncertainty with observed error.
These are useful but mainly test average calibration.



Reliability Diagrams
Reliability diagrams evaluate calibration across different uncertainty bins.
They test consistency, but are sensitive to:

bin size

sample size

data distribution




Confidence Curves
Confidence curves measure model error as predictions are filtered by uncertainty ranking.
However, the paper argues that oracle-based confidence curves are misleading, because they do not test calibration directly.
Instead, the paper proposes probabilistic reference curves.



Local Z-Variance Diagnostics
The paper proposes analysing local variance of standardized errors.
This allows detection of:

local over-confidence
local under-confidence




Local Coverage Probability
For interval predictions, local coverage probability evaluates whether predicted intervals remain valid across:

uncertainty levels
input features

text:
6. Key Findings

Average Calibration is Insufficient
A model can appear perfectly calibrated globally while being locally unreliable.



Adaptivity is Often Ignored
Most prior work evaluates calibration and consistency but does not evaluate adaptivity.
This means uncertainty models may fail under certain conditions without detection.



Many Standard Metrics Are Weak
Common scalar metrics such as:

ENCE

AUCO

do not guarantee consistency or adaptivity.
They should not be used as the sole evidence of reliable uncertainty.



Reliability Diagrams Depend on Binning
Improper binning can hide important uncertainty failures.
Careful bin selection is necessary.

7. Limitations of the Study

Framework Requires Expert Interpretation
The methodology relies heavily on diagnostic plots rather than automated metrics.
Practitioners must interpret results carefully.



Feature Selection for Adaptivity is Non-Trivial
Choosing the right feature dimension to analyse adaptivity requires domain knowledge.
In high-dimensional models this can be difficult.



Focus on Diagnosis Rather Than Correction
The paper provides tools for identifying problems but does not propose new algorithms to fix them.

text:
10. Bottom Line
The paper provides a conceptual framework for validating uncertainty quantification that goes beyond standard calibration tests.
It argues that reliable uncertainty estimates must satisfy three properties:

Calibration — correct on average

Consistency — correct across uncertainty levels

Adaptivity — correct across the input space

Many existing studies only validate the first property.
Therefore, rigorous uncertainty validation must evaluate all three dimensions to ensure that uncertainty estimates remain trustworthy in real-world applications.
